q.pt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of working in the same occupation or profession for many years
q.s: A series of related jobs in the same occupation or field that a person holds over many years is a(n)
o: position.
assignment.
shift.
career.
q.r: Career. A career is built over many years by working at related jobs in the same occupation or profession, gaining knowledge, skills and usually higher pay along the way. Careers vary in the education and training they require. A position and an assignment describe a single job or task, and a shift is a set block of working hours, so none of them describes long-term work in one field.
w: A position is one particular job a person holds, so it cannot describe a whole series of related jobs held over many years.
An assignment is a single task or project given to a worker, not the long string of related jobs the question describes.
A shift is just a set block of working hours, such as 7 a.m. to 3 p.m., and says nothing about years of work in one field.

q.pt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of working in the same occupation or profession for many years
q.s: Ramon started as a bank teller, became head teller two years later, and is now a branch manager at the same bank. Ramon's experience is an example of
o: career advancement through promotion.
a lateral move between two departments.
a career change to a new field.
job shadowing within the company.
q.r: Career advancement through promotion. Ramon has moved up to higher-level jobs with more responsibility within the same company and the same field, which is how many careers progress. A lateral move keeps a worker at the same level, and a career change means leaving one occupation for another. Job shadowing is observing a worker for a short time to learn about an occupation.
w: A lateral move keeps a worker at the same level of pay and responsibility, but Ramon moved up from teller to head teller to branch manager.
A career change means leaving one field for another, yet Ramon has stayed in banking at the same bank the whole time.
Job shadowing is briefly watching someone work to learn about a job, while Ramon actually held each job and kept moving up.

q.pt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of working in the same occupation or profession for many years
q.s: Which of the following is a possible disadvantage of working in the same occupation for many years:
o: Skills may become outdated if the field changes
Experience in the field builds steadily over time
Seniority may lead to higher pay and benefits
Deep expertise can lead to leadership roles
q.r: Skills may become outdated if the field changes. A worker who stays in one occupation for many years may rely on skills that lose value if technology or the industry changes, and income can suffer if the field shrinks. Building experience, earning higher pay through seniority, and gaining expertise that leads to leadership roles are advantages of a long career in one field, not disadvantages.
w: Building experience steadily over the years is a benefit of staying in one occupation, and the question asks for a drawback.
Higher pay and benefits from seniority reward a worker for staying in one field, so this is an advantage rather than a disadvantage.
Moving into leadership because of deep expertise is a reward of a long career in one field, not a downside of it.

q.pt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of working in the same occupation or profession for many years
q.s: Jordan moves from the marketing department to the sales department of the same company. The new job has different duties but the same pay and level of responsibility. This is a
o: promotion.
demotion.
lateral move.
career advancement.
q.r: Lateral move. A lateral move is a change to a different job at about the same level of responsibility and pay, often within the same organization. It can broaden a worker's skills even though it does not move the worker up. A promotion moves a worker to a higher-level job, and career advancement describes progress to higher positions over time. A demotion moves a worker to a lower-level job.
w: A promotion moves a worker up to a higher-level job, but Jordan's new job has the same pay and level of responsibility.
A demotion moves a worker down to a lower-level job, while Jordan kept the same pay and responsibility in the sales department.
Career advancement means progressing to higher positions over time, and Jordan's move to sales did not raise Jordan's level at all.

q.pt: Compare the education and training requirements for at least two careers
q.s: Which of the following careers generally requires the most years of education and training after high school:
o: Electrician
Physician
Bank teller
Retail sales associate
q.r: Physician. Becoming a physician typically requires a four-year college degree, four years of medical school and several years of residency training, usually 11 or more years in all. Electricians usually complete an apprenticeship of several years, while bank tellers and retail sales associates are often trained on the job. Careers vary widely in their education and training requirements, which affects both cost and income potential.
w: Electricians usually train for several years through an apprenticeship, which is far shorter than the college, medical school and residency a physician needs.
Bank tellers are often trained on the job after high school, so this career needs much less schooling than becoming a physician.
Retail sales associates usually learn on the job with little formal schooling, far less than the decade or more a physician spends training.

q.pt: Compare the education and training requirements, income potential, and primary duties of at least two jobs available to high school students
q.s: Ava is choosing between working as a lifeguard and working as a retail cashier this summer. Which difference between the two jobs should she expect?
o: The cashier job requires a two-year college degree
The lifeguard job involves no safety duties
The cashier job requires a state-issued business license
The lifeguard job requires certification training first
q.r: The lifeguard job requires certification training first. Lifeguards must complete a certification course, usually including CPR and first aid, before they can work. Retail cashiers are typically trained on the job. A cashier does not need a college degree or a state business license, and a lifeguard's primary duty is watching swimmers and keeping them safe, so the other choices are incorrect.
w: Retail cashiers are usually trained on the job, so Ava would not need any college degree to work at the register.
Keeping swimmers safe is a lifeguard's main duty, so saying the job has no safety duties gets the role backwards.
A business license is something a business owner may need, not an employee working the register, so a cashier needs none.

q.pt: Compare the education and training requirements, income potential, and primary duties of at least two jobs available to high school students
q.s: Liam earns $13.00 an hour as a restaurant host, and Zoe earns $15.50 an hour as a tutor. If each works 12 hours this week, how much more will Zoe earn than Liam?
q.r: $30.00. Zoe earns $2.50 more per hour ($15.50 − $13.00). Over 12 hours, the difference is 12 × $2.50 = $30.00. Another way: Zoe earns 12 × $15.50 = $186.00 and Liam earns 12 × $13.00 = $156.00, and $186.00 − $156.00 = $30.00. The option $186.00 is Zoe's total pay, not the difference, and $25.00 and $36.00 come from arithmetic errors.
w: $25.00 is what you get by multiplying the $2.50 hourly difference by 10 hours instead of the 12 hours each person works.
$36.00 comes from rounding the hourly difference up to $3.00 before multiplying by 12, but $15.50 minus $13.00 is exactly $2.50.
$186.00 is Zoe's total pay for 12 hours, but the question asks how much more Zoe earns than Liam, so Liam's $156.00 must be subtracted.

q.pt: Compare the education and training requirements, income potential, and primary duties of at least two jobs available to high school students
q.s: Why is a restaurant server's weekly income likely to vary more than a library aide's?
o: The server is paid a fixed annual salary
Much of the server's income comes from tips
The library aide earns a commission on each book
The library aide receives tips each week
q.r: Much of the server's income comes from tips. Tips depend on how busy the restaurant is and how generous customers are, so a server's income can change a great deal from week to week. A library aide is usually paid an hourly wage, which is more predictable. Servers are not usually paid a fixed salary, and library aides do not earn commissions or tips.
w: A fixed annual salary would make the server's pay steady from week to week, which is the opposite of what the question describes.
Library aides are usually paid an hourly wage and do not sell anything, so there is no commission on books to make their pay vary.
Library aides do not usually receive tips, and even if they did, that would not explain why the server's income varies more.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: Which U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics resource describes occupations' duties, required education, pay and projected job growth?
o: The Consumer Price Index
The Federal Register
The Occupational Outlook Handbook
The Survey of Consumer Finances
q.r: The Occupational Outlook Handbook. This free government resource from the Bureau of Labor Statistics is a reliable source of current employment and occupation trends, including what workers do, the education they need, typical pay and job outlook. The Consumer Price Index measures changes in prices, the Federal Register publishes federal rules and notices, and the Survey of Consumer Finances studies household finances, not occupations.
w: The Consumer Price Index tracks changes in the prices of goods and services over time, not the duties, education or pay of occupations.
The Federal Register publishes federal rules and official notices, so it does not describe what workers in different occupations do or earn.
The Survey of Consumer Finances studies households' income, savings and debts, not the duties or job growth of particular occupations.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: Jada arranges a 20-minute meeting with a physical therapist to ask about the therapist's daily duties and how she entered the field. What is the main benefit of this informational interview?
o: Receiving a formal job offer during the meeting
Earning school credit for hours worked
Completing a required licensing step
Learning about the field and possible openings
q.r: Learning about the field and possible openings. An informational interview is a conversation with someone working in a career field. It gives an inside view of the work, the education path and the challenges, and it can reveal job openings that are never advertised. It is not a job interview, so an offer is not expected. It does not earn school credit or count toward a professional license.
w: An informational interview is a fact-finding conversation rather than a job interview, so Jada should not expect a job offer at the meeting.
Jada is having a short conversation, not working, so the meeting does not count as hours worked for school credit.
Talking with a therapist for 20 minutes is not part of any licensing process, which requires formal education and exams.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: Building and using relationships with people who can share career information, advice and job leads is called
o: networking.
prospecting.
recruiting.
mentoring.
q.r: Networking. Networking means building relationships with people such as teachers, employers, family friends and professionals who can share information and job leads. Many openings are filled through contacts before they are advertised. Prospecting is a selling term for finding potential customers, and recruiting is an employer's search for job candidates. Mentoring is one experienced person guiding another's growth, not a broad web of contacts.
w: Prospecting is a sales term for finding potential customers, not for building relationships that bring career advice and job leads.
Recruiting is an employer's search for job candidates, while the question describes a person building contacts to help his or her own career.
Mentoring is one experienced person guiding another, while the question describes a wide web of contacts who share information and job leads.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: Carmen wants to become a registered nurse. Which action would best help her move steadily toward that goal?
o: Write a career action plan with steps and deadlines
Wait until after graduation to begin researching nursing
Take whichever classes her friends choose
Apply only for the highest-paying jobs now
q.r: Write a career action plan with steps and deadlines. A career action plan is proactive: it lists the goal and the education, training and experience needed to reach it, with a timeline for each step. Waiting to research the field, choosing classes based on friends, or chasing the highest pay today does not prepare Carmen for nursing school or licensing.
w: Waiting until after graduation to start researching wastes years Carmen could use to take the right classes and plan for nursing school.
Her friends' class choices may have nothing to do with nursing, so copying them would not move Carmen toward her own goal.
Chasing the highest-paying jobs available now does nothing to build the education and licensing Carmen needs to become a registered nurse.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: What should be the first step in creating a career action plan?
o: Apply for jobs in the field
Set a specific career goal
Request letters of recommendation
Choose a college to attend
q.r: Set a specific career goal. A career action plan starts with a clear goal, based on self-assessment and research. The goal determines which education, training, experience and deadlines belong in the plan. Choosing a college, requesting recommendation letters and applying for jobs are later steps that depend on knowing which career the person is working toward.
w: Applying for jobs comes late in the plan, after a person knows which career to aim for and has gained the needed training.
Letters of recommendation are gathered later, once the person knows which school or job to apply for based on a chosen goal.
Picking a college depends on knowing what career to prepare for, so it has to come after the career goal is set.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: Nadia spends one day following an electrician from job site to job site to see what the work involves. Nadia is
o: job shadowing.
interning.
volunteering.
networking.
q.r: Job shadowing. Job shadowing means following a worker through a typical workday to observe the duties and work environment of an occupation. It helps a student decide whether a career is a good fit. An internship is a longer work experience in which the student does real work, and volunteering is unpaid service to an organization. Networking is building relationships for information and job leads.
w: An internship is a longer work experience where the student does real tasks, but Nadia spends only one day watching the electrician.
Volunteering means giving unpaid service to an organization, while Nadia is simply following and observing a worker to learn about the job.
Networking is building relationships for information and job leads, but Nadia's day is about seeing firsthand what an electrician's work involves.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: Two people begin careers in accounting. One later earns a CPA license through added education and experience; the other remains an entry-level bookkeeper. Over a lifetime, the CPA will most likely have
o: the same pay as the bookkeeper.
greater income potential and opportunities.
fewer career options than the bookkeeper has.
less need for continuing education.
q.r: Greater income potential and opportunities. Decisions about education, licensing and experience over a lifetime affect income and opportunities. A licensed CPA qualifies for higher-level work, such as auditing and tax advising, that pays more and opens more career paths. The CPA will not likely earn the same as or have fewer options than a bookkeeper. CPAs must complete continuing education to keep their licenses.
w: Earning a CPA license qualifies a person for higher-level work like auditing and tax advising, so pay is unlikely to stay equal to a bookkeeper's.
The added education and license open more doors, such as auditing and tax work, so the CPA would have more options, not fewer.
CPAs must keep taking continuing education to keep their licenses, so they actually have more need for ongoing learning, not less.

q.pt: Conduct research on a specific career field. Describe the education, job, or career decisions individuals in this field might make over their lifetime and explain how this could affect their income potential and opportunities
q.s: Which of the following is a good reason to research employment trends before choosing a career field:
o: Trend data tells you your exact future salary
Shrinking fields usually offer the most new job openings
Trend data replaces the need for job training
Fields with strong growth may offer more job openings
q.r: Fields with strong growth may offer more job openings. Employment trends show whether the number of jobs in an occupation is expected to grow or shrink. Choosing a growing field can make it easier to find work and advance. Trend data gives averages and projections, not an exact salary. Shrinking fields usually have fewer openings, and trend data does not replace the education or training a career requires.
w: Trend data shows averages and projections for an occupation, so it cannot tell any one person exactly what he or she will earn.
Shrinking fields are losing jobs, so they usually offer fewer new openings, which is the reverse of this statement.
Knowing that a field is growing does not teach anyone the skills to do the work, so training is still required.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: An honest evaluation of your own interests, abilities, values and personality to identify careers that suit you is called a(n)
o: performance evaluation.
self-assessment.
job analysis.
reference check.
q.r: Self-assessment. A self-assessment helps a person understand his or her aptitudes, skills, interests and values so they can be matched with suitable careers. A performance evaluation is an employer's review of a worker's job performance, and a job analysis studies the tasks a job requires. A reference check is an employer contacting people who know a job applicant.
w: A performance evaluation is an employer reviewing how well a worker does a job, not a person studying his or her own interests to pick a career.
A job analysis studies the tasks and skills a particular job requires, not the interests and personality of the person choosing a career.
A reference check is an employer contacting people who know a job applicant, not a person honestly evaluating himself or herself.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: Gabe wants to find out which careers fit the abilities he is naturally good at. His school counselor should suggest that he take a(n)
o: employment application.
aptitude assessment.
resume workshop.
salary survey.
q.r: Aptitude assessment. An aptitude assessment measures a person's natural abilities, such as mechanical, verbal or numerical reasoning, and shows which kinds of work he or she could learn and do well. It is a useful tool for matching skills to career interests. An employment application and a resume workshop help a person apply for jobs, and a salary survey reports pay, but none measures abilities.
w: An employment application is a form for applying to a specific job, so it does not measure what abilities Gabe is naturally good at.
A resume workshop helps a person present his or her experience to employers, but it does not reveal Gabe's natural abilities.
A salary survey reports how much different jobs pay, so it tells Gabe nothing about which abilities come naturally to him.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: Owen completes a strengths assessment and learns that he is highly organized and detail-oriented. How can this information best support his career success?
o: He can target roles that use his strongest talents
He can choose a career based mainly on starting pay
He can stop developing his weaker skills
He can avoid asking others for feedback
q.r: He can target roles that use his strongest talents. A strengths self-assessment helps a person apply his or her talents where they are best suited, such as accounting or project coordination for someone organized and detail-oriented. Choosing mainly by pay ignores fit. Weaker skills still need attention, and feedback from others helps confirm whether a self-assessment is accurate.
w: Starting pay says nothing about whether a job fits Owen's strengths, so choosing mainly by pay ignores what his assessment revealed.
Knowing his strengths does not mean Owen can stop improving his weaker skills, which most jobs will still require him to use.
Feedback from others helps confirm whether a self-assessment is accurate, so avoiding it would weaken rather than support Owen's career success.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: A natural ability to learn a particular skill quickly and well, such as working with numbers or drawing, is a(n)
o: interest.
value.
aptitude.
credential.
q.r: Aptitude. An aptitude is a natural talent for learning a certain kind of skill. Knowing your aptitudes helps you choose careers in which you are likely to succeed. An interest is something a person enjoys, which may or may not match his or her abilities. A value is a belief about what is important, and a credential, such as a certificate, shows completed training.
w: An interest is something a person enjoys doing, which may or may not match what he or she naturally learns quickly and well.
A value is a belief about what is important, such as helping others, rather than a natural talent for a skill like numbers or drawing.
A credential, such as a certificate, proves completed training, while the question describes a natural ability a person has before any training.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: Marco answers a survey about activities he enjoys, such as building things and solving puzzles. He then receives a list of occupations whose workers enjoy similar activities. Marco completed a(n)
o: aptitude test.
interest inventory.
achievement test.
performance review.
q.r: Interest inventory. An interest inventory compares the activities a person likes with those of workers in different occupations and suggests career matches. It measures likes and preferences, not ability. An aptitude test measures natural abilities, and an achievement test measures what a person has already learned. A performance review is an employer's evaluation of an employee's work.
w: An aptitude test measures natural abilities, but Marco's survey asked which activities he enjoys, which is about likes rather than talents.
An achievement test measures what a person has already learned, while Marco's survey focused on the activities he likes to do.
A performance review is an employer's evaluation of an employee's work, and Marco simply answered a survey about what he enjoys.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: Sam's self-assessment shows that he enjoys working outdoors, is skilled with hand tools and likes seeing the results of his work each day. Which career best matches his results?
o: Medical billing clerk
Call center agent
Landscape installer
Data entry clerk
q.r: Landscape installer. Matching self-assessment results to careers means looking for work that uses a person's interests and skills. A landscape installer works outdoors, uses hand and power tools, and can see finished projects at the end of each day. A medical billing clerk, a call center agent and a data entry clerk work mainly indoors at computers or phones, so these careers do not fit Sam's interests or skills.
w: A medical billing clerk works mostly indoors at a computer, which does not match Sam's love of outdoor work and hand tools.
A call center agent spends the day indoors on the phone, so the job uses none of Sam's outdoor interests or tool skills.
A data entry clerk types information into a computer indoors, so it would not use Sam's hand-tool skills or his wish to work outside.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: Leah's assessment results show strong mechanical aptitude, but her interest inventory shows that she most enjoys helping people. What is the best way for Leah to use these results?
o: Explore careers that combine both strengths and interests
Choose a mechanical career, since aptitude outweighs interest
Ignore both results and choose by starting pay
Retake the tests until the two results match
q.r: Explore careers that combine both strengths and interests. Self-assessment results work best together. Careers such as medical equipment technician or physical therapy assistant could use Leah's mechanical aptitude while letting her help people, which supports both success and satisfaction. Relying on aptitude alone, ignoring the results, or retaking tests until they agree defeats the purpose of an objective self-assessment.
w: Ignoring Leah's strong interest in helping people could lead to a career she is good at but does not enjoy, so aptitude alone is not enough.
Choosing by starting pay throws away the useful information Leah gained about her abilities and interests, which is the point of the assessments.
Aptitude and interest measure different things, so they need not match, and retaking tests until they agree defeats an honest self-assessment.

q.pt: Assess personal skills and interests and match them to various career options
q.s: After a group project, Tomas asks two teammates and his teacher to describe what he does well and where he could improve. Tomas is gathering information to identify his
o: strengths and weaknesses.
career goals.
references for job applications.
work values.
q.r: Strengths and weaknesses. Asking others for honest feedback is part of an objective self-assessment, because others may notice abilities and problem areas that a person does not see. Knowing strengths and weaknesses helps in choosing careers and planning improvement. Career goals are outcomes a person wants to reach, job references vouch for a person to employers, and work values are what a person finds important in a job.
w: Career goals are outcomes a person wants to reach, but Tomas is asking what he does well and where he could improve.
References vouch for a person to employers, while Tomas is collecting feedback for himself about what he does well and poorly.
Work values are what a person finds important in a job, but Tomas is asking others about his abilities and problem areas.

q.pt: Investigate training opportunities that can increase a person's ability to obtain higher paid employment during high school
q.s: Every Saturday, Sofia walks dogs and cleans kennels at a nonprofit animal shelter without pay to support its mission and gain experience caring for animals. Sofia is gaining work experience through
o: an apprenticeship.
freelancing.
a part-time job.
volunteering.
q.r: Volunteering. Volunteering is giving time and work without pay to help an organization or cause. It builds skills, references and work experience that can lead to paid jobs later. An apprenticeship is paid training under skilled workers, and a part-time job pays wages. Freelancing is self-employed work done for paying clients, so none of these fits unpaid service at a nonprofit.
w: An apprenticeship is paid training under skilled workers in a trade, while Sofia works without pay to support a nonprofit shelter.
Freelancing is self-employed work done for paying clients, but Sofia receives no pay and works for a nonprofit's mission.
A part-time job pays wages, but Sofia walks dogs and cleans kennels at the shelter every Saturday without any pay at all.

q.pt: Investigate training opportunities that can increase a person's ability to obtain higher paid employment during high school
q.s: Kenji completes a summer internship at an accounting firm and impresses his supervisors. What is a likely outcome of his strong internship performance?
o: An exemption from future job training
An automatic professional license
An offer of employment from the firm
A promotion to partner in the firm
q.r: An offer of employment from the firm. Employers often use internships to find and test future employees, so a strong internship can lead to a full-time job offer. The experience also builds skills and contacts. An internship does not excuse a person from future training or grant a professional license, which requires education and exams. Partner is a senior position earned over many years.
w: No internship, however strong, excuses a worker from future job training, since new jobs and changing fields keep requiring new skills.
A professional license, such as a CPA license, requires education and exams, so a summer internship cannot grant one automatically.
Partner is a senior ownership position earned over many years, so a summer intern would not be promoted straight to it.

q.pt: Investigate training opportunities that can increase a person's ability to obtain higher paid employment during high school
q.s: Which training would most directly help a 16-year-old qualify for a higher-paying summer job at a public pool?
o: Completing a food handler course
Completing a keyboarding and typing skills course
Completing a lifeguard certification course
Completing a cashier training course
q.r: Completing a lifeguard certification course. A pool must hire certified lifeguards, and lifeguard jobs often pay more than entry-level jobs that need no certification. Specific skills training like this increases a teen's human capital and income-earning potential. Food handler, keyboarding and cashier training can help with other jobs, but they do not qualify a person to work as a lifeguard.
w: A food handler course prepares someone to work with food, which may help at a snack stand but does not qualify a teen to lifeguard.
Keyboarding skills help with office work, but they have nothing to do with the safety duties of a higher-paying pool job.
Cashier training can help at a pool's front desk, but that is an entry-level job, not the higher-paying certified lifeguard position.

q.pt: Investigate training opportunities that can increase a person's ability to obtain higher paid employment during high school
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a student receiving paid training while working under skilled workers:
o: An apprenticeship with a plumbing contractor
A weekend volunteer shift at a community food bank
A one-day job shadow at a local hospital
An informational interview with a chef
q.r: An apprenticeship with a plumbing contractor. An apprenticeship combines paid, on-the-job training under skilled workers with classroom instruction, and it is a common path into the skilled trades. A volunteer shift is unpaid service. A job shadow and an informational interview help a student learn about an occupation but do not involve paid work or structured training.
w: Volunteering at a food bank is unpaid service, so it does not match the paid training under skilled workers the question describes.
A one-day job shadow lets a student watch a worker, but it involves no pay and no structured training under skilled workers.
An informational interview is a conversation to learn about a career, not paid work or training under skilled workers.

q.pt: Investigate training opportunities that can increase a person's ability to obtain higher paid employment during high school
q.s: Mia takes a weekend CPR and first-aid course before advertising her babysitting services. How is this training most likely to affect her earning potential?
o: She will need to charge less to cover the course
Parents may pay her more because she is certified
She will no longer need references from past families
She will be required to babysit fewer hours
q.r: Parents may pay her more because she is certified. Certification in CPR and first aid shows parents that Mia can handle emergencies, which makes her more valuable and can justify higher rates or more jobs. This is an example of training increasing human capital and income-earning potential. The course does not require lower rates or fewer hours, and families will still want references.
w: A course fee does not force Mia to lower her rates; certification makes her more valuable, which usually supports charging more.
Certification adds to Mia's qualifications, but parents will still want to hear from families she has babysat for before hiring her.
Nothing about the course limits her work hours, and being certified may actually help Mia get more babysitting jobs, not fewer.

q.pt: Investigate training opportunities that can increase a person's ability to obtain higher paid employment during high school
q.s: Elena can work 10 more hours a week at her grocery job or accept an unpaid internship at a marketing agency in the field she hopes to enter. Which reason best supports choosing the internship?
o: It pays more per hour than her grocery job
It requires less effort than her grocery job
It builds career skills and professional contacts
It lets her skip the college courses her field requires
q.r: It builds career skills and professional contacts. Although the internship pays nothing now, it builds human capital and a network in Elena's chosen field, which can raise her future income-earning potential and lead to a job offer. Its opportunity cost is the grocery pay she gives up. An unpaid internship pays less, not more, may require more effort, and does not replace the education her field requires.
w: The internship is unpaid, so it pays less per hour than the grocery job, not more, which is why this reason cannot support it.
An internship in a new field is likely to take as much effort as grocery work or more, so ease is not a good reason to choose it.
Internship experience adds to Elena's skills, but it does not replace the college courses her chosen field requires.

q.pt: Explain why adults with a college education may earn more than adults with no education beyond high school
q.s: Why do adults with a college degree tend to earn more than adults with no education beyond high school?
o: Their added skills make them more productive to employers
Employers are required by federal law to pay graduates more
College graduates pay lower income tax rates
A degree removes the need for work experience
q.r: Their added skills make them more productive to employers. College builds knowledge and skills, or human capital, that increase a worker's productivity, and employers pay more for more productive workers. No law requires employers to pay graduates more, and income tax rates depend on income, not education. Graduates still need work experience to advance in most careers.
w: No federal law requires employers to pay college graduates more, so the earnings gap comes from skills and productivity, not a legal rule.
Income tax rates depend on how much a person earns, not on education, so a degree does not lower a graduate's tax rate.
Most graduates still need work experience to advance, so a degree does not replace experience or explain higher pay that way.

q.pt: Explain why adults with a college education may earn more than adults with no education beyond high school
q.s: On average, as a person's level of education increases, his or her earnings tend to __________ and his or her chance of being unemployed tends to __________.
o: decrease; increase
increase; increase
increase; decrease
stay the same; decrease
q.r: Increase; decrease. Government labor data consistently show that workers with more education have higher median earnings and lower unemployment rates. More education builds skills employers value, which raises both pay and job security. The other pairs reverse or misstate this relationship, since more education is linked with higher pay and less, not more, unemployment.
w: This pair reverses the real pattern, since more education is linked with higher earnings and a lower chance of unemployment, not the reverse.
Earnings do tend to increase with more education, but unemployment tends to go down, not up, for more educated workers.
Unemployment does tend to fall with more education, but earnings rise rather than staying the same as education increases.

q.pt: Explain why adults with a college education may earn more than adults with no education beyond high school
q.s: Some workers without college degrees earn more than some college graduates. Which explanation is most consistent with this fact?
o: Education has no link to a worker's earnings
College degrees lower a worker's productivity
Employers usually pay more to workers with fewer skills
Valuable skills, training and experience also raise pay
q.r: Valuable skills, training and experience also raise pay. Averages show that more education is linked with higher earnings, but individual pay also depends on skills, certifications, experience and demand for an occupation. A skilled electrician may earn more than a graduate in a low-paying field. Education is still strongly linked to earnings, degrees do not lower productivity, and employers pay more for more skills, not fewer.
w: Education is still strongly linked to higher average earnings, so the exceptions in the question do not mean the link has disappeared.
College builds knowledge and skills that tend to raise productivity, so degrees do not make workers less productive.
Employers generally pay more for more skills, not fewer, so this choice gets the relationship between skills and pay backwards.

q.pt: Discuss how specific skills training can improve a young person's human capital, productivity, and income-earning potential
q.s: The knowledge, skills, education and experience that make a worker productive are called
o: financial capital.
human capital.
physical capital.
venture capital.
q.r: Human capital. Human capital is the value a person brings to work through education, training and experience. Increasing human capital raises productivity and income-earning potential. Financial capital is money used to start or run a business, and physical capital is tools, equipment and buildings. Venture capital is money that investors provide to new, fast-growing businesses in exchange for ownership.
w: Financial capital is money used to start or run a business, not the knowledge and skills a worker brings to a job.
Physical capital means tools, equipment and buildings, while the question describes the skills and experience inside a person.
Venture capital is money investors put into new, fast-growing businesses, which has nothing to do with a worker's education or skills.

q.pt: Discuss how specific skills training can improve a young person's human capital, productivity, and income-earning potential
q.s: Gwen built customer-service and problem-solving skills as a restaurant server. She now uses the same skills in her new job as a bank teller. These skills are best described as
o: technical skills.
job-specific skills.
transferable skills.
aptitudes.
q.r: Transferable skills. Transferable skills, such as communication, customer service and problem solving, can be used in many different jobs and industries, so they add to a worker's human capital wherever the worker goes. Technical and job-specific skills apply mainly to the tasks of one occupation, such as running a register or operating equipment. An aptitude is a natural talent for learning a skill, not a skill developed through work.
w: Technical skills apply to specific tools or equipment in one type of work, but Gwen's customer-service skills carried over from serving to banking.
Job-specific skills apply mainly to one occupation, such as running a restaurant's ordering system, while Gwen used the same skills in a different industry.
An aptitude is a natural talent for learning, but Gwen built these skills through work experience and then used them in a new job.

q.pt: Discuss how specific skills training can improve a young person's human capital, productivity, and income-earning potential
q.s: What is a major benefit to workers who take part in ongoing job training?
o: Fewer duties for the same level of pay
Better chances for career advancement
An exemption from performance reviews
Lower payroll deductions on each check
q.r: Better chances for career advancement. Ongoing training keeps a worker's skills current and adds new ones, which increases productivity and makes the worker a stronger candidate for promotions and raises. Training does not reduce a worker's duties or excuse him or her from performance reviews, and it has no direct effect on payroll deductions.
w: Training adds to what a worker can do; it does not cut duties while keeping pay the same.
Trained workers are still reviewed on their performance, so ongoing training does not excuse anyone from performance reviews.
Payroll deductions depend on pay, taxes and chosen benefits, so ongoing training has no direct effect on how much is withheld.

q.pt: Discuss how specific skills training can improve a young person's human capital, productivity, and income-earning potential
q.s: Darius, a licensed electrician, takes evening classes each year to keep up with new wiring codes and technologies. Darius is participating in
o: an internship.
job shadowing.
an apprenticeship.
continuing education.
q.r: Continuing education. Continuing education is learning that a person pursues after completing formal schooling or training, often to keep a license or to stay current in a field. It helps workers remain productive as technology changes. An apprenticeship is the training that comes before licensing, an internship is temporary work experience for students, and job shadowing is observing a worker for a short time.
w: An internship is temporary work experience, usually for students, but Darius is already a licensed electrician taking yearly classes.
Job shadowing is briefly watching someone work, while Darius takes regular evening classes to keep up with new codes in the electrical field.
An apprenticeship is the training that comes before becoming licensed, but Darius is already a licensed electrician who is keeping that license current.

q.pt: Discuss how specific skills training can improve a young person's human capital, productivity, and income-earning potential
q.s: Why should employees develop interpersonal skills as well as job-specific skills?
o: Interpersonal skills can replace technical knowledge
Job-specific skills matter mainly for new hires
Both kinds of skills support career progression
Interpersonal skills are used mainly in sales jobs
q.r: Both kinds of skills support career progression. Occupational skills let a worker do the job, while interpersonal skills, such as communication and teamwork, let the worker cooperate, lead and serve customers. Employers look for both when deciding on promotions. Interpersonal skills do not replace technical knowledge, technical skills matter throughout a career, and nearly every job requires working with others.
w: Communication and teamwork skills cannot take the place of knowing how to do the actual work, so interpersonal skills do not replace technical knowledge.
Job-specific skills matter throughout a career, not only for new hires, because workers keep using and updating them as they advance.
Sales jobs do use interpersonal skills heavily, but nearly every job requires working with coworkers, supervisors or customers.

q.pt: Discuss how specific skills training can improve a young person's human capital, productivity, and income-earning potential
q.s: Learning a job from a supervisor or experienced coworker while performing the work is called
o: on-the-job training.
continuing education.
job shadowing.
classroom instruction.
q.r: On-the-job training. On-the-job training teaches workers the skills of a job while they are doing it, usually under the guidance of a supervisor or experienced coworker. It builds human capital without taking the worker away from work. Continuing education usually takes place in courses, job shadowing is observing rather than working, and classroom instruction is separate from performing the job.
w: Continuing education usually happens in courses after formal schooling, while the question describes learning a job while doing it.
Job shadowing means watching a worker rather than performing the work, but the question describes learning while actually doing the job.
Classroom instruction takes place apart from the job, while the question describes learning from a supervisor while performing the work.

q.pt: Explain why wages or salaries vary among employees in different types of jobs and among workers in the same jobs
q.s: Priya and Cole hold the same job title at a sign shop. After taking a design-software course, Priya completes custom orders faster and with fewer errors than Cole. Why might Priya now earn more than Cole?
o: Her job title now ranks above his
Her training increased her productivity
Her payroll deductions are smaller than his
She works fewer hours each week than he does
q.r: Her training increased her productivity. Employers generally pay more to workers who produce more, better work in the same time. Priya's training added to her human capital, so she is worth more to the business even though her job title has not changed. The two share a title, payroll deductions affect take-home pay rather than earnings, and working fewer hours would lower her pay.
w: The question says Priya and Cole hold the same job title, so a higher-ranking title cannot explain her higher pay.
Payroll deductions affect take-home pay after earnings are figured, so they do not explain why the shop would pay Priya more.
Working fewer hours would usually lower Priya's pay, and the question says nothing about her hours, only her faster, better work.

q.pt: Gather data on the average wage or salary for different jobs and explain how they differ by the level of education, job skill, or years of experience
q.s: Which of the following best explains why an experienced welder usually earns more per hour than a newly hired welder:
o: Years of experience increase skill and productivity
New hires are not legally allowed to weld alone
Experienced workers pay a lower federal income tax rate
New welders are paid by commission instead
q.r: Years of experience increase skill and productivity. Wage data show that pay usually rises with experience because experienced workers complete work faster, make fewer mistakes and handle harder jobs. The other choices are not accurate explanations. Tax rates depend on income, not years of experience, and welders are typically paid hourly wages rather than commissions.
w: Nothing in the question suggests a legal rule against new welders working alone, and such a rule would not explain differences in hourly pay.
Income tax rates depend on how much a person earns, not on years of experience, so taxes do not explain the higher hourly pay.
Welders are usually paid hourly wages, not commissions, and the question compares pay per hour for both welders.

q.pt: Gather data on the average wage or salary for different jobs and explain how they differ by the level of education, job skill, or years of experience
q.s: A manufacturer pays a base wage of $17.00 an hour and adds $1.50 an hour for each industry certification a worker holds. Jamal holds two certifications. What is his hourly wage?
q.r: $20.00. Two certifications add 2 × $1.50 = $3.00 an hour, so Jamal earns $17.00 + $3.00 = $20.00 an hour. This shows how job skills and training can raise pay. The option $18.50 counts only one certification, and $19.50 and $21.00 result from arithmetic errors. Certifications are one way workers increase their human capital and wages.
w: $18.50 adds the $1.50 raise for only one certification, but Jamal holds two, so $3.00 should be added to the $17.00 base.
$19.50 adds $2.50 to the base, which is not two $1.50 raises; two certifications add $3.00 for a total of $20.00.
$21.00 adds $4.00, as if each certification were worth $2.00, but each adds only $1.50, so the total raise is $3.00.

q.pt: Gather data on the average wage or salary for different jobs and explain how they differ by the level of education, job skill, or years of experience
q.s: Wage data for one occupation show annual pay ranging from $38,000 to $71,000. What most likely explains this difference within the same occupation?
o: Differences in each worker's federal tax bracket
Differences in Social Security tax rates
Differences in how often workers are paid
Differences in experience, skills and education
q.r: Differences in experience, skills and education. Workers in the same occupation earn different wages because some have more years on the job, specialized skills, advanced credentials or higher productivity. Tax brackets and Social Security rates affect taxes owed, not what an employer pays. How often a worker is paid, such as weekly or monthly, changes the size of each check, not annual pay.
w: A tax bracket affects how much income tax a worker owes, not how much the employer pays the worker in the first place.
The Social Security tax rate is the same percentage for nearly all employees, so it cannot explain a wide range of annual pay.
Being paid weekly or monthly changes the size of each paycheck, not the total a worker earns over the year.

q.pt: Describe the opportunity costs of attending a training course on babysitting, lifeguarding, or first aid
q.s: Ruby skips 15 hours of her $12-an-hour job to take a $200 first-aid and babysitting course. What is the total cost of the course, including the earnings she gives up?
q.r: $380.00. The opportunity cost of training includes the wages given up as well as the fee. Ruby gives up 15 × $12 = $180 in wages, and the course costs $200, so the total cost is $180 + $200 = $380. The option $180.00 counts only lost wages, $200.00 counts only the fee, and $20.00 is the difference between them.
w: $20.00 is just the difference between the $200 fee and the $180 in lost wages, but the total cost adds them together.
$180.00 counts only the wages Ruby gives up, 15 times $12, and leaves out the $200 she pays for the course.
$200.00 counts only the course fee and ignores the $180 in wages Ruby gives up by skipping work.

q.pt: Compare the costs of post-secondary education with the potential increase in income for a career of choice
q.s: A one-year certificate program costs $9,000 and is expected to raise Dani's pay by $3,000 a year. Ignoring other factors, how many years of higher pay will it take to recover the cost?
o: 2 years
3 years
4 years
9 years
q.r: 3 years. Dividing the cost by the yearly increase in income shows the payback period: $9,000 ÷ $3,000 = 3 years. After that, the added pay is a return on the investment. Comparing the cost of education with the increase in income is a key step in deciding whether training is worthwhile. The other options result from dividing incorrectly.
w: Two years of $3,000 raises recovers only $6,000, which falls short of the $9,000 the program costs.
Four years of $3,000 raises would bring back $12,000, so this overshoots; $9,000 divided by $3,000 is exactly 3 years.
Nine years would be right only if the raise were $1,000 a year; with a $3,000 raise, the $9,000 is recovered in 3 years.

q.pt: Explain why families/caregivers might choose to help pay for education and training of younger family members
q.s: Why might parents choose to help pay for a teenager's welding certificate program?
o: The program removes the teen's need to work
The payments lower the teen's tax rate
The parents are entitled to the teen's future wages
The training can raise the teen's future earnings
q.r: The training can raise the teen's future earnings. Families often help pay for education and training as an investment in a young person's human capital, which can lead to better jobs, higher income and greater financial independence. The training is meant to prepare the teen for work, not replace it. Paying for training does not change the teen's tax rate, and the teen keeps his or her own wages.
w: A welding certificate prepares the teen for work rather than replacing it, so the program does not remove any need to earn money.
Paying for a teen's training does not change the teen's tax rate, which depends on how much income the teen earns.
Helping pay for training does not give parents a right to the teen's future paychecks; the real payoff is the teen's higher earning power and independence.

q.pt: Differentiate between gross and net income
q.s: The total amount a worker earns in a pay period before any deductions are taken out is
o: net pay.
taxable income.
tax liability.
gross pay.
q.r: Gross pay. Gross pay is the full amount earned, such as hours worked times the hourly rate, before taxes and other deductions are withheld. Net pay, or take-home pay, is what remains after deductions. Taxable income is the portion of income subject to tax after allowable deductions, and tax liability is the total tax owed.
w: Net pay is what is left after deductions are taken out, while the question asks for the amount earned before any deductions.
Taxable income is the part of income that is subject to tax after allowable deductions, not the full amount earned in one pay period.
Tax liability is the total amount of tax a person owes, not the worker's full earnings before deductions.

q.pt: Differentiate between gross and net income
q.s: Dana works 32 hours this week at a rate of $15.50 an hour. What is her gross pay for the week?
q.r: $496.00. Gross pay for an hourly worker equals hours worked times the hourly rate: 32 × $15.50 = $496.00. This is the amount before any taxes or deductions are taken out. The option $480.00 uses $15.00 an hour, $465.00 uses 30 hours, and $512.00 uses $16.00 an hour, so each reflects a calculation error.
w: $465.00 multiplies $15.50 by 30 hours, but Dana worked 32 hours, so two hours of pay are missing.
$480.00 multiplies 32 hours by $15.00, dropping the extra 50 cents per hour that Dana actually earns.
$512.00 multiplies 32 hours by $16.00, which rounds Dana's $15.50 rate up and overstates her pay by $16.00.

q.pt: Differentiate between gross and net income
q.s: Mateo earns $18.00 an hour and is paid 1.5 times his hourly rate for hours over 40 in a week. If he works 44 hours this week, what is his gross pay?
q.r: $828.00. Regular pay is 40 × $18.00 = $720.00. Overtime pay is 4 hours × ($18.00 × 1.5) = 4 × $27.00 = $108.00. Gross pay is $720.00 + $108.00 = $828.00. The option $720.00 leaves out overtime, $792.00 pays all 44 hours at the regular rate, and $1,188.00 pays all 44 hours at the overtime rate.
w: $720.00 is only Mateo's pay for the first 40 hours and leaves out the 4 overtime hours at $27.00 each.
$792.00 pays all 44 hours at the regular $18.00 rate, forgetting that the 4 hours over 40 earn 1.5 times the rate.
$1,188.00 pays all 44 hours at the $27.00 overtime rate, but only the 4 hours beyond 40 qualify for overtime pay.

q.pt: Differentiate between gross and net income
q.s: Keisha's gross pay is $1,200.00. Her employer withholds $96.00 for federal income tax, $50.40 for state income tax, 6.2% for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare. What is her net pay?
q.r: $961.80. Social Security is $1,200.00 × 6.2% = $74.40, and Medicare is $1,200.00 × 1.45% = $17.40. Total deductions are $96.00 + $50.40 + $74.40 + $17.40 = $238.20, so net pay is $1,200.00 − $238.20 = $961.80. The option $1,053.60 leaves out Social Security and Medicare, $1,108.20 leaves out income taxes, and $1,438.20 adds the deductions instead of subtracting them.
w: $1,053.60 subtracts only the federal and state income taxes and forgets the $74.40 Social Security and $17.40 Medicare deductions.
$1,108.20 subtracts Social Security and Medicare but leaves out the $96.00 federal and $50.40 state income tax withholdings.
$1,438.20 adds the $238.20 in deductions to gross pay instead of subtracting them, so it is larger than Keisha's earnings.

q.pt: Differentiate between gross and net income
q.s: On a pay stub, which figure shows the amount actually deposited into the worker's bank account?
o: Gross pay
Year-to-date gross
Hourly rate
Net pay
q.r: Net pay. Net pay, or take-home pay, is the amount left after taxes and other payroll deductions are subtracted from gross pay, and it is what the worker actually receives. Gross pay is earnings before deductions, year-to-date gross is total earnings so far this year, and the hourly rate is the pay for one hour of work.
w: Gross pay is the amount earned before taxes and other deductions are taken out, so it is larger than what reaches the bank account.
Year-to-date gross is total earnings so far this year before deductions, not the amount deposited for this one paycheck.
The hourly rate shows pay for a single hour of work, not the total amount deposited after deductions.

q.pt: Identify common types of payroll deductions
q.s: Amounts an employer withholds from a worker's gross pay for taxes, insurance and retirement savings are called
o: payroll deductions.
tax credits.
employee bonuses.
sales taxes.
q.r: Payroll deductions. Payroll deductions are amounts subtracted from gross pay, including income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes, health insurance premiums and retirement contributions. They explain why net pay is smaller than gross pay. A tax credit reduces taxes owed, a bonus is extra pay, and sales tax is charged on purchases rather than withheld from paychecks.
w: A tax credit lowers the tax a person owes when filing, while the question describes amounts withheld from each paycheck.
A bonus is extra pay added to earnings, which is the opposite of amounts taken out of gross pay.
Sales tax is charged when you buy goods, not withheld from a worker's paycheck for taxes, insurance or retirement.

q.pt: Identify common types of payroll deductions
q.s: Which of the following is a voluntary payroll deduction:
o: Social Security tax
A contribution to a 401(k) retirement plan
Medicare tax
Federal income tax withheld based on Form W-4
q.r: A contribution to a 401(k) retirement plan. Employees choose whether to save in an employer retirement plan and how much to contribute, so it is a voluntary deduction. Social Security tax, Medicare tax and federal income tax withholding are required by law for most employees, and the employer must withhold them from each paycheck.
w: Social Security tax is required by law for most employees, so the worker cannot choose to skip it, which makes it mandatory rather than voluntary.
Medicare tax must be withheld from most employees' pay by law, so it is a required deduction, not one the worker chooses.
Form W-4 affects how much federal income tax is withheld, but withholding itself is required by law, so it is not voluntary.

q.pt: Identify common types of payroll deductions
q.s: Which of the following payroll deductions helps fund federal health insurance mainly for people age 65 and older:
o: Social Security tax
State income tax
Medicare tax
Health insurance premium
q.r: Medicare tax. Medicare tax is withheld from wages at 1.45%, and the employer pays a matching 1.45%, to fund Medicare, the federal health insurance program mainly for people 65 and older. Social Security tax funds retirement, disability and survivors benefits, and state income tax supports state government. A health insurance premium pays for the worker's own employer-sponsored coverage, not the federal program.
w: Social Security tax funds retirement, disability and survivors benefits, not the federal health insurance program for people 65 and older.
State income tax pays for state government services, so it does not fund federal health insurance for older people.
A health insurance premium pays for the worker's own employer coverage, not the federal health program for people 65 and older.

q.pt: Identify common types of payroll deductions
q.s: Lucia notices a $42.50 deduction labeled "Medical/Dental" on her pay stub. This deduction most likely pays for her
o: federal income taxes.
share of health insurance premiums.
Social Security benefits.
contributions to a 401(k) retirement plan.
q.r: Share of health insurance premiums. Many employers offer health and dental insurance and deduct the employee's share of the premium from each paycheck. This is a common payroll deduction. Federal income taxes and Social Security taxes appear as separate tax lines on a pay stub, and 401(k) contributions are listed as retirement savings, not medical or dental coverage.
w: Federal income tax appears as its own tax line on a pay stub, so a deduction labeled Medical/Dental is not a tax payment.
Social Security is a payroll tax listed separately on the stub, and it does not pay for Lucia's medical or dental coverage.
A 401(k) deduction goes into retirement savings and would be labeled that way, not as Medical/Dental.

q.pt: Explain how taxes impact take-home pay
q.s: Ellie can take a job with the same gross pay in either of two states. Only one of the states has a state income tax. In the state without it, Ellie's take-home pay will most likely be
o: lower, because federal taxes replace the state tax.
the same, because the employer pays all state taxes.
the same, because only federal taxes affect net pay.
higher, because less tax is withheld from her pay.
q.r: Higher, because less tax is withheld from her pay. Take-home pay is gross pay minus taxes and other deductions. With no state income tax withheld, fewer dollars are subtracted, so net pay is larger. Federal income tax and Social Security and Medicare taxes do not rise to replace the missing state tax. State income tax is withheld from the worker's own pay rather than paid by the employer, and it does reduce net pay.
w: Federal taxes do not rise to make up for a missing state income tax, so Ellie's pay would not be lower in the no-tax state.
State income tax is withheld from the worker's own pay, not covered by the employer, so it does change Ellie's take-home pay.
State income tax withholding also reduces net pay, so the two jobs would not leave Ellie with the same take-home amount.

q.pt: Explain how taxes impact take-home pay
q.s: Why is a teen's first paycheck usually smaller than his or her hours worked times the hourly rate?
o: Taxes and other deductions are withheld
The employer subtracts the cost of training
Overtime is always paid one period later
Tips are subtracted from the hourly wages
q.r: Taxes and other deductions are withheld. Hours times the hourly rate equals gross pay. Before paying the worker, the employer withholds payroll deductions such as Social Security and Medicare taxes and, when required, income taxes, so the check shows the smaller net pay. Employers do not subtract training costs from pay, overtime timing varies, and tips are added to income, not subtracted.
w: Employers do not normally take training costs out of a new worker's pay, so this does not explain the smaller first paycheck.
Overtime timing varies by employer, and a teen's first check may have no overtime at all, so it cannot explain the usual gap.
Tips are extra income added on top of wages, so they would never be subtracted from the hourly pay on a paycheck.

q.pt: Complete IRS Form W-4
q.s: Max updates his Form W-4 so that more federal income tax is withheld from each paycheck. How will this change affect his paychecks?
o: His gross pay per check will decrease
His net pay per check will decrease
His Social Security tax will increase
His hourly wage will decrease
q.r: His net pay per check will decrease. Form W-4 tells an employer how much federal income tax to withhold. Withholding more tax means a larger deduction from gross pay, which leaves less take-home pay in each check, though it may mean a smaller tax bill or a larger refund later. Gross pay, the hourly wage and the Social Security tax rate do not change.
w: Gross pay is what Max earns before deductions, and changing his W-4 only changes how much tax is withheld, not what he earns.
The Social Security tax rate is set by law and is not affected by Form W-4, which covers only federal income tax withholding.
His hourly wage is set by his employer, and a W-4 change only affects the tax taken out of his pay.

q.pt: Identify the different groups of people who qualify for Social Security benefits
q.s: Social Security pays income benefits to which of the following groups:
o: Retired workers, disabled workers and survivors
New hires, student interns and seasonal workers
Business owners who earn large annual profits
Workers who change to new careers
q.r: Retired workers, disabled workers and survivors. Social Security is a federal program funded by payroll taxes that provides retirement, disability and survivors benefits to qualified workers and their dependents, such as spouses and children. Starting a job, earning business profits or changing careers does not qualify a person for benefits. Benefits are based on a worker's earnings record and circumstances such as age or disability.
w: Simply starting a job, interning or working a season does not qualify anyone for benefits, which depend on age, disability or a worker's death.
Earning large business profits does not make someone eligible, since Social Security pays benefits for retirement, disability or a worker's death.
Changing careers is a normal job decision, not retirement, disability or a family member's death, so it does not qualify a person for benefits.

q.pt: Identify the different groups of people who qualify for Social Security benefits
q.s: Alana's father, who worked for many years, died last year. Alana, age 12, now receives monthly Social Security payments based on her father's work record. These payments are
o: survivors benefits.
disability benefits.
retirement benefits.
unemployment benefits.
q.r: Survivors benefits. Social Security pays survivors benefits to eligible family members, such as children and spouses, of a worker who has died. Disability benefits go to workers who cannot work because of a serious medical condition, and retirement benefits go to workers who have reached retirement age. Unemployment benefits are a separate program for workers who lose their jobs.
w: Disability benefits go to workers who cannot work because of a serious medical condition, but Alana receives payments because her father died.
Retirement benefits go to workers who reach retirement age, while Alana is a 12-year-old receiving payments after her father's death.
Unemployment benefits are a separate program for people who lose their jobs, not payments to a child based on a parent's work record.

q.pt: Given information on a worker's income and today's Social Security tax rates, calculate what the worker and the worker's employer will pay in Social Security taxes
q.s: Corinne earns a salary of $42,000 a year. The Social Security tax rate is 6.2% for the employee and 6.2% for the employer. How much Social Security tax will Corinne and her employer each pay for the year?
q.r: $2,604.00. Corinne pays $42,000 × 6.2% = $2,604.00, and her employer pays a matching $2,604.00. The option $609.00 uses the 1.45% Medicare rate, $3,213.00 uses the combined 7.65% FICA rate, and $5,208.00 is the total that Corinne and her employer pay together rather than each one's share.
w: $609.00 uses the 1.45% Medicare rate instead of the 6.2% Social Security rate that the question gives.
$3,213.00 uses the combined 7.65% rate for Social Security and Medicare, but the question asks only about Social Security tax.
$5,208.00 is what Corinne and her employer pay together, but the question asks how much each one pays separately.

q.pt: Research the Social Security tax rate for someone who is self-employed vs. someone who is working for an employer
q.s: How does the Social Security tax rate for a self-employed person compare with the rate for an employee?
o: The self-employed person pays 12.4%, covering both shares
Both pay 6.2%, and the government pays the rest
The self-employed person pays no Social Security tax on earnings
The employee pays 12.4%, and the employer pays none
q.r: The self-employed person pays 12.4%, covering both shares. An employee pays 6.2% of wages for Social Security, and the employer pays a matching 6.2%. A self-employed person has no employer, so he or she pays both halves, 12.4%, through the self-employment tax. The government does not pay a share, self-employed people are not exempt, and employers must match employees' tax.
w: An employee pays 6.2%, but the employer pays the matching share, not the government, and a self-employed person pays both shares.
Self-employed people are not exempt; they pay Social Security tax on their earnings through the self-employment tax.
An employee pays only 6.2% and the employer must match it, so the employee does not pay the full 12.4% alone.

q.pt: Research the Social Security tax rate for someone who is self-employed vs. someone who is working for an employer
q.s: Theo works as an independent contractor designing websites for several clients. In addition to income tax, he must pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on his net earnings through
o: state and local sales tax.
excise tax.
local property tax.
self-employment tax.
q.r: Self-employment tax. Independent contractors and other self-employed people pay self-employment tax, which covers both the employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare. No employer withholds it, so they must set money aside. Sales tax is charged on purchases, excise tax on specific goods such as gasoline, and property tax on real estate.
w: Sales tax is charged when customers buy goods, not on the money Theo earns from designing websites.
Excise tax is charged on specific products such as gasoline, not on a contractor's earnings for Social Security and Medicare.
Property tax is charged on real estate a person owns, so it has nothing to do with Theo's earnings from clients.

q.pt: Research the Social Security tax rate for someone who is self-employed vs. someone who is working for an employer
q.s: Rosa has $20,000 of earnings subject to self-employment tax. If the self-employment tax rate is 15.3% (12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare), how much self-employment tax does she owe?
q.r: $3,060.00. Self-employment tax is $20,000 × 15.3% = $3,060.00, because a self-employed person pays both the employee and employer shares. The option $1,530.00 uses only the 7.65% employee share, $2,480.00 includes only the 12.4% Social Security portion, and $580.00 includes only the 2.9% Medicare portion.
w: $580.00 uses only the 2.9% Medicare portion and leaves out the 12.4% Social Security part of the tax.
$1,530.00 uses just the 7.65% employee share, but a self-employed person pays both shares, for 15.3% in all.
$2,480.00 uses only the 12.4% Social Security portion and leaves out the 2.9% for Medicare.

q.pt: Illustrate the relationship between income level and income tax paid
q.s: The total amount of tax a person owes on his or her income for the year is the person's
o: tax liability.
taxable income.
gross pay.
tax refund.
q.r: Tax liability. Tax liability is the total amount of tax owed to a government for a period. It is figured by applying tax rates to taxable income and then subtracting any credits. Taxable income is the amount being taxed, not the tax itself. Gross pay is earnings before deductions, and a tax refund is money returned when more tax was withheld than was owed.
w: Taxable income is the amount of income being taxed, not the amount of tax owed on it.
Gross pay is what a worker earns before deductions in a pay period, not the total tax owed for the year.
A tax refund is money returned when more tax was withheld than was owed, so it is not the total amount owed.

q.pt: Illustrate the relationship between income level and income tax paid
q.s: Which of the following types of income is generally taxable:
o: A birthday gift from a grandparent
Wages and commissions from a job
Money borrowed through a student loan
A refund for a returned purchase
q.r: Wages and commissions from a job. People are required to pay taxes on most income, including wages, salaries, commissions, tips, investment earnings and self-employment income. A gift is generally not taxable to the person who receives it, borrowed money must be repaid and is not income, and a refund for a returned purchase simply gives back money the buyer already spent.
w: A gift from a grandparent is generally not taxable to the person who receives it, so it is not taxable income.
A student loan is borrowed money that must be paid back, so it is not income and is not taxed.
A refund for a returned item just gives back money already spent, so it is not new income to be taxed.

q.pt: Illustrate the relationship between income level and income tax paid
q.s: A tax system in which people with higher incomes pay a larger percentage of their income in tax is a
o: regressive tax.
flat tax.
excise tax.
progressive tax.
q.r: Progressive tax. Under a progressive tax, rates rise as income rises, so higher earners pay a larger share of their income. The federal income tax is progressive because it uses brackets with higher rates on higher portions of income. A regressive tax takes a larger share from lower incomes, a flat tax charges everyone the same rate, and an excise tax applies to specific goods.
w: A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from lower earners, the opposite of the pattern the question describes.
A flat tax charges everyone the same percentage, so higher earners would not pay a larger percentage of their income.
An excise tax is charged on specific goods, such as gasoline, rather than on income at rates that rise with earnings.

q.pt: Illustrate the relationship between income level and income tax paid
q.s: Which of the following describes a flat income tax:
o: Higher earners pay a higher percentage of income
Lower earners pay a higher percentage of income
Everyone pays the same percentage of income
A set tax is charged on specific products
q.r: Everyone pays the same percentage of income. A flat tax applies a single rate to all taxable income, so a person earning $40,000 and a person earning $400,000 pay the same percentage, though the higher earner pays more dollars. Higher rates for higher earners describe a progressive tax, a larger share from lower earners describes a regressive tax, and a tax on specific products is an excise tax.
w: Higher earners paying a higher percentage describes a progressive tax, not a flat tax with one rate for everyone.
Lower earners paying a higher percentage describes a regressive tax, while a flat tax uses one rate for every income.
A set tax on specific products is an excise tax, which is a tax on goods rather than a flat tax on income.

q.pt: Illustrate the relationship between income level and income tax paid
q.s: Kai gets a raise that moves part of his income into a higher federal income tax bracket. How will the raise affect his take-home pay?
o: It falls, since all his income is taxed at the higher rate
It stays the same, since higher taxes cancel the raise
It rises by the full amount of the raise
It rises, though by less than the raise
q.r: It rises, though by less than the raise. The federal income tax is progressive, and only the portion of income within the higher bracket is taxed at the higher rate. Kai's tax increases, but by less than the raise, so his take-home pay still goes up. Moving into a higher bracket does not raise the rate on all income, and the extra pay is also subject to taxes, so it is not all kept.
w: Only the part of Kai's income inside the higher bracket is taxed at the higher rate, so the rest of his income is not affected.
Only the portion of the raise in the higher bracket faces the higher rate, so the extra tax cannot wipe out the whole raise.
The added pay is also taxed, so Kai's take-home pay goes up but by less than the full amount of the raise.

q.pt: Describe how taxes are paid on tip income
q.s: Callie, a restaurant server, receives $380 in cash tips during March. What should Callie do with this tip income for tax purposes?
o: Leave the tips off all tax records
Report the tips to her employer
Report only tips paid by credit card
Give the tips to the restaurant owner
q.r: Report the tips to her employer. Tips are income. Employees who receive $20 or more in tips in a month while working for one employer must report them to that employer, who withholds Social Security and Medicare taxes and, when required, income tax. Cash tips must be reported along with card tips. Leaving tips off records can result in penalties, and the tips belong to Callie, not the owner.
w: Tips are taxable income, so leaving them off tax records breaks the rules and can lead to penalties for Callie.
Cash tips must be reported just like card tips, and all $380 of Callie's tips were cash, so reporting only card tips would leave out every dollar.
Tips belong to the server who earns them, so Callie does not hand them to the owner for tax purposes.

q.pt: Describe how taxes are paid on tip income
q.s: Tips that employees report to their employers are subject to
o: state and local sales taxes on purchases.
federal excise taxes.
local property taxes.
Social Security and Medicare taxes.
q.r: Social Security and Medicare taxes. Reported tips are treated as wages for payroll tax purposes, so Social Security and Medicare taxes apply to them, and they are reported as income. Sales taxes apply to purchases, excise taxes apply to specific goods such as gasoline, and property taxes apply to real estate, so none of these applies to tip income.
