q.r: An official vehicle history report. This type of report draws on official title, registration and accident records, so it is based on documented facts rather than opinion. That makes it more reliable than information from someone who has an interest in the sale or who cannot be identified. The seller and the ad both come from the person trying to sell the car, and an anonymous comment cannot be checked.
w: The seller wants to sell the car and may leave out problems, so their own description is less reliable than official records.
A classified ad is written by the seller to attract buyers, so it is promotional and may not reveal accidents or title problems.
An anonymous forum user cannot be identified or checked, so their comment is far less reliable than a report based on official records.

q.pt: Assess strengths and weaknesses of various online and printed sources of product information
q.s: Compared with a printed consumer magazine, a major strength of online product information is that it
o: is always reviewed by independent experts.
is updated quickly and easy to search.
is never influenced by advertisers.
never contains errors or outdated facts.
q.r: Is updated quickly and easy to search. Online sources can be updated quickly as new models, prices and recalls appear, and they are easy to search and compare. Printed magazines are slower to update but often go through careful editing. Online information is not always reviewed by experts, is often influenced by advertisers and sponsors, and can contain errors, so consumers still need to judge each source's reliability.
w: Online information is not always checked by independent experts; anyone can publish online, which is why readers must judge each source.
Many online sources are paid for by advertisers or sponsors, so online information is often influenced by advertisers rather than free of it.
Online information can contain mistakes and outdated facts like any source; its strength is fast updating and easy searching, not perfect accuracy.

q.pt: Assess strengths and weaknesses of various online and printed sources of product information
q.s: A major weakness of social media posts as a source of product information is that they
o: are always older than printed reviews.
cannot include photos or video.
are written only by manufacturers.
may be unverified paid promotions.
q.r: May be unverified paid promotions. Social media posts are easy to publish and often are not checked for accuracy. Some are paid promotions or sponsored content, which gives the poster an incentive to praise the product. Consumers should verify such claims with independent sources. Social media posts are often more current than printed reviews, commonly include photos and video, and are written by many people besides manufacturers.
w: Social media posts are often newer than printed reviews because they can be published instantly, so being older is not their weakness.
Social media posts commonly include photos and video, so this is not a limitation; the real concern is that claims may be paid or unchecked.
Social media posts come from many people, including customers and influencers, not only manufacturers, so this does not describe their weakness.

q.pt: Identify sources of product information that are less useful for buying decisions due to incentive conflicts of the information provider
q.s: Which source of product information is most likely to be influenced by an incentive to make a sale?
o: A salesperson paid on commission
An independent product-testing laboratory
A government product-recall database
A nonprofit consumer magazine with no ads
q.r: A salesperson paid on commission. Commission pay rises when customers buy, especially higher-priced items, so a commissioned salesperson's advice may favor making the sale over the customer's best interest. This is an incentive conflict. Independent testing labs, government recall databases and ad-free nonprofit magazines do not profit from a particular sale, so their information is generally more objective.
w: An independent testing lab does not earn money when a product sells, so it has little reason to slant its results toward making a sale.
A government recall database exists to warn the public about unsafe products, and the agency does not profit from any sale.
A nonprofit magazine with no ads does not depend on sellers or advertisers, so it has no incentive to push a particular sale.

q.pt: Identify sources of product information that are less useful for buying decisions due to incentive conflicts of the information provider
q.s: A popular influencer praises a skin-care brand in a video, and the caption includes #ad. A careful consumer should recognize that the influencer
o: has tested every competing product.
has a paid incentive to promote it.
is required to recommend only the best product.
cannot legally share personal opinions.
q.r: Has a paid incentive to promote it. The #ad label tells viewers that the post is a paid promotion. The Federal Trade Commission expects influencers to disclose such relationships because payment gives them an incentive to speak favorably about the product. The disclosure does not mean the influencer tested competing products or must recommend the best one, and influencers may legally share opinions as long as paid relationships are disclosed.
w: The #ad label shows a paid relationship; it says nothing about whether the influencer has tested competing skin-care brands.
No rule requires influencers to recommend only the best product; the #ad tag simply discloses that the brand is paying for the promotion.
Influencers can legally share personal opinions; the law expects them to disclose paid relationships, which is what the #ad tag does.

q.pt: Identify sources of product information that are less useful for buying decisions due to incentive conflicts of the information provider
q.s: Why is a manufacturer's website less useful than an independent review site for comparing different brands?
o: Manufacturers' websites never list product prices
The manufacturer wants consumers to buy its own products
Manufacturers' websites are always out of date
Independent sites are paid by every brand they review
q.r: The manufacturer wants consumers to buy its own products. A manufacturer's website is a good source of specifications, but the company has a strong incentive to present its own products favorably and is unlikely to point out where competitors do better. Independent review sites compare brands without a stake in the sale. Many manufacturer sites list prices and are kept current, and reputable independent reviewers are not paid by every brand they review.
w: Many manufacturer websites do list prices, so this is not the reason; the problem is that a maker favors its own products over competitors.
Manufacturer websites are often kept current, so being out of date is not the issue; the issue is the company's interest in selling its own brand.
Reputable independent review sites are not paid by every brand they review; their value comes from comparing brands without a stake in the sale.

q.pt: Explain the difference between a debit card and a credit card
q.s: When Emeka pays for gas with a plastic card, the money comes directly out of his checking account. Emeka is paying with a
o: debit card.
credit card.
gift card.
charge card.
q.r: Debit card. A debit card takes money directly from the cardholder's checking account at the time of purchase, so Emeka is spending money he already has. A credit card and a charge card let the user borrow money from the card issuer and repay it later. A gift card is prepaid with a set amount and is not linked to a checking account.
w: A credit card lets Emeka borrow from the card issuer and pay later, but his payment comes straight out of his checking account.
A gift card is preloaded with a set amount and is not linked to a checking account, so the money would not come from Emeka's account.
A charge card lets the user borrow and pay the full bill later, so the money does not come directly from Emeka's checking account.

q.pt: Explain the difference between a debit card and a credit card
q.s: What is the main difference between a debit card and a credit card?
o: A debit card always charges interest on purchases
A credit card draws money from a savings account
A debit card builds the user's credit history
A credit card lets the user borrow money
q.r: A credit card lets the user borrow money. With a credit card, the card issuer lends the user money up to a credit limit, to be repaid later with interest on any balance not paid in full. A debit card spends money already in the user's checking account. Debit cards do not charge interest on purchases and do not build a credit history, and credit cards are not linked to savings accounts.
w: Debit cards spend money already in a checking account, so purchases do not carry interest; that is not what separates them from credit cards.
Credit cards are not linked to savings accounts; they let the user borrow from the card issuer up to a credit limit.
Debit card use generally does not appear on credit reports, so it does not build credit history; credit cards are what can do that.

q.pt: Explain the difference between a debit card and a credit card
q.s: Pilar pays her credit card balance in full by the due date every month. What is the result?
o: She pays a higher interest rate than other users
Her credit card works like a debit card
She avoids interest and builds a positive credit history
Each purchase immediately lowers her checking balance
q.r: She avoids interest and builds a positive credit history. When a cardholder pays the full statement balance by the due date, no interest is charged on purchases, and the record of on-time payments builds a positive credit history. This is the smartest way to use a credit card. Paying in full does not raise the interest rate, and the card is still a borrowing tool: purchases do not come out of checking until Pilar pays the bill.
w: Paying in full on time does not raise Pilar's interest rate; it means she pays no interest at all on her purchases.
Her card is still a credit card: Pilar borrows when she buys and repays later, while a debit card takes money from checking at the moment of purchase.
Credit card purchases do not come out of checking right away; Pilar's checking balance drops only when she pays her monthly card bill.

q.pt: Explain how various payment methods are used to purchase goods and services
q.s: A written order directing a bank to pay a specific amount from the writer's account to a named person or business is a
o: debit card.
money order.
check.
credit card.
q.r: Check. A check is a written, signed order telling the writer's bank to pay a stated amount from the writer's checking account to the payee. It leaves a paper record of the payment. A debit card is a plastic card that electronically withdraws money from checking. A money order is a prepaid payment bought with cash, not drawn on the writer's own account, and a credit card borrows money.
w: A debit card withdraws money electronically from checking; it is a plastic card, not a written, signed order to the bank naming who gets paid.
A money order is bought in advance with cash, so it is prepaid rather than drawn from the writer's own bank account like the payment described.
A credit card borrows money from the card issuer, while the payment described comes straight from the writer's own bank account by written order.

q.pt: Explain how various payment methods are used to purchase goods and services
q.s: Ruby pays a friend back for lunch by sending money through an app on her phone that is linked to her bank account. Ruby is using a
o: cashier's check.
cash advance.
money order.
mobile payment.
q.r: Mobile payment. A mobile payment uses a smartphone app or digital wallet to transfer money, here from Ruby's linked bank account to her friend's account. Peer-to-peer apps are fast and convenient, but users should send money only to people they know. A cashier's check is a check guaranteed by a bank, a cash advance borrows cash against a credit card, and a money order is a prepaid paper payment.
w: A cashier's check is a paper check guaranteed by a bank, not an app on Ruby's phone that sends money instantly to her friend.
A cash advance is borrowing cash against a credit card, while Ruby is sending her own money from her linked bank account.
A money order is a prepaid paper payment bought at a store or post office, not an app-based transfer from Ruby's bank account.

q.pt: Summarize the advantages, disadvantages, risks, and protections of various payment methods
q.s: Which payment method generally gives a consumer the strongest legal protection against unauthorized purchases if it is lost or stolen?
o: Debit card
Prepaid gift card
Credit card
Cash
q.r: Credit card. Federal law limits a credit cardholder's liability for unauthorized charges to $50, and many issuers charge nothing. Because the money is borrowed, the cardholder's own funds are not at risk while the issue is resolved. Debit card protection depends on how quickly the loss is reported, and stolen money leaves the checking account right away. Lost gift cards and cash usually cannot be recovered.
w: Debit cards do have some protection, but it depends on how quickly the loss is reported, and stolen money leaves the checking account right away.
A lost or stolen gift card usually works like cash, so whoever has it can spend it and the owner often cannot get the money back.
Lost or stolen cash is usually gone for good, so it offers the least protection of any payment method, not the strongest.

q.pt: Summarize the advantages, disadvantages, risks, and protections of various payment methods
q.s: A major disadvantage of paying with cash is that
o: lost or stolen cash usually cannot be recovered.
cash is accepted almost everywhere.
cash purchases are charged interest.
cash payments lower a person's credit score.
q.r: Lost or stolen cash usually cannot be recovered. Cash offers no protection: once it is lost or stolen, it is usually gone, and paying with cash leaves no automatic record unless the buyer keeps receipts. Acceptance almost everywhere is an advantage of cash, not a disadvantage. Cash purchases never carry interest, and because cash does not involve borrowing, it does not affect a credit score at all.
w: Being accepted almost everywhere is an advantage of cash, not a disadvantage, so it does not describe a drawback.
Cash is not borrowed, so no interest is ever charged on cash purchases; interest applies to credit, not cash.
Cash payments do not involve borrowing, so they do not show up on credit reports and do not lower a credit score.

q.pt: Choose and justify a preferred payment method for purchases of at least three different types of goods and services
q.s: Nora is buying a $1,100 laptop online from a seller she has never used before. Which payment method would best protect her if the laptop never arrives?
o: A credit card, because she can dispute the charge
A debit card, because the money leaves her account at once
A wire transfer, because it is fast and final
A gift card, because it limits how much she can spend
q.r: A credit card, because she can dispute the charge. A credit card is usually the safest way to pay an unfamiliar seller online. Under federal law, Nora can dispute a charge for goods that are not delivered, and the money in her bank account is never at risk while the dispute is resolved. Debit card money leaves her account immediately, and wire transfers and gift cards are favorite tools of scammers because the money is very hard to get back.
w: The money leaving her account at once is actually a risk: if the laptop never arrives, Nora's own cash is already gone while she tries to recover it.
A wire transfer is fast, but being final means Nora can rarely get the money back if the seller never ships the laptop.
Gift cards are very hard to trace or refund, so paying an unknown seller this way gives Nora almost no protection if the laptop never arrives.

q.pt: Explain how pre-purchase research encourages consumers to avoid impulse buying
q.s: Hailey often buys things she had not planned on when she visits the mall. Which strategy would best help her avoid these purchases?
o: Bringing extra cash in case she finds a good deal
Shopping when she feels bored or stressed
Signing up for every store's text alerts
Researching what she needs before she goes
q.r: Researching what she needs before she goes. Pre-purchase research and planning are the best defenses against impulse buying. When Hailey decides in advance what she needs, compares options and sets a limit, she is far less likely to buy on the spur of the moment. Extra cash, shopping to relieve boredom or stress and constant store promotions all make unplanned purchases more likely.
w: Bringing extra cash makes it easier to buy unplanned items, which is the opposite of what Hailey needs to curb her impulse spending.
Shopping when bored or stressed often leads to buying for comfort, which would increase Hailey's unplanned purchases rather than reduce them.
Store text alerts push sales and promotions, which tempt shoppers to buy things they had not planned, making Hailey's problem worse.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Money set aside to pay for unexpected costs, such as a car repair or a sudden medical bill, is a(n)
o: emergency fund.
retirement account.
college fund.
down payment.
q.r: Emergency fund. An emergency fund is savings reserved for unexpected expenses, such as car repairs, medical bills or a job loss. Having one lets a person handle surprises without borrowing or falling behind on bills. A retirement account builds income for later in life, a college fund pays future education costs, and a down payment is the cash paid upfront on a large planned purchase.
w: A retirement account builds savings for later in life, not money set aside for surprise costs like a car repair or sudden medical bill.
A college fund is saved for future education costs, a planned expense, rather than for unexpected bills like a car repair.
A down payment is cash paid upfront on a large planned purchase, such as a car or home, not a reserve for sudden expenses.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Which of the following expenses would be the most appropriate use of a person's emergency fund:
o: A car repair needed to get to work
Tickets to a popular sold-out concert
Gifts for a planned holiday shopping trip
A new phone to replace one that works
q.r: A car repair needed to get to work. An emergency fund exists to cover unexpected, necessary expenses, such as a sudden repair, a medical bill or a job loss, without borrowing. A breakdown that threatens a person's ability to get to work is exactly that kind of expense. Concert tickets, holiday gifts and an upgrade to a phone that still works are wants or planned purchases, so they belong in the regular budget or in separate savings goals, not in the emergency fund.
w: Concert tickets are a want, not an unexpected necessity, so they belong in the regular budget or a fun-money goal rather than the emergency fund.
Holiday gifts are a planned, expected expense, so they should come from the regular budget or a holiday savings goal, not the emergency fund.
Replacing a phone that still works is an upgrade, a want rather than an emergency, so it should not be paid from the emergency fund.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a short-term savings goal:
o: Buying a house in ten years
Retiring comfortably at age 65
Paying for a weekend trip next summer
Paying for a child's college education
q.r: Paying for a weekend trip next summer. This is a short-term savings goal because it can be reached in about a year or less. Short-term goals are usually funded by saving in a safe, easy-to-reach account. Buying a house in ten years, retiring at 65 and paying for a child's college education are long-term goals that take many years of saving and investing.
w: Buying a house in ten years is a long-term goal because it takes many years of saving, while short-term goals are reached in about a year or less.
Retiring at 65 is usually decades away for a saver, making it a long-term goal rather than one reached within about a year.
Paying for a child's college education usually takes many years of saving, so it is a long-term goal, not a short-term one.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Ines, 22, puts $300 a month into an account she plans to use for buying a home in about eight years. This is an example of a
o: long-term savings goal.
short-term savings goal.
variable expense.
emergency fund.
q.r: Long-term savings goal. A long-term savings goal takes several years or more to reach. Ines is saving for a home purchase about eight years away, so it is a long-term goal. Short-term goals are reached in about a year or less. A variable expense is spending that changes month to month, and an emergency fund is set aside for unexpected costs rather than a planned purchase.
w: Short-term goals are reached in about a year or less, but Ines plans to buy her home in about eight years.
A variable expense is spending that changes month to month, while Ines is putting a steady $300 into savings for a future home.
An emergency fund is reserved for unexpected costs, but Ines is saving for a planned home purchase about eight years away.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Mr. and Mrs. Okafor deposit money each month into an account set aside to pay their daughter's future tuition. This account is a
o: emergency fund.
checking account.
pension.
college fund.
q.r: College fund. A college fund is savings set aside specifically for future education costs, such as tuition, fees and books. Families often use tax-advantaged accounts such as 529 plans for this purpose. An emergency fund covers unexpected expenses, a checking account is used for everyday payments, and a pension is a retirement plan that pays income to former employees.
w: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs, while the Okafors are saving specifically for their daughter's future tuition.
A checking account is used for everyday payments and bills, not an account set aside specifically for a child's future tuition.
A pension is a retirement plan that pays income to former employees, not savings parents set aside for their child's education.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Which habit will best help a young worker build enough savings to support himself or herself in retirement?
o: Saving part of every paycheck, starting now
Spending freely now and starting to save after age 50
Counting on a future inheritance to cover retirement
Keeping all of his or her savings in cash at home
q.r: Saving part of every paycheck, starting now. Securing retirement income depends on regularly spending less than one earns and saving the difference, starting early so compounding has decades to work. Waiting until 50 leaves far less time for growth. An inheritance is uncertain and may never arrive, and cash kept at home earns no interest, loses value to inflation and can be lost or stolen.
w: Waiting until 50 gives savings far fewer years to grow, so the worker would need to save much more later to catch up.
An inheritance is uncertain and may never come or be smaller than expected, so counting on one is not a reliable retirement plan.
Cash kept at home earns no interest, loses buying power to inflation and can be lost or stolen, so it will not grow enough for retirement.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Erica started saving $200 a month at age 25. Mason started saving $200 a month at age 40. If they earn the same rate of return, who is likely to have more at age 65?
o: Mason, because he saved when his income was higher
Erica, because her money has more time to compound
Neither, because they save the same monthly amount
Mason, because later savings earn higher interest
q.r: Erica, because her money has more time to compound. Erica will likely have much more. She saves for 40 years and Mason for 25, so she contributes more, and her early deposits have decades to earn interest on interest. Starting early is the most powerful advantage a saver has. Mason's higher income at 40 does not change his $200 deposits, equal monthly amounts do not mean equal results, and later savings do not earn higher interest.
w: Mason's higher income at 40 does not matter here because he saves the same $200 a month; Erica saves 15 more years and gets more compounding.
Equal monthly deposits do not mean equal results; Erica saves for 40 years and Mason for 25, so she deposits more and earns more interest.
Saving later does not earn a higher interest rate; the question says both earn the same rate, so Erica's extra years give her the edge.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Kiara is saving $600 for a trip she will take in four months. Where should she keep the money?
o: In individual company stocks
In an insured savings account
In a long-term retirement account
In a five-year certificate of deposit
q.r: In an insured savings account. Money needed within a year should be kept safe and easy to reach, so a traditional, federally insured savings account is the best choice for Kiara's trip fund. Stocks can lose value in the short run, retirement accounts are meant for long-term goals and may carry penalties for early withdrawals, and a five-year CD charges a penalty if the money is withdrawn before the term ends.
w: Stocks can drop in value over a few months, so Kiara could have less than $600 right when she needs it for her trip.
Retirement accounts are meant for goals decades away and may charge penalties for early withdrawals, which does not suit a trip in four months.
A five-year CD locks up the money for five years and charges a penalty for early withdrawal, while Kiara needs the money in only four months.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Which statement best describes when a person should save and when he or she should invest?
o: Save for short-term goals; invest for long-term goals
Invest for short-term goals; save for long-term goals
Save only when interest rates are high
Invest money that will be needed within a year
q.r: Save for short-term goals; invest for long-term goals. Saving keeps money safe and available for short-term goals, while investing in assets such as stocks and mutual funds offers greater growth for long-term goals, because there is time to recover from short-term drops in value. Reversing the two exposes short-term money to losses at the wrong time. Saving makes sense at any interest rate, and money needed within a year should not be invested.
w: This reverses the rule: investing money needed soon risks a drop in value right before it is needed, while long-term money can ride out ups and downs.
Saving makes sense at any interest rate, because the main purpose is keeping money safe and available for near-term needs.
Money needed within a year should be kept safe in savings, since investments can lose value in the short run.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Many financial experts recommend that an emergency fund hold enough money to cover
o: one week of planned entertainment spending.
the full purchase price of a new home.
three to six months of essential expenses.
ten years of the person's take-home pay.
q.r: Three to six months of essential expenses. A widely used guideline is that an emergency fund should cover three to six months of essential living expenses, such as rent, food, utilities and transportation. That amount can carry a person through a job loss or major repair. One week of entertainment spending is far too little, while the price of a home or ten years of pay are long-term goals, not emergency reserves.
w: One week of entertainment money is far too small to cover rent, food and bills during a job loss or major repair.
The full price of a home is a large long-term goal, not an emergency reserve, and far more than most experts suggest keeping for emergencies.
Ten years of take-home pay is far beyond what an emergency fund needs; that much money would be better invested for long-term goals.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Why should an emergency fund be kept in a highly liquid account?
o: Liquid accounts pay the highest returns
Liquid accounts block withdrawals before a set date
The money is fully protected from inflation
The money can be reached quickly without losing value
q.r: The money can be reached quickly without losing value. Liquidity is how quickly and easily an asset can be turned into cash without losing value. Emergencies do not wait, so an emergency fund belongs in a liquid account, such as an insured savings account, where the money is available immediately. Liquid accounts usually pay lower returns than long-term investments, they do not block withdrawals, and low-interest savings can still lose purchasing power to inflation.
w: Liquid accounts, such as savings accounts, usually pay lower returns than long-term investments; they are chosen for quick access, not high returns.
An account that blocks withdrawals before a set date is the opposite of liquid, and emergency money must be available right away.
Low-interest savings can still lose buying power to inflation, so liquidity does not mean protection from rising prices.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Paulo, 17, wants to buy a used car next year, help pay for college in two years and eventually retire. Which goal is best suited to investing in a diversified stock fund?
o: The used car
Retirement
College in two years
All three goals equally
q.r: Retirement. Retirement is decades away, so Paulo has time to ride out short-term drops in the stock market and benefit from its higher long-term growth. Money for the car next year and for college in two years is needed soon, so it should be kept in safe, liquid savings where its value will not fall right before he needs it. Treating all three goals the same ignores their different time frames.
w: Paulo needs the car money next year, and stocks could fall right before the purchase, so this short-term goal belongs in safe savings.
College is only two years away, which is too little time to recover if stock prices drop, so this money should stay in safe savings.
The three goals have very different time frames, and only retirement is far enough away to ride out stock market drops.

q.pt: Identify the most common reasons that people save money for the future
q.s: Why do many people save for months or years before buying a car or a home?
o: To avoid paying any sales tax on the purchase
Because lenders do not make car or home loans
To qualify for a higher interest rate on the loan
To make a larger down payment and borrow less
q.r: To make a larger down payment and borrow less. Saving ahead for a large purchase lets a buyer make a larger down payment, the cash paid upfront, so less must be borrowed. Borrowing less means smaller loan payments and less interest paid over the life of the loan, and lenders often offer better terms to buyers with larger down payments. Saving does not eliminate sales tax, lenders do make car and home loans, and a higher loan rate would cost the buyer more.
w: Saving ahead does not remove sales tax; tax is still owed on a car purchase no matter how the buyer pays.
Lenders do make car and home loans; people save first so they can make a bigger down payment and borrow less.
A higher interest rate on a loan would cost the buyer more, so no one saves in order to get one; a bigger down payment can help earn a lower rate.

q.pt: Create a savings plan that will allow someone to make a large purchase in one year, 5 years, and 10 years
q.s: Theo wants to save $1,440 for a used e-bike in 12 months. Ignoring interest, how much must he save each month?
q.r: $120. A savings plan divides the goal by the number of months until the deadline: $1,440 ÷ 12 = $120 a month. Saving $100 a month would leave him $240 short after a year. The figure $144 divides by 10 instead of 12, and $240 would reach the goal in only six months, more than Theo needs to save.
w: $100 a month for 12 months adds up to only $1,200, leaving Theo $240 short of his $1,440 goal.
$144 comes from dividing $1,440 by 10 instead of by the 12 months Theo actually has.
$240 a month would reach $1,440 in just six months, so it is more than Theo needs to save over 12 months.

q.pt: Create a savings plan that will allow someone to make a large purchase in one year, 5 years, and 10 years
q.s: Brianna wants $6,000 for a car down payment in five years. Ignoring interest, how much should she save each month?
q.r: $100. Convert years to months first: 5 years × 12 = 60 months. Then divide the goal by the months: $6,000 ÷ 60 = $100 a month. The figure $1,200 is the amount she must save each year, not each month. Saving $60 or $75 a month would leave her short of her down payment goal at the end of five years.
w: $60 a month for 60 months adds up to only $3,600, well short of Brianna's $6,000 goal.
$75 a month for 60 months totals $4,500, leaving Brianna $1,500 short of her $6,000 goal.
$1,200 is what Brianna must save each year ($6,000 / 5), not each month; the yearly figure still needs to be divided by 12.

q.pt: Create a savings plan that will allow someone to make a large purchase in one year, 5 years, and 10 years
q.s: Marcus wants $18,000 toward a home down payment in 10 years. He already has $3,000 saved. Ignoring interest, how much must he save each month?
q.r: $125. First subtract what Marcus already has: $18,000 − $3,000 = $15,000 still needed. Then divide by the number of months: 10 years × 12 = 120 months, and $15,000 ÷ 120 = $125 a month. The figure $150 ignores the $3,000 already saved, and $1,250 and $1,500 divide by 12 months instead of 120.
w: $150 divides the full $18,000 by 120 months and ignores the $3,000 Marcus has already saved.
$1,250 divides the $15,000 still needed by 12 months instead of the 120 months in 10 years.
$1,500 divides the full $18,000 by 12 months, ignoring both the $3,000 already saved and the 10-year time frame.

q.pt: Create a savings plan that will allow someone to make a large purchase in one year, 5 years, and 10 years
q.s: Jalen plans to save $50 a week for 26 weeks toward a $1,500 goal. How much more will he need at the end of the 26 weeks?
q.r: $200. Jalen will save $50 × 26 = $1,300 in 26 weeks. His goal is $1,500, so he will still need $1,500 − $1,300 = $200. To close the gap, he could save about $8 more each week or extend his deadline by four weeks. The figure $1,300 is what he will have saved, and $100 and $250 do not match the arithmetic.
w: $100 is too small a gap: $50 x 26 = $1,300 saved, which leaves Jalen $200, not $100, short of $1,500.
$250 would be the gap after only 25 weeks of saving ($1,250); over the full 26 weeks Jalen saves $1,300 and needs $200 more.
$1,300 is what Jalen will have saved after 26 weeks, not how much more he still needs to reach $1,500.

q.pt: Create a savings plan that will allow someone to make a large purchase in one year, 5 years, and 10 years
q.s: Iris wants $2,400 for a trip and can save $80 a month. Ignoring interest, how many months will it take her to reach the goal?
o: 20 months
24 months
30 months
36 months
q.r: 30 months. Divide the goal by the monthly savings amount: $2,400 ÷ $80 = 30 months, or two and a half years. Knowing how long a goal will take helps a saver decide whether to save more each month or adjust the target date. Twenty and 24 months would require saving $120 and $100 a month, and 36 months is longer than she needs.
w: Reaching $2,400 in 20 months would require saving $120 a month, but Iris can save only $80.
Reaching $2,400 in 24 months would require saving $100 a month, more than the $80 Iris can save.
At $80 a month, 36 months would add up to $2,880, more than Iris needs; she reaches $2,400 after 30 months.

q.pt: Create a savings plan that will allow someone to make a large purchase in one year, 5 years, and 10 years
q.s: What is the first step in creating a savings plan for a large purchase?
o: Apply for a new credit card
Buy the item now and repay it later
Choose the riskiest available investment
Set a specific goal amount and deadline
q.r: Set a specific goal amount and deadline. A savings plan begins with a specific goal: how much money is needed and by when. With those two numbers, a saver can calculate how much to set aside each week or month and choose a suitable account. Applying for credit or buying now and repaying later is borrowing, not saving, and picking the riskiest investment could cause losses right when the money is needed.
w: A new credit card is a way to borrow, not to save, and it does not tell the saver how much is needed or by when.
Buying now and repaying later is borrowing, which skips saving altogether and adds interest costs to the purchase.
The riskiest investment could lose value right when the money is needed, and choosing investments comes after the goal and deadline are set.

q.pt: Explain how the saving strategy "pay yourself first" can help people achieve their saving goals
q.s: Which action would best help Aiyana stick to her plan to save $75 from every paycheck?
o: Setting up an automatic transfer to savings on payday
Saving whatever is left at the end of the month
Keeping her savings in an envelope in her wallet
Linking her savings to her debit card for easy spending
q.r: Setting up an automatic transfer to savings on payday. An automatic transfer on payday puts the pay-yourself-first strategy into action: savings come out before Aiyana has a chance to spend the money. Automating removes the need for willpower each time. Saving whatever is left often means saving nothing, cash in a wallet is easy to spend and can be lost, and linking savings to a debit card makes the money easier to spend.
w: Saving only what is left at month's end often means saving little or nothing, because spending tends to use up whatever money is available.
Cash in a wallet is easy to spend on the spot and can be lost or stolen, which makes it harder for Aiyana to protect her $75 savings.
Linking savings to a debit card makes the money easy to spend, which works against Aiyana's goal of keeping $75 from each paycheck saved.

q.pt: Compare personal attitudes toward saving to those of a friend or relative
q.s: Sofia saves most of her birthday money, while her brother spends his as soon as he receives it. This difference most likely reflects their different
o: interest rates.
tax brackets.
financial institutions.
attitudes toward saving.
q.r: Attitudes toward saving. People's attitudes toward saving vary with their personalities, values and experiences, even within the same family. Sofia values having money for the future, while her brother prefers to enjoy his money now. Interest rates, tax brackets and the choice of bank do not explain why one sibling saves a gift and the other spends it at once.
w: Interest rates affect how fast savings grow, but they do not explain why one sibling saves birthday money and the other spends it right away.
Birthday gifts are generally not taxed to the person who receives them, so tax brackets cannot explain the difference between Sofia's saving and her brother's spending.
Which bank someone uses does not decide whether they save or spend a gift; the difference comes from each sibling's own feelings about money.

q.pt: Explain how a person's personality type might affect their willingness to save or to stick to a savings plan
q.s: A person who values instant gratification and loves spending on new experiences is most likely to find it harder to
o: open a checking account.
use a debit card.
make a purchase decision.
stick to a savings plan.
q.r: Stick to a savings plan. Personality affects saving. People who prefer instant gratification feel a strong pull to spend now, so delaying rewards to follow a savings plan is more difficult for them. Strategies such as automatic transfers can help. Opening a checking account and using a debit card are simple tasks unrelated to personality, and a spender typically finds making purchase decisions easy rather than hard.
w: Opening a checking account is a simple, one-time task that has little to do with whether someone prefers to spend now or later.
Using a debit card is easy for anyone and does not depend on personality, so it is not what a spender would struggle with.
Someone who loves spending usually finds buying decisions easy, not hard; the struggle comes with delaying rewards to keep saving.

q.pt: Explain how a person's personality type might affect their willingness to save or to stick to a savings plan
q.s: A naturally cautious person who worries about the future is most likely to
o: build savings consistently.
make frequent impulse purchases.
avoid setting any financial goals.
rely on credit cards for daily needs.
q.r: Build savings consistently. Cautious, future-focused people tend to feel more secure when they have savings, so they are more likely to build savings consistently and stick to a plan. Frequent impulse purchases, avoiding goals and relying on credit for daily needs are habits more often linked to people who focus on the present and give less thought to future risks.
w: Frequent impulse purchases fit someone focused on enjoying the moment, not a cautious person who worries about future needs.
A person who worries about the future is more likely to set goals to feel secure, not avoid them.
Relying on credit for daily needs creates debt and future risk, which a cautious, future-focused person would usually try to avoid.

q.pt: Identify life situations that can make it difficult for a person to save or to stick to a savings plan
q.s: Which life situation would most likely make it difficult for a person to stick to a savings plan?
o: A raise at work
Paying off a car loan
Receiving a tax refund
A sudden job loss
q.r: A sudden job loss. Losing a job cuts off income, so a person may need to stop saving and even use savings to pay for necessities. Illness, a new baby and large unexpected bills can have similar effects. A raise, paying off a car loan and receiving a tax refund all free up money, which makes it easier, not harder, to stick to a savings plan.
w: A raise increases income, which gives a person more room to save, so it makes a savings plan easier to keep, not harder.
Paying off a car loan ends a monthly payment and frees up money that can go into savings, making the plan easier to follow.
A tax refund is extra money that can be added to savings, so it helps a savings plan rather than making it difficult.

q.pt: Identify life situations that can make it difficult for a person to save or to stick to a savings plan
q.s: After an unexpected medical bill, Grace cannot save her usual $100 this month. What is her best response?
o: Give up on her savings goal entirely
Pay the bill with a high-interest payday loan
Adjust her plan and resume saving later
Skip her rent payment so she can keep saving
q.r: Adjust her plan and resume saving later. Life situations sometimes interrupt a savings plan. The best response is to adjust temporarily, perhaps saving less this month or extending the deadline, and then resume regular saving. Giving up the goal entirely wastes the progress already made, a payday loan adds very high interest costs, and skipping rent creates late fees and the risk of eviction.
w: Giving up entirely throws away the progress Grace has already made, when one missed month only calls for a short pause or adjustment.
Payday loans charge extremely high fees and interest, so using one would turn a single medical bill into a bigger, costlier debt for Grace.
Skipping rent to keep saving risks late fees and eviction, putting a basic need at risk to protect a savings goal.

q.pt: Discuss how savings decisions can affect financial well-being
q.s: How does having savings most directly improve a person's financial well-being?
o: It guarantees a higher salary in the future
It reduces stress and the need to borrow
It eliminates the need for insurance
It prevents prices in the economy from rising
q.r: It reduces stress and the need to borrow. Savings give a person a cushion for emergencies and a way to pay for goals without borrowing. That lowers stress, avoids interest costs and expands future choices, all signs of financial well-being. Savings do not affect a person's salary, they do not replace insurance against large losses such as a house fire, and individual savings cannot stop inflation.
w: Savings do not change what an employer pays; salary depends on a person's job, skills and work, not on how much is in the bank.
Savings can cover small emergencies, but insurance is still needed for large losses, such as a house fire, that savings could not cover.
Prices across the economy rise or fall because of nationwide forces, so one person's savings cannot stop inflation.

q.pt: Discuss how savings decisions can affect financial well-being
q.s: Leah has no savings, so she charges a $900 car repair to a credit card she cannot pay off right away. The most likely effect on her financial well-being is
o: a higher credit score next month.
a larger emergency fund over time.
added debt and interest costs.
no change, because the repair was needed.
q.r: Added debt and interest costs. Without savings, an unexpected expense often turns into high-interest debt. Leah will owe the card issuer the $900 plus interest on any balance she carries, which strains her future budget and makes saving harder. Carrying a large balance does not raise a credit score and can lower it. Borrowing does nothing to build an emergency fund, and a necessary expense still affects well-being when it must be paid with credit.
w: Carrying a large unpaid balance does not raise a credit score and can lower it by increasing how much of her credit limit Leah is using.
Charging the repair is borrowing, which does nothing to build an emergency fund; Leah ends up owing money instead of saving it.
Even a necessary repair hurts Leah's finances when it goes on a card she cannot pay off, because she now owes $900 plus interest.

q.pt: Compare and contrast different types of financial institutions and their products and services
q.s: A not-for-profit financial institution owned by its members, who share in its earnings, is a
o: commercial bank.
savings and loan association.
sales finance company.
credit union.
q.r: Credit union. A credit union is a not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members, who usually share a common bond such as an employer or community. Earnings are returned to members through higher savings rates, lower loan rates and lower fees. Commercial banks are for-profit and owned by stockholders, savings and loan associations specialize in savings and mortgages, and sales finance companies finance specific purchases.
w: A commercial bank is a for-profit business owned by stockholders, not a not-for-profit owned by its members.
Savings and loan associations traditionally focus on savings deposits and home mortgages, and the description of a member-owned not-for-profit fits a credit union instead.
A sales finance company makes loans for specific purchases, such as cars or appliances, and is not a member-owned not-for-profit.

q.pt: Compare and contrast different types of financial institutions and their products and services
q.s: Which type of financial institution is a for-profit, full-service business owned by stockholders that offers checking, savings and many kinds of loans?
o: Commercial bank
Credit union
Sales finance company
Pawnshop
q.r: Commercial bank. A commercial bank is a for-profit, full-service institution owned by stockholders. It offers a wide range of products, including checking and savings accounts, CDs, credit cards and business, auto and home loans. A credit union is owned by its members and operates as a not-for-profit. A sales finance company finances specific purchases, and a pawnshop makes small loans secured by personal property.
w: A credit union does offer checking, savings and loans, but it is a not-for-profit owned by its members rather than for-profit and owned by stockholders.
A sales finance company finances specific purchases, such as cars, and does not offer checking and savings accounts.
A pawnshop makes small loans backed by personal items left as collateral, not a full range of checking, savings and loan services.

q.pt: Compare and contrast different types of financial institutions and their products and services
q.s: Savings and loan associations have traditionally specialized in
o: insuring the deposits of other banks.
issuing stock for large corporations.
accepting savings and making home mortgages.
buying installment contracts from car dealers.
q.r: Accepting savings and making home mortgages. Savings and loan associations, sometimes called thrifts, were created to gather savings deposits and use them to make home mortgage loans, and that remains their traditional specialty. Insuring deposits is the role of federal agencies such as the FDIC, helping corporations issue stock is done by investment banks, and buying installment contracts from car dealers describes a sales finance company.
w: Insuring other banks' deposits is the job of federal agencies such as the FDIC, not the traditional business of savings and loan associations.
Helping large corporations issue stock is the work of investment banks, not savings and loans, which focus on savings and home loans.
Buying installment contracts from car dealers is what sales finance companies do, not the traditional focus of savings and loan associations.

q.pt: Compare and contrast different types of financial institutions and their products and services
q.s: Compared with a commercial bank, a credit union often
o: is owned by outside stockholders.
has its deposits insured by the FDIC instead of the NCUA.
serves anyone with no membership requirements.
pays more on savings and charges less on loans.
q.r: Pays more on savings and charges less on loans. Because credit unions are not-for-profit and owned by their members, they often return earnings through higher savings rates, lower loan rates and fewer fees than commercial banks. Commercial banks, not credit unions, are owned by stockholders. Federally insured credit union deposits are protected by the NCUA rather than the FDIC, and credit unions require membership, usually based on a common bond.
w: Credit unions are owned by their members, not outside stockholders; stockholder ownership describes commercial banks.
This reverses the facts: federally insured credit union deposits are protected by the NCUA, while bank deposits are protected by the FDIC.
Credit unions require membership, usually based on a common bond such as an employer or community, so they do not serve just anyone.

q.pt: Compare the interest rate paid by a financial institution on savings accounts to the interest charged by the same institution on loans
q.s: Northfield Bank pays 2% interest on savings accounts. Which interest rate is it most likely to charge on new car loans?
q.r: 7%. Financial institutions charge borrowers higher interest rates than they pay depositors. The difference, called the spread, covers the bank's costs and the risk that some loans will not be repaid, and provides a profit. A bank paying 2% on savings would therefore charge more, such as 7%, on car loans. Lending at 0%, 1% or 2% would leave the bank unable to cover its costs.
w: A 0% car loan would earn the bank nothing while it still pays savers 2%, so it would lose money on every loan.
Charging 1% on loans while paying 2% on savings would mean the bank pays out more than it earns, so it could not cover its costs.
Charging the same 2% it pays savers leaves no spread to cover the bank's costs, unpaid loans and profit.

q.pt: Compare the interest rate paid by a financial institution on savings accounts to the interest charged by the same institution on loans
q.s: A bank pays 3% interest on $100,000 of deposits and lends the same money at 8%. In one year, how much more does the bank earn in loan interest than it pays depositors?
q.r: $5,000. The bank earns $100,000 × 0.08 = $8,000 in loan interest and pays $100,000 × 0.03 = $3,000 to depositors. The difference is $8,000 − $3,000 = $5,000, which helps cover the bank's operating costs and losses on unpaid loans and provides its profit. The figures $3,000 and $8,000 are only one side of the calculation, and $11,000 adds them instead of subtracting.
w: $3,000 is only the interest the bank pays depositors ($100,000 x 0.03), not the difference between what it earns and what it pays.
$8,000 is only the loan interest the bank earns ($100,000 x 0.08); the $3,000 paid to depositors still must be subtracted.
$11,000 adds the $8,000 earned and the $3,000 paid instead of subtracting to find the difference.

q.pt: Explain how financial institutions get the money to pay interest to their customers who deposit money in savings accounts
q.s: Where does a bank get most of the money it uses to pay interest to savings depositors?
o: From the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
From federal income tax refunds
From printing new currency
From interest that borrowers pay on loans
q.r: From interest that borrowers pay on loans. Banks lend much of the money deposited with them to borrowers, who pay interest on their loans. That loan interest is the main source of the money banks use to pay interest to depositors. The FDIC insures deposits but does not pay interest. Tax refunds go to taxpayers, and only the federal government, not a bank, can issue currency.
w: The FDIC insures deposits in case a bank fails, but it does not pay the everyday interest that savers earn.
Tax refunds go from the government to taxpayers, not to banks, so they are not a source of the interest banks pay savers.
Banks cannot print money; only the federal government issues currency, so this is not where depositors' interest comes from.

q.pt: Explain how financial institutions get the money to pay interest to their customers who deposit money in savings accounts
q.s: When a person deposits money in a savings account, the bank typically
o: keeps every dollar untouched in its vault.
lends much of it to borrowers.
invests it in stocks in the saver's name.
sends it to the U.S. Treasury for safekeeping.
q.r: Lends much of it to borrowers. Banks act as go-betweens for savers and borrowers. They keep part of their deposits available for withdrawals and lend much of the rest to people and businesses, charging interest. In return, they pay savers interest for the use of their money. Banks do not leave all deposits in a vault, do not buy stocks in savers' names and do not send deposits to the Treasury.
w: Banks keep only part of deposits on hand for withdrawals; leaving every dollar in a vault would earn nothing to pay savers interest.
A savings deposit is not used to buy stocks in the saver's name; buying stocks would be the saver's own investing, through an investment account.
Banks do not send deposits to the U.S. Treasury for safekeeping; they keep some on hand and lend much of the rest to borrowers.

q.pt: Differentiate between principal and interest
q.s: The original amount of money a person deposits in a savings account is the
o: principal.
interest.
dividend.
capital gain.
q.r: Principal. The principal is the original amount of money deposited, invested or borrowed, not counting any interest. Interest is the money the bank pays for the use of the principal. A dividend is a share of a company's profits paid to stockholders, and a capital gain is the profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price.
w: Interest is the extra money earned on the deposit, not the original amount the person put into the account.
A dividend is a share of a company's profits paid to stockholders, not the original amount deposited in a savings account.
A capital gain is profit from selling an asset for more than it cost, not the original amount placed in a savings account.

q.pt: Differentiate between principal and interest
q.s: Money that a bank pays a depositor for the use of the depositor's money is
o: principal.
interest.
a fee.
a premium.
q.r: Interest. Interest is the price paid for the use of money. A bank pays interest to depositors because it uses their deposits to make loans, and borrowers pay interest to the bank. The principal is the original amount deposited. A fee is a charge the customer pays to the bank, and a premium is the amount paid for an insurance policy.
w: Principal is the original amount the depositor put in, not the extra money the bank pays for using it.
A fee is a charge the customer pays to the bank, which moves money in the opposite direction from what the question describes.
A premium is the amount paid to buy an insurance policy, not money a bank pays a depositor for using their deposit.

q.pt: Differentiate between principal and interest
q.s: Tomas deposits $800 in a savings account. One year later, with no other deposits or withdrawals, the balance is $824. Which statement is correct?
o: The principal is $824, and the interest is $24
The principal is $24, and the interest is $800
The principal is $800, and the interest is $824
The principal is $800, and the interest is $24
q.r: The principal is $800, and the interest is $24. The principal is the original $800 Tomas deposited. Interest is the amount the account earned: $824 − $800 = $24, which is a 3% annual rate ($24 ÷ $800 = 0.03). The $824 is the new balance, which combines principal and interest. The other choices mix up the original deposit, the interest earned and the ending balance.
w: The interest is $24, but $824 is the new balance, which combines the original $800 deposit with the interest earned.
This swaps the two: Tomas's original deposit of $800 is the principal, and the $24 the account earned over the year is the interest.
The principal is $800, but $824 is the ending balance; the interest is only the $24 the account earned.

q.pt: Differentiate between principal and interest
q.s: Lena has $2,500 in a savings account that pays 3% annual interest. How much interest will she earn in the first year?
q.r: $75. Interest earned equals the interest rate times the balance: $2,500 × 0.03 = $75. Converting the percentage to a decimal (3% = 0.03) is the critical step. The figure $7.50 misplaces the decimal, $25 is 1% of the balance, and $750 is 30% of the balance, so all three reflect errors in converting or applying the rate.
w: $7.50 comes from misplacing the decimal point and using 0.003 instead of 0.03 for 3%, which makes the interest ten times too small.
$25 is only 1% of $2,500, so it uses the wrong rate instead of the 3% the account pays.
$750 is 30% of $2,500, which happens when 3% is converted to 0.30 instead of 0.03.

q.pt: Demonstrate how earning a higher interest rate on money in a savings account will help a person to reach their savings goal sooner
q.s: Saving for a large purchase will take less time when a saver
o: earns a higher interest rate on the savings.
makes smaller monthly deposits.
withdraws money from the account often.
keeps the money in an account with no interest.
q.r: Earns a higher interest rate on the savings. A higher interest rate means the account earns more money each year, so the balance grows faster and reaches the goal sooner, even with the same deposits. Smaller deposits and frequent withdrawals slow progress toward the goal. An account with no interest grows only by what the saver deposits, so it takes the longest of all.
w: Smaller deposits add less money each month, so the balance grows more slowly and the goal takes longer to reach.
Frequent withdrawals take money out of the account, pulling the balance backward and delaying the purchase.
An account with no interest grows only by what the saver puts in, so it reaches the goal more slowly than one that earns interest.

q.pt: Demonstrate how earning a higher interest rate on money in a savings account will help a person to reach their savings goal sooner
q.s: Which of the following best illustrates the time value of money:
o: A $1,000 deposit growing to $1,030 in a year
A $20 bill found in a coat pocket a year later
Prices that stay the same for ten years
A paycheck that arrives on the same day each month
q.r: A $1,000 deposit growing to $1,030 in a year. The time value of money is the idea that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future because money available now can be saved or invested to earn interest. A deposit that earns interest and grows over a year shows this directly. Finding a $20 bill, stable prices and a regular payday do not show money growing over time.
w: Finding a forgotten $20 bill shows money that sat unused and did not grow, the opposite of earning interest over time.
Prices staying the same for ten years describes stable prices, not money growing because it was saved or invested.
A regular payday shows when income arrives, not how money grows over time by earning interest.

q.pt: Demonstrate how earning a higher interest rate on money in a savings account will help a person to reach their savings goal sooner
q.s: Two savings accounts each start with $5,000. Account A earns 2% a year, and Account B earns 5% a year. After one year, how much more interest will Account B have earned?
q.r: $150. Account A earns $5,000 × 0.02 = $100, and Account B earns $5,000 × 0.05 = $250. The difference is $250 − $100 = $150 in just one year, and the gap grows each year as interest compounds. This is why a higher rate helps a saver reach a goal sooner. The figures $100 and $250 are each account's interest alone, and $300 does not match the calculation.
w: $100 is the interest Account A earns alone ($5,000 x 0.02), not how much more Account B earns.
$250 is the interest Account B earns alone ($5,000 x 0.05); Account A's $100 must be subtracted to find the difference.
$300 doubles the correct $150 difference; the 3-point gap in rates on $5,000 is only $150 for one year.

q.pt: Use the Rule of 72 to approximate how many years it will take for savings to double in value at different rates of interest
q.s: According to the Rule of 72, to estimate how many years it will take money to double, a person should divide 72 by the
o: annual interest rate.
original principal.
monthly deposit amount.
current account balance.
q.r: Annual interest rate. The Rule of 72 is a shortcut for estimating doubling time: divide 72 by the annual interest rate. At 6%, for example, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. The rule uses only the interest rate, so the principal, monthly deposits and current balance do not enter the calculation, and dividing by them would give meaningless results.
w: The Rule of 72 does not use the starting amount; any sum doubles in the same time at a given rate, so dividing by the principal gives a meaningless result.
Monthly deposits do not enter the Rule of 72, which estimates doubling time from the annual interest rate alone.
The current balance does not affect doubling time under the Rule of 72; only the annual interest rate goes into the shortcut.

q.pt: Use the Rule of 72 to approximate how many years it will take for savings to double in value at different rates of interest
q.s: Using the Rule of 72, about how long will it take $3,000 to double at 6% annual interest?
o: 6 years
8 years
12 years
18 years
q.r: 12 years. Under the Rule of 72, divide 72 by the annual interest rate: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years for $3,000 to grow to about $6,000. The amount being doubled does not change the answer. Six years confuses the rate with the time, 8 years would require a 9% rate and 18 years would require a 4% rate.
w: 6 years confuses the 6% rate with the number of years; the Rule of 72 divides 72 by 6 to get about 12 years.
8 years would be the doubling time at about 9% (72 / 9), not at the 6% rate in the question.
18 years would be the doubling time at about 4% (72 / 4), so it is too long for money earning 6%.

q.pt: Use the Rule of 72 to approximate how many years it will take for savings to double in value at different rates of interest
q.s: Carlos wants his savings to double in 9 years. Using the Rule of 72, about what annual interest rate must he earn?
q.r: 8%. The Rule of 72 also works backward: divide 72 by the number of years to find the rate needed. 72 ÷ 9 = 8%, so Carlos needs to earn about 8% a year. Choosing 9% confuses the number of years with the rate. At 6% his money would take about 12 years to double, and at 12% it would take about 6 years.
w: At 6% the Rule of 72 gives 72 / 6 = 12 years to double, which is three years slower than the 9-year goal Carlos set.
Using 9% mixes up the number of years with the rate; the rule asks you to divide 72 by those 9 years, which gives 8%.
At 12% money doubles in about 72 / 12 = 6 years, so Carlos would not need a rate that high to double his savings in 9 years.

q.pt: Use the Rule of 72 to approximate how many years it will take for savings to double in value at different rates of interest
q.s: Aaliyah invests $4,000 at 8% annual interest, compounded annually. Using the Rule of 72, about how much will she have after 18 years?
q.r: $16,000. At 8%, money doubles about every 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. In 18 years it doubles twice: $4,000 becomes about $8,000 after 9 years and about $16,000 after 18 years. The figure $8,000 counts only one doubling, $12,000 adds the original amount twice instead of doubling, and $32,000 counts three doublings, which would take about 27 years.
w: $8,000 counts only one doubling; at 8% money doubles about every 9 years, so 18 years allows Aaliyah's $4,000 to double twice.
$12,000 adds $4,000 in each 9-year period, as if growth were simple, instead of doubling the larger $8,000 balance in the second period.
$32,000 counts three doublings, which would take about 27 years at 8%, not the 18 years Aaliyah keeps her money invested.

q.pt: Explain the benefit of compound interest as compared with simple interest
q.s: Interest earned on both the original principal and the interest already earned is
o: compound interest.
simple interest.
a stock dividend.
a capital gain.
q.r: Compound interest. Compound interest is earned on the principal plus all interest already added to the account, so the balance grows faster each year: interest earns interest. Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal. A dividend is a share of a company's profits paid to stockholders, and a capital gain is the profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price.
w: Simple interest is figured only on the original principal, so it never earns interest on interest already paid, which is exactly what the question describes.
A stock dividend is a share of company profits paid to stockholders, not interest that builds on a principal and on earlier interest.
A capital gain is profit from selling an asset for more than it cost, not interest earned on a deposit and its past interest.

q.pt: Explain the benefit of compound interest as compared with simple interest
q.s: Ben's account pays him $30 of interest every year on his original $1,000 deposit, and the yearly interest never changes. Ben is earning
o: simple interest.
compound interest.
variable interest.
dividends.
q.r: Simple interest. Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal, so the dollar amount earned stays the same every year: $1,000 × 3% = $30. With compound interest, Ben's yearly interest would grow because he would also earn interest on past interest. Variable interest describes a rate that changes over time, and dividends are company profits paid to stockholders, not interest on deposits.
w: With compound interest, Ben's yearly interest would grow because each year's interest would also earn interest, but his payment stays at $30 every year.
Variable interest means the rate changes over time, yet Ben's interest never changes from $30 on his original $1,000.
Dividends are company profits paid to stockholders, while Ben is earning interest on money he deposited in an account.

q.pt: Explain the benefit of compound interest as compared with simple interest
q.s: Why do financial experts urge young people to begin saving for retirement as early as possible?
o: Banks pay higher interest rates to younger savers
Their money has more years to compound
Retirement accounts close to people over age 30
Young savers do not pay taxes on their wages
q.r: Their money has more years to compound. Starting early gives savings more years to compound. Each year's interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself, so money saved in a person's twenties can grow far more than larger amounts saved later. Banks do not pay higher rates based on age, retirement accounts remain open to older workers, and young workers do pay taxes on their wages.
w: Banks do not set savings rates based on a customer's age, so the benefit of starting young comes from extra years of compounding, not a better rate.
Retirement accounts stay open to workers of all ages; starting early matters because it gives money more time to grow, not because the door closes at 30.
Young workers pay income and payroll taxes on wages just like older workers, so taxes do not explain why early saving pays off.

q.pt: Demonstrate how annual interest earned increases over time when both the original principal and earned interest are left in a savings account
q.s: Dev deposits $2,000 in an account that earns 5% interest compounded annually. If he makes no other deposits or withdrawals, what will his balance be after two years?
q.r: $2,205. With annual compounding, Year 1: $2,000 × 1.05 = $2,100. Year 2: $2,100 × 1.05 = $2,205. Dev earns $100 in the first year and $105 in the second because interest is earned on the earlier interest. The figure $2,100 is only one year, $2,200 uses simple interest, and $2,210 is not supported by the calculation.
w: $2,100 is Dev's balance after just one year; the second year adds another $105 in interest because it is earned on the larger $2,100 balance.
$2,200 uses simple interest, adding $100 each year on the original $2,000 and ignoring the interest earned on the first year's interest.
$2,210 would require $105 of interest in both years, but in the first year there is no earlier interest yet, so Dev earns only $100.

q.pt: Demonstrate how annual interest earned increases over time when both the original principal and earned interest are left in a savings account
q.s: Darius deposits $1,000 at 10% interest for three years. How much more will he earn if the interest is compounded annually rather than calculated as simple interest?
q.r: $31. Simple interest is $1,000 × 0.10 × 3 = $300. With annual compounding, the balance grows to $1,100, then $1,210, then $1,331, so interest totals $331. The difference is $331 − $300 = $31. The figure $21 is only the third year's difference, and $300 and $331 are each method's total interest rather than the difference between them.
w: $21 is only the gap in the third year ($121 versus $100); the question asks for the extra interest over all three years combined.
$300 is the total simple interest Darius would earn, not how much more compounding earns compared with simple interest.
$331 is the total interest from annual compounding; subtracting the $300 of simple interest shows the extra amount is only $31.

q.pt: Demonstrate how annual interest earned increases over time when both the original principal and earned interest are left in a savings account
q.s: Sam leaves both his principal and earned interest in his savings account. Why does the amount of interest he earns increase each year?
o: The bank must raise its rate every year by law
The balance earning interest grows every year
His principal decreases each year
Interest is paid only on new deposits
q.r: The balance earning interest grows every year. When earned interest stays in the account, it becomes part of the balance that earns interest the next year. Because the balance keeps growing, each year's interest is larger than the last; this is how compound interest works. No law requires banks to raise rates each year, Sam's principal does not shrink, and interest is paid on the whole balance, not only on new deposits.
w: No law forces banks to raise savings rates every year; Sam's interest grows because the balance earning interest keeps getting larger.
Sam leaves his principal and interest in the account, so his balance grows rather than shrinks, and a smaller principal would lower his interest, not raise it.
Banks pay interest on the whole account balance, not only on new deposits, and Sam's growth comes from interest added back into that balance.

q.pt: Explain the importance of federal deposit insurance
q.s: Which federal agency insures deposits at banks?
o: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
q.r: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) is the federal agency that insures deposits at member banks and savings associations up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. The FTC protects consumers from deceptive and unfair business practices, the IRS collects federal taxes, and the SEC regulates the securities markets.
w: The Federal Trade Commission guards consumers against deceptive and unfair business practices, but it does not insure money kept in bank accounts.
The Internal Revenue Service collects federal taxes; it has no role in protecting deposits if a bank fails.
The Securities and Exchange Commission oversees stock and bond markets and investor disclosures, but it does not insure bank deposits.

q.pt: Explain the importance of federal deposit insurance
q.s: Why is federal deposit insurance important to savers?
o: It guarantees a minimum interest rate on savings
It protects stock investments from market losses
It replaces cash lost from a person's wallet
It protects insured deposits if a bank fails
q.r: It protects insured deposits if a bank fails. Federal deposit insurance repays depositors, up to the coverage limit, if an insured bank or credit union fails. Because deposits are protected, people can trust banks with their savings, which supports a stable banking system. Deposit insurance does not set interest rates, does not cover investments such as stocks, and does not replace cash that a person loses.
w: Deposit insurance does not set or guarantee interest rates; banks choose their own rates, and the insurance only protects the deposit if the bank fails.
Stocks are investments, not deposits, so deposit insurance never covers market losses, even on stocks bought through a bank.
Deposit insurance covers money held in an insured bank account, not cash that a person loses or has stolen from a wallet.

q.pt: Explain the importance of federal deposit insurance
q.s: Hector has $310,000 in one individual savings account, his only account at an FDIC-insured bank. If the bank failed, how much of his deposit would be insured?
q.r: $250,000. The FDIC's standard coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category. Hector has one single-owner account, so $250,000 is insured and the remaining $60,000 is not. To protect the full amount, he could spread money across different insured banks or ownership categories. The $100,000 figure is an outdated limit, and the full $310,000 and $500,000 exceed the coverage limit.
w: $100,000 was the old coverage limit; today the standard FDIC limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
Hector's full $310,000 is more than the $250,000 standard limit, so the extra $60,000 in his single account would not be insured.
$500,000 is far above the $250,000 limit for one person's single-owner account at one bank, and Hector does not even have that much deposited.

q.pt: Compare Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) insurance coverage limits for checking and savings accounts offered at financial institutions
q.s: Which federal agency insures deposits at federally insured credit unions?
o: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA)
Federal Reserve System
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
q.r: National Credit Union Administration (NCUA). The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) charters and supervises federal credit unions and insures deposits at federally insured credit unions through its share insurance fund. The FDIC insures deposits at banks, not credit unions. The Federal Reserve is the nation's central bank, and the CFPB enforces consumer financial protection laws but does not insure deposits.
w: The FDIC does insure deposits, but at banks and savings associations; credit unions are covered by a separate fund run by the NCUA.
The Federal Reserve is the nation's central bank that manages monetary policy, and it does not insure deposits at credit unions.
The CFPB enforces consumer financial protection laws, but it does not insure the money members keep at credit unions.

q.pt: Compare Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) insurance coverage limits for checking and savings accounts offered at financial institutions
q.s: How does the standard insurance limit for a savings account at an NCUA-insured credit union compare with the standard limit at an FDIC-insured bank?
o: Credit union $125,000; bank $250,000
Credit union $250,000; bank $100,000
Both are $100,000 per depositor
Both are $250,000 per depositor
q.r: Both are $250,000 per depositor. The NCUA and FDIC provide the same standard coverage: $250,000 per depositor, per insured institution, for each account ownership category. Savers receive equal protection whether they choose a federally insured credit union or an insured bank. The credit union limit is not half the bank limit, and $100,000 was the standard limit for both before it was permanently raised to $250,000 in 2010.
w: Credit union coverage is not half of bank coverage; the NCUA matches the FDIC's $250,000 standard limit per depositor.
$250,000 is correct for credit unions, but banks are not limited to $100,000; both kinds of institutions share the same $250,000 standard limit.
$100,000 was the standard limit for both before it was permanently raised; today both banks and credit unions insure $250,000 per depositor.

q.pt: Identify types of accounts that do not offer deposit insurance
q.s: Which of the following is NOT protected by FDIC deposit insurance, even when it is purchased through an insured bank:
o: Stock mutual fund shares
A regular savings account
A certificate of deposit
A checking account
q.r: Stock mutual fund shares. Mutual fund shares are investments, not deposits, so they are not covered by FDIC insurance even if bought through a bank, and their value can fall. Stocks, bonds, annuities, life insurance and cryptocurrency are likewise uninsured. Savings accounts, certificates of deposit and checking accounts are deposit products covered up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
