Bodily injury liability coverage pays for injuries the policyholder causes to other people, including their medical bills, lost wages and legal costs, up to the policy limits. Collision pays to repair Tessa's own car, comprehensive covers damage to her car from causes such as theft or hail, and uninsured motorist coverage protects Tessa if a driver without insurance injures her.
w: Collision coverage pays to repair Tessa's own car after a crash, not the medical bills of the other driver who was injured.
Comprehensive covers damage to Tessa's own car from non-crash events like theft or hail, not injuries Tessa causes to other people.
Uninsured motorist coverage protects Tessa when an uninsured driver causes an injury to Tessa, not when Tessa is the one who injures someone else.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: While backing out of a driveway, Andre hits his neighbor's fence and damages it. Which auto insurance coverage pays to repair the fence?
o: Bodily injury liability
Property damage liability
Collision
Comprehensive
q.r: Property damage liability. Property damage liability pays for damage the policyholder causes to someone else's property, such as another car, a fence or a mailbox. Bodily injury liability covers injuries to other people, not property. Collision would pay to repair Andre's own car after the impact, and comprehensive covers damage to his car from non-collision events such as theft, fire or hail.
w: Bodily injury liability pays for injuries Andre causes to other people, but the fence is property, not a person.
Collision would pay to repair Andre's own car after hitting the fence, not the neighbor's fence.
Comprehensive covers non-crash damage to Andre's own car, such as theft or hail, not damage he causes to a neighbor's property.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: Noor's car slides on an icy road and hits a guardrail. No one else is involved. Which auto insurance coverage pays to repair Noor's car?
o: Comprehensive
Property damage liability
Collision
Bodily injury liability
q.r: Collision. Collision coverage pays to repair the policyholder's own vehicle when it strikes another vehicle or an object, such as a guardrail, regardless of who is at fault. Comprehensive covers damage from causes other than a collision, such as theft or hail. Property damage liability and bodily injury liability pay for harm the driver causes to other people and their property, not for repairs to the driver's own car.
w: Comprehensive covers damage from events other than a crash, like hail or theft, while Noor's car hit a guardrail.
Property damage liability pays for damage Noor causes to someone else's property, not for repairs to Noor's own car after hitting the guardrail.
Bodily injury liability pays for injuries Noor causes to other people, and no one else was involved in this crash.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: A hailstorm dents the hood and cracks the windshield of Caleb's parked car. Which auto insurance coverage pays for the repairs?
o: Comprehensive
Collision
Property damage liability
Uninsured motorist
q.r: Comprehensive. Comprehensive coverage pays for damage to the policyholder's car from events other than a collision, such as hail, fire, flood, theft, vandalism or hitting an animal. Collision applies when the car strikes another vehicle or object. Property damage liability pays for damage Caleb causes to others' property, and uninsured motorist coverage applies when a driver without insurance injures Caleb.
w: Collision applies when a car hits another vehicle or object, but Caleb's car was parked and damaged by hail.
Property damage liability pays for damage Caleb causes to other people's property, not for storm damage to Caleb's own parked car.
Uninsured motorist coverage helps when a driver without insurance injures Caleb, and a hailstorm involves no other driver.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: Rosa is injured when a driver with no auto insurance runs a stop sign and hits her car. Which part of Rosa's own policy helps pay for her injuries?
o: Comprehensive coverage
Property damage liability
Collision coverage
Uninsured motorist coverage
q.r: Uninsured motorist coverage. Uninsured motorist coverage protects the policyholder when an at-fault driver has no insurance to pay for the injuries they cause. Comprehensive covers non-collision damage such as theft or hail, property damage liability pays for damage Rosa causes to others, and collision pays to repair Rosa's car but not her medical bills.
w: Comprehensive covers non-crash damage to Rosa's car, such as theft or hail, not her injuries from being hit by another driver.
Property damage liability pays for damage Rosa causes to someone else's property, but she was the one hit.
Collision coverage may pay to repair Rosa's car, but it does not cover her medical bills from the injury.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: Auto liability insurance pays for
o: repairs to the policyholder's own car after any crash.
injuries and damage the policyholder causes to others.
the policyholder's car if it is stolen.
routine maintenance such as oil changes.
q.r: Injuries and damage the policyholder causes to others. Liability coverage protects the policyholder's finances when he or she is legally responsible for harm to others. Bodily injury liability pays for other people's injuries, and property damage liability pays for damage to their property, up to the policy limits. Repairs to the policyholder's own car after a crash are covered by collision, theft by comprehensive, and routine maintenance is not covered by insurance.
w: Repairs to the policyholder's own car after a crash are covered by collision, while liability pays for harm done to others.
A stolen car is covered by comprehensive, not liability, which pays when the policyholder harms other people or their property.
Routine maintenance like oil changes is a normal cost of owning a car, and no auto insurance coverage pays for it.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: A kitchen fire badly damages the walls and roof of the Okafor family's house. Which part of their homeowners policy pays to repair the structure?
o: Personal property coverage
Personal liability coverage
Dwelling coverage
Loss-of-use coverage
q.r: Dwelling coverage. Dwelling coverage pays to repair or rebuild the house itself, including walls, roof and built-in systems, after a covered loss such as fire. Personal property coverage pays for belongings such as furniture and clothing. Personal liability coverage pays when the homeowner is responsible for injuring someone or damaging their property, and loss-of-use coverage pays extra living costs while the home is repaired.
w: Personal property coverage pays for belongings such as furniture and clothing, not the walls and roof of the house.
Personal liability coverage pays when the Okafors injure someone or damage another person's property, not for fire damage to their own home.
Loss-of-use coverage pays extra living costs, like a hotel, while the house is being repaired, not for fixing the structure itself.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: How does auto insurance protect a policyholder financially after an at-fault crash?
o: It pays covered costs up to the limits of the policy
It prevents the injured driver from filing a lawsuit
It guarantees that the driver's premium will not increase
It pays for damage the driver chooses not to report
q.r: It pays covered costs up to the limits of the policy. Auto insurance transfers the financial risk of driving to the insurer. After an at-fault crash, the policy pays covered costs, such as other people's injuries, property damage and, with collision coverage, repairs to the driver's car, up to the policy limits. Insurance does not stop lawsuits, premiums often rise after an at-fault claim, and insurers pay only for losses that are reported as claims.
w: Insurance cannot stop an injured driver from suing; it helps pay legal defense and damages up to the policy limits.
Premiums often go up after an at-fault crash, so insurance does not guarantee the driver's cost will stay the same.
Insurers pay only for losses that are reported as claims, so damage the driver never reports will not be covered.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: A standard homeowners policy does not pay for damage caused by rising floodwater. A specific type of loss that a policy does not cover is called a(n)
o: deductible.
endorsement.
claim.
exclusion.
q.r: Exclusion. An exclusion is a loss, cause or item that an insurance policy specifically does not cover. Standard homeowners policies exclude flood and earthquake damage, so homeowners must buy separate coverage, such as flood insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program. A deductible is the amount paid before coverage begins, an endorsement adds or changes coverage, and a claim is a request for payment.
w: A deductible is the amount the policyholder pays before coverage starts, not a type of loss the policy refuses to cover.
An endorsement adds to or changes a policy's coverage, which is close to the opposite of a loss the policy leaves out.
A claim is a request for payment after a loss, not a type of loss the policy excludes.

q.pt: Explain what might happen to people who cannot afford to buy insurance for a particular risk or who choose not to buy it
q.s: Which of the following is a likely result for a family with no health insurance when one member needs emergency surgery:
o: Having the hospital cancel the bill automatically
Paying the entire bill and possibly taking on debt
Having the government pay the full cost automatically
Having the family's auto insurer pay the bill
q.r: Paying the entire bill and possibly taking on debt. People who go without insurance retain the full risk of a loss. A large medical bill can drain savings, lead to debt or collection actions and, in severe cases, contribute to bankruptcy. Hospitals do not automatically cancel bills, government programs such as Medicaid cover only people who qualify, and auto insurance covers medical costs only for injuries related to auto accidents.
w: Hospitals do not automatically cancel bills for uninsured patients, so the family would still owe the cost of the surgery.
Government programs such as Medicaid cover only people who qualify, so the government will not automatically pay this family's full bill.
Auto insurance covers medical costs only for injuries from car accidents, not emergency surgery unrelated to driving.

q.pt: Explain what might happen to people who cannot afford to buy insurance for a particular risk or who choose not to buy it
q.s: Ellis drives without auto insurance and causes a crash that injures another driver. What is Ellis most likely to face?
o: No financial responsibility because he had no policy
Payment of all costs by the other driver's insurer with no consequences
Personal responsibility for the other driver's costs plus legal penalties
Coverage from his parents' homeowners policy
q.r: Personal responsibility for the other driver's costs plus legal penalties. Without liability insurance, Ellis must pay the injured driver's medical bills, lost wages and other damages himself and may be sued. Driving uninsured also breaks the law in most states and can bring fines and license suspension. Lacking a policy does not remove responsibility. The other driver's insurer may pay its own customer and then seek repayment from Ellis, and homeowners policies exclude auto accidents.
w: Having no policy does not remove Ellis's responsibility; he still owes the injured driver's costs and broke the law by driving uninsured.
The other driver's insurer may pay its customer, but it can then seek repayment from Ellis, who also faces legal penalties.
Homeowners policies exclude auto accidents, so his parents' policy would not cover a crash Ellis caused.

q.pt: Explain what might happen to people who cannot afford to buy insurance for a particular risk or who choose not to buy it
q.s: People who choose not to buy insurance for a particular risk are
o: retaining the risk and paying any loss themselves.
transferring the risk to the government instead.
avoiding the risk entirely by staying uninsured.
sharing the risk with other policyholders.
q.r: Retaining the risk and paying any loss themselves. Choosing not to insure means retaining the risk: if a loss happens, the person pays the full cost out of savings, income or borrowing. The government does not take on that risk automatically. The person still faces the risk, so it is not avoided, and sharing risk with other policyholders through a pool of premiums happens only when a person buys insurance.
w: The government does not take on a person's risk just because that person skipped insurance; the person pays any loss.
Being uninsured does not make the risk go away; the person still faces it and simply has no protection.
Sharing risk with other policyholders happens only when someone buys insurance and joins a pool of premium payers.

q.pt: Describe ways in which having insurance can protect a person from financial loss
q.s: A formal request to an insurance company for payment of a covered loss is a(n)
o: premium.
policy.
endorsement.
claim.
q.r: Claim. A claim is the policyholder's request for the insurer to pay for a covered loss, such as a car crash or a stolen laptop. The insurer reviews the claim and pays according to the policy terms, after any deductible. A premium is the price paid for coverage, a policy is the written insurance contract, and an endorsement is a change or addition to a policy's coverage.
w: A premium is the price paid for insurance coverage, not a request for payment after a loss.
A policy is the written insurance contract itself, not the request to be paid for a covered loss.
An endorsement adds to or changes the coverage in a policy, while a request for payment after a covered loss is a claim.

q.pt: Discuss how people use insurance to share the risk of financial loss
q.s: An insurance company can afford to pay large claims to a few customers because it
o: borrows from the government after each loss.
pools premiums from many policyholders.
bills each claimant for the full cost later.
insures only people who never file claims.
q.r: Pools premiums from many policyholders. Insurance works by risk pooling. Many policyholders each pay a relatively small premium, and only a few of them will suffer a loss in a given year, so the pooled premiums are enough to pay those claims. Insurers do not depend on government loans, do not bill claimants for the full cost of their losses afterward, and cannot know in advance who will never file a claim.
w: Insurers do not depend on government loans; they pay claims mainly from the premiums many customers have paid in.
Claimants are not billed later for their losses; that would defeat the purpose of transferring risk to an insurer.
Insurers cannot know in advance who will never file a claim, so they rely on many people's premiums to cover the few who do.

q.pt: Discuss how people use insurance to share the risk of financial loss
q.s: Besides collecting premiums, how do insurance companies earn money that helps them pay claims?
o: By charging interest on the claims they pay
By receiving grants from the FDIC
By investing premiums until the money is needed for claims
By keeping each policyholder's deductible as profit
q.r: By investing premiums until the money is needed for claims. Insurers collect premiums before most claims are paid, so they invest that money, often in bonds and other securities, and use the investment earnings along with premiums to pay claims and operating costs. Claim payments are not loans, so no interest is charged. The FDIC insures bank deposits and does not fund insurers. A deductible is the policyholder's share of a loss, not money the insurer collects.
w: Claim payments are not loans, so insurers do not charge interest on the money they pay out for covered losses.
The FDIC insures deposits at banks and does not give grants to insurance companies, so it is not a source of money for paying claims.
A deductible is the policyholder's share of a loss that reduces what the insurer pays, not money the insurer collects as profit.

q.pt: Explain why insurers commonly charge higher premiums to people who are higher risk (e.g., auto insurance for drivers with a bad accident record, flood insurance for houses on the coastline)
q.s: Which driver would most likely pay the highest auto insurance premium?
o: A 17-year-old with two recent speeding tickets
A 45-year-old with a clean driving record
A 35-year-old who drives fewer than 5,000 miles a year
A 50-year-old who completed a defensive driving course
q.r: A 17-year-old with two recent speeding tickets. Insurers charge higher premiums to people who are more likely to file claims. Teen drivers have higher crash rates, and recent speeding tickets signal risky driving, so this driver presents the greatest risk. A clean record, low annual mileage and completing a defensive driving course all lower the likelihood of a claim and often qualify drivers for lower premiums.
w: A 45-year-old with a clean record is a lower risk to the insurer, so this driver would usually pay less than a teen with tickets.
Driving fewer than 5,000 miles a year lowers the chance of a crash, which often lowers the premium.
Completing a defensive driving course signals safer driving and often earns a discount, so this driver would likely pay less.

q.pt: Explain why insurers commonly charge higher premiums to people who are higher risk (e.g., auto insurance for drivers with a bad accident record, flood insurance for houses on the coastline)
q.s: Why does flood insurance on a house near the coastline usually cost more than flood insurance on a similar house far inland?
o: Coastal homeowners file fewer insurance claims
Insurance laws require equal premiums for all homes
Coastal houses are worth less than inland homes
The coastal house has a greater chance of a costly loss
q.r: The coastal house has a greater chance of a costly loss. Premiums reflect risk. Homes near the coastline face a higher chance of storm surge and flooding, so insurers expect to pay more and larger claims on them and charge higher premiums to cover that expected cost. Coastal owners do not file fewer claims, premiums are not required to be equal for all homes, and a lower home value would reduce the premium, not raise it.
w: Coastal homes actually face more storm and flood claims, not fewer, and an insurer would charge less, not more, if claims were rare.
Insurers are allowed to price by risk, so no law forces every home to pay the same flood premium regardless of how close it sits to the water.
A lower home value would usually mean a smaller possible payout and a lower premium, so it cannot explain why the coastal policy costs more.

q.pt: Explain why insurers commonly charge higher premiums to people who are higher risk (e.g., auto insurance for drivers with a bad accident record, flood insurance for houses on the coastline)
q.s: The process an insurer uses to evaluate an applicant's risk and decide whether to offer coverage, and at what premium, is called
o: claims adjusting.
underwriting.
diversification.
coinsurance.
q.r: Underwriting. Underwriting is how insurers assess risk. Underwriters review information such as driving records, a home's location and condition, or health history to decide whether to issue a policy and how much to charge. Claims adjusting is investigating and settling a claim after a loss. Diversification spreads investment risk, and coinsurance is a policyholder's percentage share of covered costs.
w: Claims adjusting happens after a loss, when the insurer checks and settles a claim, while the question describes judging an applicant before any policy is issued.
Diversification means spreading investments across many holdings to reduce investment risk, not reviewing one applicant to decide on coverage and price.
Coinsurance is the percentage of covered costs a policyholder pays after the deductible, not the insurer's process for deciding whether to offer a policy.

q.pt: Describe how each of the following out-of-pocket insurance costs affects policyholders: premium, deductible, copayment, and coinsurance
q.s: The amount a policyholder pays, usually monthly or yearly, to keep an insurance policy in force is the
o: deductible.
copayment.
premium.
coinsurance.
q.r: Premium. The premium is the price of insurance coverage. It must be paid on schedule, such as monthly, every six months or yearly, or the policy can be canceled. The deductible is paid only when a claim is made, a copayment is a flat fee for a specific service such as a doctor visit, and coinsurance is a percentage of covered costs shared after the deductible.
w: A deductible is paid only when the policyholder makes a claim, not on a regular schedule just to keep the policy active.
A copayment is a flat fee paid each time a specific service is used, like a doctor visit, not the regular charge that keeps coverage in force.
Coinsurance is a percentage share of a covered bill after the deductible, paid only when care is used, not the regular price of keeping the policy.

q.pt: Describe how each of the following out-of-pocket insurance costs affects policyholders: premium, deductible, copayment, and coinsurance
q.s: The amount a policyholder must pay out of pocket on a claim before the insurance company pays is the
o: deductible.
premium.
copayment.
policy limit.
q.r: Deductible. A deductible is the portion of a covered loss the policyholder pays before the insurer pays the rest. For example, with a $500 deductible and $2,000 of covered damage, the insurer pays $1,500. The premium is the regular price of the policy, a copayment is a flat fee for a service, and the policy limit is the most the insurer will pay.
w: The premium is the regular price paid to keep the policy active, whether or not a claim is ever filed, not the share paid on a claim first.
A copayment is a flat fee for a specific service, such as an office visit, rather than the amount paid on a claim before the insurer starts paying.
The policy limit is the most the insurer will pay on a claim, which is the ceiling on coverage rather than the amount the policyholder pays first.

q.pt: Describe how each of the following out-of-pocket insurance costs affects policyholders: premium, deductible, copayment, and coinsurance
q.s: Each time Ruby visits her doctor, she pays a flat $25 at the front desk, and her health plan pays the rest of the covered visit. The $25 is a
o: deductible.
premium.
coinsurance payment.
copayment.
q.r: Copayment. A copayment, or copay, is a fixed dollar amount the insured pays for a specific covered service, such as an office visit or prescription. A deductible is the amount paid before the plan starts sharing costs, a premium is the regular price of the coverage itself, and coinsurance is a percentage of the bill rather than a flat fee.
w: A deductible is the amount Ruby would pay before her plan shares costs, not a fixed fee she pays at every visit while the plan covers the rest.
A premium is the regular price of the health plan itself, paid whether or not Ruby sees a doctor, not a charge collected at the front desk.
Coinsurance is a percentage of the bill, so it would change with the cost of each visit instead of staying a flat $25 every time.

q.pt: Describe how each of the following out-of-pocket insurance costs affects policyholders: premium, deductible, copayment, and coinsurance
q.s: After meeting her deductible, Leila pays 20% of each covered medical bill and her insurer pays 80%. Leila's 20% share is called
o: a copayment.
coinsurance.
a premium.
an exclusion.
q.r: Coinsurance. Coinsurance is the percentage of covered costs the policyholder pays after the deductible has been met. In an 80/20 plan, the insurer pays 80% and the insured pays 20% until the out-of-pocket maximum is reached. A copayment is a flat dollar fee, a premium is the price of the policy, and an exclusion is a loss the policy does not cover.
w: A copayment is a flat dollar fee for a service, while Leila pays a percentage of each bill, which is what makes her share coinsurance.
A premium is the regular price Leila pays to keep her plan, not the 20% portion of each medical bill she pays after meeting the deductible.
An exclusion is a type of loss the policy does not cover at all, but Leila's bills are covered and simply split 80/20 with the insurer.

q.pt: Describe how each of the following out-of-pocket insurance costs affects policyholders: premium, deductible, copayment, and coinsurance
q.s: What is one purpose of a deductible in an insurance policy?
o: To pay the insurance agent's commission on the policy
To set the most the insurer will pay for a loss
To have the policyholder share in the cost of losses
To refund premiums to people who file no claims
q.r: To have the policyholder share in the cost of losses. Deductibles make policyholders pay the first part of each loss, which discourages small claims, encourages care, and cuts the insurer's processing costs, helping keep premiums lower. Agent commissions are paid by the insurer from premiums. The maximum the insurer will pay is the policy limit, and deductibles have nothing to do with refunding premiums.
w: Agent commissions are paid by the insurer out of premiums, so a deductible has nothing to do with paying the agent who sold the policy.
The most an insurer will pay is set by the policy limit, while the deductible is the first part of a loss the policyholder pays.
A deductible is money the policyholder pays toward a loss, not a refund of premiums for people who go a year without filing claims.

q.pt: Given information about premiums, deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance, calculate out-of-pocket costs for a hypothetical insured loss
q.s: Owen's auto policy has a $500 collision deductible. He backs into a pole, causing $2,300 of damage to his car. How much will the insurance company pay?
q.r: $1,800. The policyholder pays the deductible and the insurer pays the rest of the covered loss: $2,300 − $500 = $1,800. Owen pays $500 himself. $500 is Owen's share, not the insurer's, $2,300 ignores the deductible, and $2,800 wrongly adds the deductible to the damage instead of subtracting it.
w: $500 is the deductible, which is the part of the damage Owen pays himself, not the amount the insurance company pays.
$2,300 is the full repair cost, so this figure forgets to subtract Owen's $500 deductible before the insurer pays.
$2,800 comes from adding the $500 deductible to the $2,300 of damage, when the deductible should be subtracted from it.

q.pt: Given information about premiums, deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance, calculate out-of-pocket costs for a hypothetical insured loss
q.s: Grace's health plan has a $1,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance and a $5,000 out-of-pocket maximum. She has paid nothing toward her deductible this year when she receives a $6,000 covered hospital bill. How much does Grace pay?
q.r: $2,000. Grace first pays the $1,000 deductible, leaving $6,000 − $1,000 = $5,000. She then pays 20% coinsurance on that amount: 0.20 × $5,000 = $1,000. Her total is $1,000 + $1,000 = $2,000, which is below her $5,000 out-of-pocket maximum, so the cap does not apply. $1,200 applies 20% to the whole bill, $2,200 adds both, and $1,000 is only the deductible.
w: $1,000 is only Grace's deductible; it leaves out the 20% coinsurance she still owes on the remaining $5,000 of the bill.
$1,200 takes 20% of the whole $6,000 bill and skips the deductible, but coinsurance applies only to the $5,000 left after the deductible.
$2,200 adds the $1,000 deductible to 20% of the full $6,000, which charges coinsurance on money already covered by the deductible.

q.pt: Given information about premiums, deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance, calculate out-of-pocket costs for a hypothetical insured loss
q.s: Lena pays $150 a month in health insurance premiums. This year she also made four doctor visits with a $30 copayment each. What were Lena's total out-of-pocket insurance costs for the year?
q.r: $1,920. Annual premiums: $150 × 12 = $1,800. Copayments: $30 × 4 = $120. Total: $1,800 + $120 = $1,920. Premiums and copayments are both out-of-pocket costs of having insurance. $1,800 counts only premiums, $270 adds one month's premium to the copayments, and $1,950 adds an extra month's premium instead of the copayments.
w: $270 adds just one month's $150 premium to the $120 in copays, but Lena paid premiums for all twelve months of the year.
$1,800 counts a full year of premiums but leaves out the $120 Lena paid in copayments for her four doctor visits.
$1,950 adds a thirteenth $150 premium to the yearly $1,800 instead of adding the $120 in copayments from Lena's four visits.

q.pt: Describe types of purchases where extended warranties are typically offered as an add-on purchase
q.s: Which of the following purchases is most commonly offered with an extended warranty as an add-on:
o: A new laptop computer
A tank of gasoline
A week of groceries
A movie ticket
q.r: A new laptop computer. Extended warranties, also called service contracts, are typically offered on durable goods that can break down, such as electronics, appliances and vehicles. They pay for certain repairs after the manufacturer's warranty ends. Gasoline, groceries and movie tickets are consumed or used up quickly and have no mechanical parts that could fail later, so no warranty is offered on them.
w: Gasoline is used up within days and has no parts that can break later, so there is nothing for an extended repair contract to cover.
Groceries are eaten within a week, so there is no long-lasting product that might need repairs after a manufacturer's warranty ends.
A movie ticket is used once and then it is gone, so it is not a durable product that could need repairs covered by a warranty.

q.pt: Analyze the costs and benefits of purchasing an extended warranty on a specific item (e.g., cellphone, laptop, or vehicle)
q.s: A store offers Dante a $90 extended warranty on a $300 tablet. Which question would best help Dante decide whether the warranty is worth buying?
o: Will the warranty lower the tablet's purchase price?
Will the warranty make the tablet run faster?
Can the warranty be traded in on a future purchase?
How likely is the tablet to need a costly repair?
q.r: How likely is the tablet to need a costly repair? An extended warranty is worth buying only if its price is reasonable compared with the likelihood of failure and the cost of repair or replacement. Dante should also check what the manufacturer's warranty and his credit card already cover. A warranty adds to the purchase cost rather than lowering it, does not change the tablet's performance, and is not a store credit.
w: An extended warranty is an extra charge on top of the $300 price, so it adds to Dante's cost rather than lowering what the tablet costs.
A warranty only pays for certain repairs; it does nothing to change how fast the tablet runs, so speed is not part of the decision.
A warranty is a repair contract, not store credit, so whether it can be traded in has nothing to do with whether it is worth $90.

q.pt: Explain methods used by identity thieves to obtain personal information to commit a crime
q.s: Using another person's personal information, such as a Social Security number, without permission to commit fraud is called
o: phishing.
skimming.
identity theft.
insurance fraud.
q.r: Identity theft. Identity theft is the crime of using someone else's identifying information, such as a name, Social Security number or account number, to open accounts, make purchases, file tax returns or commit other fraud. Phishing and skimming are methods thieves use to steal that information, not the crime itself. Insurance fraud involves false claims or fake policies.
w: Phishing is one trick thieves use to steal personal information through fake messages, but the question asks for the crime of misusing that information.
Skimming is a way to steal card data with a hidden device, which is a method of gathering information rather than the fraud crime itself.
Insurance fraud means making false claims or selling fake policies, while the question describes using someone else's Social Security number without permission.

q.pt: Explain methods used by identity thieves to obtain personal information to commit a crime
q.s: Lauren receives an email that looks like it came from her bank. It asks her to click a link and confirm her account password. This is an example of
o: skimming.
phishing.
dumpster diving.
shoulder surfing.
q.r: Phishing. Phishing uses fake emails or websites that appear to come from trusted organizations to trick people into revealing passwords, account numbers or other personal information. Banks do not ask customers to confirm passwords through email links. Skimming copies card data with a hidden device, dumpster diving searches trash for documents, and shoulder surfing is watching someone enter a PIN or password.
w: Skimming copies card data with a hidden device on a card reader, but Lauren is being tricked by a fake email asking for her password.
Dumpster diving means digging through trash for papers with personal details, while Lauren's threat arrives as an email that pretends to be her bank.
Shoulder surfing is secretly watching someone type a PIN or password, but in this case no one is watching; a fake email asks Lauren directly.

q.pt: Explain methods used by identity thieves to obtain personal information to commit a crime
q.s: A thief attaches a hidden device to a gas pump's card reader to copy customers' card numbers. This method of stealing information is called
o: skimming.
phishing.
pretexting.
smishing.
q.r: Skimming. Skimming uses a device placed on or inside a card reader, often at gas pumps or ATMs, to capture card data that thieves use to make counterfeit cards or unauthorized purchases. Phishing uses fake emails, smishing uses fake text messages, and pretexting involves a thief pretending to be someone else, such as a bank employee, to talk a person into revealing information.
w: Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick people into giving up information, but this thief uses a hidden device on the gas pump instead.
Pretexting means pretending to be someone trustworthy to talk a person into sharing information, while this thief never speaks to the customers at all.
Smishing uses fake text messages to fool people, but this thief copies card numbers with a device attached to the pump's card reader.

q.pt: Explain methods used by identity thieves to obtain personal information to commit a crime
q.s: Which of the following behaviors most exposes a person's credit card information to theft:
o: Using a password manager for online accounts
Turning on purchase alerts for a card
Logging out after banking on a home network
Shopping online over unsecured public Wi-Fi
q.r: Shopping online over unsecured public Wi-Fi. Unsecured public Wi-Fi networks do not encrypt traffic, so thieves on the same network can intercept card numbers and login information. Sensitive transactions should use a secure network or a mobile data connection. Using a password manager, turning on alerts and logging out after banking on a secure home network all protect personal information rather than expose it.
w: A password manager helps people keep strong, different passwords for each account, so it protects card information rather than exposing it.
Purchase alerts tell the cardholder about each charge right away, which helps catch theft quickly rather than making the card easier to steal.
Logging out after banking on a home network is a safe habit that keeps others from using the session, so it does not expose card details.

q.pt: Explain methods used by identity thieves to obtain personal information to commit a crime
q.s: Identity thieves who search through trash for bank statements and preapproved credit offers are using a method called
o: phishing.
skimming.
dumpster diving.
smishing.
q.r: Dumpster diving. Dumpster diving is searching through garbage for discarded documents that contain names, account numbers or Social Security numbers. Shredding financial documents before throwing them away prevents it. Phishing and smishing use fake emails and text messages to trick people into sharing information, and skimming copies card data with a hidden device on a card reader.
w: Phishing uses fake emails to trick people into sharing information, while these thieves dig through trash for papers that were thrown away.
Skimming copies card numbers with a hidden device on a card reader, not by searching garbage for bank statements and credit offers.
Smishing is phishing by text message, but these thieves are not contacting anyone; they are pulling documents out of the trash.

q.pt: Explain methods used by identity thieves to obtain personal information to commit a crime
q.s: Which of the following is a warning sign of tax-related identity theft:
o: Your employer sends you a Form W-2 in late January
The IRS says a return was already filed in your name
Your tax refund arrives by direct deposit
You receive a reminder that taxes are due in mid-April
q.r: The IRS says a return was already filed in your name. When a thief files a fraudulent tax return with a stolen Social Security number to claim a refund, the real taxpayer's return is often rejected as a duplicate, or the IRS sends a notice about a return the person never filed. Receiving a W-2 from an employer, getting a refund by direct deposit and being reminded of the filing deadline are all normal parts of filing taxes.
w: Employers are required to send W-2 forms by the end of January, so getting one then is a normal part of tax season, not a sign of theft.
Many taxpayers choose to receive refunds by direct deposit, so a refund arriving that way is routine and does not suggest someone stole an identity.
Reminders that taxes are due in mid-April are normal and sent to everyone, so they do not signal that a thief has misused a Social Security number.

q.pt: List actions that an individual can take to protect personal identification information
q.s: What is the safest way to get rid of old bank statements and other documents that show account numbers?
o: Shred them with a cross-cut shredder
Tear them in half and recycle them
Throw them in the household trash
Store them in the car's glove compartment
q.r: Shred them with a cross-cut shredder. Shredding, especially with a cross-cut shredder that cuts paper into small pieces, makes documents unreadable and prevents dumpster diving. Torn pages can be taped back together, documents tossed in the trash or recycling can be retrieved by thieves, and a glove compartment is an easy target if the car is broken into or stolen.
w: Tearing pages in half leaves account numbers readable, and a thief could pull the pieces from recycling and tape them back together.
Documents tossed in household trash stay whole and readable, which is exactly what dumpster-diving thieves are hoping to find.
Keeping statements in the glove compartment does not get rid of them, and anyone who breaks into or steals the car could take them.

q.pt: List actions that an individual can take to protect personal identification information
q.s: Which of the following is the strongest password for an online banking account:
o: Password123
Jordan2009
qwertyuiopasdfghjkl
Vq7#t%m2Rz9&Lp4w
q.r: Vq7#t%m2Rz9&Lp4w. Strong passwords are long, random and mix uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols, and each account should have its own. The 16-character random string meets all of these tests. Password123 is a common password that thieves try first, Jordan2009 combines a name and year that could be guessed from social media, and qwertyuiopasdfghjkl is long but is simply two rows of keyboard keys, a pattern that cracking tools try early.
w: Password123 is one of the most common passwords, so it is among the first guesses thieves and cracking programs try.
Jordan2009 is just a name and a year, details a thief might find on social media, so it is much easier to guess than a random string.
This password is long, but it is only two rows of keys typed in order, a pattern that cracking tools check early, and it has no numbers or symbols.

q.pt: List actions that an individual can take to protect personal identification information
q.s: Which habit would help Carlos detect identity theft the earliest?
o: Checking his credit score once every five years
Writing his debit card PIN on the back of the card
Reviewing his account transactions every week
Waiting for his bank to call him about problems
q.r: Reviewing his account transactions every week. Regularly reviewing account activity and statements lets a person spot unauthorized charges quickly, often while they are small, and report them before losses grow. Checking credit only every five years would let fraud go unnoticed for years. Writing a PIN on the card invites theft, and banks do not catch every fraudulent transaction, so consumers must monitor their own accounts.
w: Checking credit only once every five years could let fraud go unnoticed for years, which is the opposite of catching identity theft early.
Writing a PIN on the card makes theft easier if the card is lost or stolen, and it does nothing to help Carlos notice fraud sooner.
Banks do not catch every fraudulent charge, so waiting for a call means Carlos might not learn about theft until the losses have grown.

q.pt: List actions that an individual can take to protect personal identification information
q.s: Turning on multifactor authentication for an online bank account protects the account because
o: it removes the need to create and remember a password.
a stolen password alone is not enough to log in.
it makes the account invisible to hackers online.
it insures the account balance against all losses.
q.r: A stolen password alone is not enough to log in. Multifactor authentication requires a second proof of identity, such as a code sent to the user's phone or a fingerprint, in addition to the password. Even if a thief obtains the password through phishing or a data breach, the thief cannot log in without that second factor. It does not replace passwords, hide accounts from hackers or insure balances against losses.
w: Multifactor authentication adds a second step on top of the password; the account still needs a password, so it does not remove that need.
Hackers can still find and target the account; multifactor authentication just stops them from logging in with a stolen password alone.
Multifactor authentication is a login security step, not insurance, so it does not promise to repay the account balance after any loss.

q.pt: Describe steps people can take to safely manage their finances using mobile technology
q.s: Which practice is safest when managing money on a smartphone?
o: Using the bank's official app with a screen lock
Banking over free public Wi-Fi at the airport
Downloading banking apps from links in text messages
Saving account passwords in a phone's notes app
q.r: Using the bank's official app with a screen lock. Downloading the bank's official app from a trusted app store avoids fake apps, and a screen lock keeps a lost or stolen phone from being used to reach the account. Turning on transaction alerts adds another layer by flagging suspicious activity quickly. Public Wi-Fi can expose login information, links in texts may install fake apps, and passwords saved in an unprotected notes app are easy to steal.
w: Free public Wi-Fi at an airport is often unsecured, so other people on the network may be able to capture banking logins and account details.
Links in text messages can lead to fake banking apps that steal logins, so banking apps should come only from a trusted app store.
A regular notes app is not protected like a password manager, so anyone who gets into the phone could read the saved passwords.

q.pt: Describe steps people can take to safely manage their finances using mobile technology
q.s: Tyler gets a text saying his package is delayed and he must enter his card number at a link to reschedule delivery. Tyler should
o: click the link and enter his card number quickly.
reply with his home address to confirm his identity.
forward the link to friends to see whether it is real.
ignore the link and contact the shipper directly.
q.r: Ignore the link and contact the shipper directly. This message has the signs of smishing, a phishing scam sent by text: urgency, a link and a request for card information. The safe response is not to click or reply, to delete or report the message, and to contact the company through its official website or app. Entering a card number gives it to thieves, replying confirms the number is active, and forwarding the link spreads the scam to others.
w: Clicking the link and entering his card number would hand Tyler's card information straight to the scammer who sent the fake delivery text.
Replying with his home address gives the scammer more personal information and confirms that Tyler's phone number is active.
Forwarding the link spreads the scam to friends and puts them at risk, and it does not tell Tyler whether the message is real.

q.pt: Explain the primary types of losses covered by auto, homeowner's, and renter's insurance policies
q.s: While their home is repaired after a storm, the Nguyen family must stay in a hotel. Which part of their homeowners policy helps pay the hotel bill?
o: Dwelling coverage
Personal liability coverage
Loss-of-use coverage
Medical payments coverage
q.r: Loss-of-use coverage. Loss-of-use coverage, also called additional living expenses, pays the extra costs of living elsewhere, such as hotel bills and restaurant meals, while a home damaged by a covered loss is being repaired. Dwelling coverage pays to repair the house itself. Personal liability coverage pays when the homeowner is responsible for harm to others, and medical payments coverage pays minor medical bills for guests hurt on the property.
w: Dwelling coverage pays to repair the damaged house itself, not the hotel costs the Nguyens face while they cannot live there.
Personal liability coverage pays when the homeowners are responsible for harming someone else, but the hotel bill comes from the storm damage to their own home.
Medical payments coverage pays small medical bills for guests hurt on the property, while the Nguyens need help with hotel costs during repairs.

q.pt: Explain the primary types of losses covered by auto, homeowner's, and renter's insurance policies
q.s: Jasmine rents an apartment. A burst pipe in her unit ruins her laptop, clothes and furniture. Which insurance would pay to replace her belongings?
o: Her renters insurance
Her landlord's property insurance
Her auto insurance
Her landlord's liability insurance
q.r: Her renters insurance. Renters insurance covers a tenant's personal property, along with liability and loss of use. The landlord's property policy covers the building, not tenants' belongings, and the landlord's liability coverage applies only when the landlord is responsible for harm to others. Auto insurance covers vehicles and driving, not household possessions, so Jasmine needs her own renters policy.
w: The landlord's property insurance protects the building itself, not the laptop, clothes and furniture that belong to Jasmine as a tenant.
Auto insurance covers cars and driving, so it would not pay for household belongings ruined by a burst pipe in Jasmine's apartment.
The landlord's liability insurance pays when the landlord is responsible for harm to others, and it does not replace a tenant's own belongings.

q.pt: Research the minimum auto liability insurance required in the state they live in and whether it is sufficient to cover typical auto accident financial losses
q.s: Kai's auto policy has bodily injury liability limits of $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident. Kai causes a crash that injures one person, whose medical bills total $65,000. How much will Kai's insurer pay for that person's injuries?
q.r: $50,000. The per-person limit caps what the insurer pays for any one injured person, so the insurer pays $50,000 even though the bills total $65,000. Kai is personally responsible for the remaining $15,000. The $100,000 per-accident limit is the most the insurer pays for all injured people in one crash combined. This is why low minimum limits may not cover the cost of a serious accident.
w: $15,000 is the amount left over after the insurer pays its limit, which is Kai's own share of the bills, not what the insurer pays.
$65,000 is the full medical bill, but the $50,000 per-person limit caps what the insurer will pay for any one injured person.
$100,000 is the per-accident limit for all injured people combined; with only one person hurt, the $50,000 per-person limit applies.

q.pt: Discuss the benefits and costs of purchasing life insurance on the primary earners in a household
q.s: Which type of life insurance covers a person for a set number of years at a relatively low premium and builds no cash value?
o: Whole life insurance
Universal life insurance
Disability insurance
Term life insurance
q.r: Term life insurance. Term life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries only if the insured dies during the policy term, such as 20 years. Because it provides pure protection with no savings feature, it costs much less than permanent coverage. Whole life and universal life are permanent policies that build cash value and charge higher premiums. Disability insurance replaces income, not life.
w: Whole life insurance is permanent coverage that builds cash value and costs more, so it does not match a low-cost policy for a set number of years.
Universal life insurance is a type of permanent coverage with a cash value account, not temporary coverage that builds no savings.
Disability insurance replaces part of a worker's income during an illness or injury, so it is not a type of life insurance at all.

q.pt: Discuss why most states mandate auto liability coverage
q.s: Most states require drivers to carry auto liability insurance mainly to
o: pay others for injuries and damage the driver causes.
pay for repairs to the at-fault driver's own car.
lower the price of new cars for all drivers.
fund the building and repair of roads.
q.r: Pay others for injuries and damage the driver causes. Mandatory liability coverage protects the public. Without it, people injured in crashes caused by drivers with no money or insurance could be left with medical bills and repair costs they did not cause. Liability coverage pays others, not the at-fault driver's car repairs, which require collision coverage. Insurance requirements do not lower car prices, and road projects are funded mainly by taxes such as fuel taxes.
w: Paying for the at-fault driver's own car is the job of collision coverage, while required liability insurance pays the people that driver harms.
Insurance rules do not change what car makers charge, so lowering new car prices is not why states require liability coverage.
Roads are paid for mainly through taxes such as fuel taxes, not through the liability insurance that drivers are required to buy.

q.pt: Explain why homeowners' insurance is required by a lender when a homeowner takes out a mortgage
q.s: Why does a mortgage lender require a homeowner to carry homeowners insurance?
o: Insurance lowers the interest rate the Federal Reserve sets
The house is collateral, so the lender wants it protected
Insurance pays the mortgage if the borrower loses a job
Insurance is needed to obtain a building permit
q.r: The house is collateral, so the lender wants it protected. A mortgage is secured by the home, so if the house were destroyed by fire or another covered loss, the lender's collateral would disappear. Requiring homeowners insurance ensures that money is available to repair or rebuild the home. The Federal Reserve's policy rates are not tied to one homeowner's insurance, homeowners insurance does not pay the mortgage after a job loss, and building permits do not require it.
w: The Federal Reserve sets interest rate policy for the whole economy, and one homeowner's insurance has no effect on the rates it sets.
Homeowners insurance pays for damage to the house, not mortgage payments after a job loss, so that is not why the lender requires it.
Building permits are for construction projects, not home purchases, so a lender's insurance requirement has nothing to do with getting a permit.

q.pt: Explain why taking a safe driving course can lower a driver's auto insurance premium
q.s: Why might completing a defensive driving course lower a driver's auto insurance premium?
o: The course provider pays part of the premium
The course replaces the need for liability coverage
Safer driving habits reduce the likelihood of a claim
The course automatically raises the deductible
q.r: Safer driving habits reduce the likelihood of a claim. Insurers base premiums on the expected cost of claims. Drivers who complete a defensive driving course are expected to drive more safely and be involved in fewer crashes, so many insurers offer a discount. Course providers do not pay premiums, the course does not replace legally required liability coverage, and deductibles are chosen by the policyholder rather than changed by taking a course.
w: Course providers charge drivers for the class; they do not pay any part of the driver's insurance premium afterward.
Liability coverage is required by law in most states, and a safety course cannot replace it, so the discount does not come from dropping coverage.
The policyholder picks the deductible, and finishing a driving course does not change it, so the lower premium is not caused by a deductible change.

q.pt: Discuss the pros and cons of buying an auto insurance policy with a higher deductible
q.s: Choosing an auto insurance policy with a higher deductible will usually
o: raise the premium and lower out-of-pocket costs.
lower both the premium and out-of-pocket costs.
have no effect on the premium the driver pays.
lower the premium but raise costs per claim.
q.r: Lower the premium but raise costs per claim. With a higher deductible, the policyholder agrees to pay more of each loss, so the insurer's expected cost falls and the premium drops. The tradeoff is that the policyholder pays more when a claim occurs, so a high deductible makes sense only for someone with enough savings to cover it. A higher deductible cannot lower both costs, and it does affect the premium.
w: A higher deductible does the reverse: the driver pays more when a claim happens, which is why the insurer can lower the premium.
A higher deductible lowers the premium, but the driver pays more out of pocket on each claim, so both costs cannot go down together.
The deductible is a major factor in pricing, so agreeing to pay more of each loss does change the premium, usually by lowering it.

q.pt: Compare disability coverage offered by individual policies, employee benefit plans, Social Security, workers' compensation, and temporary disability programs (in some states)
q.s: Marisol, a self-employed electrician, breaks her arm and cannot work for three months. Which type of insurance would replace part of her lost income?
o: Life insurance
Disability insurance
Renters insurance
Liability insurance
q.r: Disability insurance. Disability insurance replaces a portion of a worker's income when illness or injury prevents the person from working. Because Marisol is self-employed, she has no employer plan, so a private disability policy protects her paycheck. Life insurance pays beneficiaries after a death, renters insurance covers a tenant's belongings, and liability insurance pays for harm the policyholder causes to others.
w: Life insurance pays beneficiaries when the insured person dies, so it would not replace Marisol's income while she recovers from a broken arm.
Renters insurance covers a tenant's belongings and liability, not the paychecks Marisol loses while she is too injured to work.
Liability insurance pays for harm Marisol causes to other people, not for her own lost income when she is the one who is injured.

q.pt: Explain the steps an identity theft victim should take to limit losses and restore personal security
q.s: Rachel finds two credit card accounts on her credit report that she never opened. Which is the best action for Rachel to take right away?
o: Report it at IdentityTheft.gov and place a fraud alert
Wait to see whether the accounts close on their own
Pay the balances so her credit score is not hurt
Close her own checking account at her bank
q.r: Report it at IdentityTheft.gov and place a fraud alert. Identity theft victims should act quickly: report the theft to the Federal Trade Commission at IdentityTheft.gov to get a recovery plan, contact the companies that opened the accounts, and place a fraud alert or credit freeze with the credit bureaus to stop new accounts. Waiting lets losses grow, paying the thief's balances accepts debts Rachel does not owe, and closing her own checking account does nothing to stop the fraudulent credit cards.
w: Fraudulent accounts do not close on their own, and waiting gives the thief more time to run up charges in Rachel's name.
The thief opened these accounts, so Rachel does not owe the balances, and paying them would accept debt that is not hers.
Closing her checking account does nothing about the fake credit cards, which were opened with separate companies in Rachel's name.

q.pt: Explain the steps an identity theft victim should take to limit losses and restore personal security
q.s: Placing a credit freeze with the three major credit bureaus helps protect an identity theft victim because it
o: deletes negative information from the credit report.
closes every existing credit card and loan account.
blocks new creditors from viewing the credit report.
raises the victim's credit score right away.
q.r: Blocks new creditors from viewing the credit report. A credit freeze restricts access to a person's credit report. Because most lenders will not open an account without checking credit, a freeze blocks thieves from opening new accounts in the victim's name. It is free under federal law and can be lifted temporarily when the person applies for credit. A freeze does not remove accurate negative information, close existing accounts or change a credit score.
w: A credit freeze limits who can see the report, but it does not remove accurate negative information from it.
A freeze leaves existing accounts open and usable; it only stops new creditors from checking the report to open new accounts.
A freeze does not change the credit score; it simply blocks access to the report so thieves cannot open new accounts.

q.pt: Describe conditions under which individuals should and should not disclose their Social Security numbers, account numbers, or other sensitive information
q.s: In which situation is it generally appropriate to give out your Social Security number?
o: Answering a surprise phone call from someone claiming to be from the IRS
Filling out new-hire tax forms for a verified employer
Entering a giveaway posted on social media
Signing up for a store's loyalty card
q.r: Filling out new-hire tax forms for a verified employer. Employers need a new worker's Social Security number to report wages and withhold taxes, so sharing it on verified hiring paperwork is appropriate. The IRS usually contacts people by mail, and unexpected callers demanding personal information are a common scam. Social media giveaways and store loyalty programs have no legitimate need for a Social Security number, so giving it out there invites identity theft.
w: The IRS usually contacts people by mail, and surprise calls demanding a Social Security number are a common scam used by identity thieves.
A social media giveaway has no real need for a Social Security number, so sharing it there invites identity theft.
A store loyalty card only tracks purchases and rewards, so the store has no legitimate need for a Social Security number.

q.pt: Identify indicators that a person has accumulated too much debt
q.s: Money that a person has borrowed and is obligated to repay is called
o: equity.
assets.
income.
debt.
q.r: Debt. Debt is the total amount a person owes to lenders or others and must pay back, usually with interest. Lenders look at a person's existing debt before approving new credit because more debt reduces the ability to repay. Equity is the value of what a person owns outright, assets are items of value a person owns, and income is money received from work or investments.
w: Equity is the value a person owns outright after subtracting what is owed, which is the opposite of borrowed money that must be repaid.
Assets are things of value a person owns, like a car or savings, not money borrowed from someone else that must be paid back.
Income is money a person receives from work or investments, while the question describes money borrowed that must be repaid.

q.pt: Identify indicators that a person has accumulated too much debt
q.s: Which of the following is a warning sign that a person has accumulated too much debt:
o: Using one credit card to make the payment on another
Paying each credit card balance in full every month
Keeping an emergency fund equal to three months of expenses
Having a car loan with a fixed interest rate
q.r: Using one credit card to make the payment on another. Borrowing on one card to pay another means the person's income no longer covers debt payments, so the debt simply moves around and keeps growing. Paying card balances in full and keeping an emergency fund are signs of healthy credit habits. A fixed-rate car loan is a normal form of borrowing and does not by itself indicate a debt problem.
w: Paying each card in full every month means the person's income covers all charges, which is a sign of healthy credit use, not too much debt.
An emergency fund worth three months of expenses shows the person is saving well, not struggling under too much debt.
A fixed-rate car loan is a normal, predictable type of borrowing and does not by itself show that someone owes more than they can handle.

q.pt: Identify indicators that a person has accumulated too much debt
q.s: Over the past year, Devon's credit card balances have grown every month. He pays only the minimum due and has stopped saving so he can keep up. These facts indicate that Devon
o: is building a strong credit history.
has a low credit utilization rate.
is using credit to invest in his future.
has accumulated too much debt.
q.r: Has accumulated too much debt. Balances that keep rising, minimum-only payments and saving that stops so the bills can be paid are classic indicators of too much debt. Devon's payments barely cover interest, so his debt grows. Rising balances raise credit utilization rather than lowering it, which weakens rather than strengthens a credit history, and everyday card spending is not an investment in future earnings.
w: Rising balances and minimum-only payments make Devon look riskier to lenders, which weakens rather than builds a strong credit history.
Credit utilization goes up as balances grow, so Devon's rising card balances point to high utilization, not low.
Investing in the future means borrowing for something like education that raises earnings, while Devon is using cards to keep up with everyday bills.

q.pt: Identify indicators that a person has accumulated too much debt
q.s: Rosa's gross monthly income is $3,200. Each month she pays $380 on a car loan, $220 on a student loan and $200 in credit card minimums. What is Rosa's debt-to-income ratio?
q.r: 25%. The debt-to-income ratio equals total monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income. Rosa's payments total $380 + $220 + $200 = $800, and $800 ÷ $3,200 = 0.25, or 25%. The higher this ratio, the more of a person's income is already committed to debt, which is an indicator of too much debt. The other percentages come from adding the payments or dividing incorrectly.
w: 20% would mean only $640 a month in debt payments, but Rosa's three payments add up to $800, which is 25% of $3,200.
30% would mean $960 a month in payments, more than Rosa's actual $800 total, so the payments were added or divided incorrectly.
40% would mean $1,280 a month in payments, far more than the $800 Rosa actually pays on her car loan, student loan and cards.

q.pt: Identify indicators that a person has accumulated too much debt
q.s: What is the strongest evidence that a borrower owes more than he or she can repay?
o: Collection agencies are calling about overdue accounts
The borrower's credit card offers a grace period
The borrower recently paid off a car loan early
The borrower's credit report shows no late payments
q.r: Collection agencies are calling about overdue accounts. Calls from collection agencies mean that accounts are seriously past due, a strong indicator that the borrower owes more than he or she can repay. A grace period is a normal credit card feature. Paying off a loan early and having no late payments are signs that a borrower is managing debt responsibly, not that the borrower has too much of it.
w: A grace period is a normal credit card feature that gives time to pay without interest, so it says nothing about owing too much.
Paying off a car loan early shows the borrower has extra money for debt, which is the opposite of owing more than can be repaid.
A credit report with no late payments shows the borrower keeps up with bills, so it is evidence of managing debt well.

q.pt: Predict the possible consequences of having a lot of debt payments relative to income
q.s: Before taking out a loan to buy a used car, Malik should first
o: make sure his budget can cover the monthly payments.
ask for the largest loan the lender will approve.
choose the longest repayment period available.
open a store credit card to pay the down payment.
q.r: Make sure his budget can cover the monthly payments. Before borrowing, a person should plan realistically for repayment by confirming that the monthly payment fits his or her budget along with other expenses and savings. Borrowing the largest amount a lender will approve can create payments Malik cannot handle. The longest term raises total interest, and using a store card for the down payment simply adds more high-rate debt.
w: Borrowing the largest amount a lender will approve could create payments bigger than Malik's budget can handle, so it is not the first step.
The longest repayment period lowers each payment but adds more total interest, and it skips checking whether the payment fits Malik's budget.
Opening a store card for the down payment adds high-interest debt on top of the car loan instead of planning for repayment first.

q.pt: Predict the possible consequences of having a lot of debt payments relative to income
q.s: Imani's work hours were cut, and she realizes she cannot make next month's full student loan payment. What should Imani do first?
o: Stop making payments until her hours return
Take out a payday loan to cover the payment
Contact her lender to discuss changing her payment plan
File for bankruptcy so that the student loan is canceled
q.r: Contact her lender to discuss changing her payment plan. When a borrower cannot keep up with payments, the first step is to contact the lender before missing a payment. Many lenders, including student loan servicers, can change the payment plan or temporarily reduce payments. Simply stopping payments leads to late fees, default and credit damage. A payday loan adds expensive new debt, and bankruptcy is a last resort that rarely cancels student loans.
w: Simply stopping payments leads to late fees, default and credit damage, while contacting the lender first may let Imani adjust the plan.
A payday loan adds expensive new debt with very high fees, so it makes Imani's problem worse rather than fixing her reduced income.
Bankruptcy is a last resort and rarely cancels student loans, so it is not the right first move for one payment Imani cannot make.

q.pt: Predict the possible consequences of having a lot of debt payments relative to income
q.s: Carter forgot to make his credit card payment by this month's due date. The most likely immediate consequence is that Carter will
o: have the balance forgiven by the issuer.
have the account sent to a collection agency.
be required to repay the entire balance at once.
be charged a late fee.
q.r: Be charged a late fee. A late fee is the usual immediate consequence of missing a payment due date, and a payment that becomes 30 days past due can also be reported to the credit bureaus. Issuers do not forgive balances because a payment is late. Accounts are typically sent to collection agencies only after several months of nonpayment, and one late payment does not normally make the full balance due immediately.
w: Card issuers do not forgive balances because a payment is late; Carter still owes the full amount plus any added fees.
Accounts usually go to collections only after several months without payment, not right after one missed due date.
One late payment does not normally make the entire balance due at once; the usual immediate result is a fee.

q.pt: Predict the possible consequences of having a lot of debt payments relative to income
q.s: When a large share of a person's income goes to debt payments, the person is most likely to
o: qualify for lower interest rates on new loans.
see his or her credit score rise quickly.
earn interest on the outstanding balances.
have little money left to save or handle emergencies.
q.r: Have little money left to save or handle emergencies. This is the predictable consequence of high debt payments relative to income. Each dollar committed to payments cannot be saved, so an unexpected expense often leads to even more borrowing. A high debt load makes lenders see the person as riskier, so new rates rise rather than fall, credit scores do not improve quickly, and borrowers pay interest rather than earn it.
w: Lenders see someone with a large share of income going to debt as riskier, so new loan rates tend to go up, not down.
Heavy debt payments do not make a credit score climb quickly, and high balances can actually hold a score down.
Borrowers pay interest on what they owe; they do not earn it, so outstanding balances cost the person money rather than making any.

q.pt: Predict the possible consequences of having a lot of debt payments relative to income
q.s: Lena's monthly debt payments already equal 45% of her income. If she applies for a new auto loan, the lender will most likely
o: charge a higher rate or deny the loan.
approve a larger loan at a lower rate.
ignore her current debts and consider only income.
require her to close her savings account first.
q.r: Charge a higher rate or deny the loan. A lender judges whether a borrower can repay. When 45% of Lena's income already goes to debt payments, adding another payment increases the risk that she will fall behind, so the lender is likely to charge a higher rate to cover that risk or to deny the application. Lenders do not reward heavy debt with better terms, they do consider existing debts, and they do not require closing savings.
w: With 45% of Lena's income already going to debt, a lender sees more risk, so it would not reward her with a bigger loan at a lower rate.
Lenders look closely at existing debt payments to judge whether a borrower can repay, so they would not ignore Lena's current debts.
Lenders do not require borrowers to close savings accounts, and savings actually make a borrower look more able to repay.

q.pt: Predict the possible consequences of having a lot of debt payments relative to income
q.s: Mason uses his credit cards to cover everyday expenses each month and pays only the minimum amounts due. Over time, what is the most likely result?
o: His credit card APRs will steadily decrease
His total debt and interest charges will keep growing
His balances will be paid off within a few months
His credit utilization rate will fall
q.r: His total debt and interest charges will keep growing. When new charges are added each month and only the minimums are paid, the balance grows and interest is charged on a larger amount, so total debt and interest charges keep growing. Card issuers do not lower APRs because of minimum payments. Minimum payments can take years to pay off a balance, and rising balances raise, rather than lower, the credit utilization rate.
w: Card issuers do not lower APRs because someone pays only the minimum, so Mason's rates would not steadily drop.
Minimum payments can take years to pay off a balance, and Mason keeps adding new charges, so his balances will not disappear in months.
Credit utilization rises as balances grow compared with credit limits, so Mason's growing balances would push it up, not down.

q.pt: Identify the types of information contained in a credit report
q.s: Which of the following types of information appears on a person's credit report:
o: A record of on-time and late payments
The person's annual salary
The person's checking account balance
The person's race and religion
q.r: A record of on-time and late payments. A credit report contains a person's payment history, showing which bills were paid on time and which were late, along with accounts, balances, inquiries and certain public records such as bankruptcies. Credit reports do not list a person's salary or bank account balances. Race and religion are never included, and federal law prohibits lenders from using them in credit decisions.
w: A credit report tracks borrowing and repayment, not how much a person earns, so annual salary does not appear on it.
Checking account balances are deposits rather than borrowing, so they are not listed on a credit report.
Race and religion are never part of a credit report, and federal law bars lenders from using them in credit decisions.

q.pt: Identify the types of information contained in a credit report
q.s: Why should consumers look for unfamiliar accounts when they review their credit reports?
o: Unfamiliar accounts may be a sign of identity theft
Unfamiliar accounts automatically raise credit scores
Lenders require consumers to close unused accounts
Credit bureaus reward consumers for finding errors
q.r: Unfamiliar accounts may be a sign of identity theft. An account the consumer never opened may mean that someone has used his or her personal information to borrow, which is identity theft or fraud. Spotting it early lets the consumer dispute the account and limit the damage. Unknown accounts, especially unpaid ones, can lower a score rather than raise it. Lenders do not require closing unused accounts, and credit bureaus do not pay rewards for reporting errors.
w: Unfamiliar accounts, especially unpaid ones a thief opened, are more likely to hurt a credit score than to raise it.
Lenders do not require consumers to close unused accounts, so that is not the reason to watch for accounts you do not recognize.
Credit bureaus do not pay rewards for finding errors; the real reason to look is to catch fraud or identity theft early.

q.pt: Identify the types of information contained in a credit report
q.s: A credit report includes a list of inquiries. Each inquiry shows
o: how much money the person has in savings.
that the person disputed an error on the report.
the person's current credit score.
that a business requested the person's credit report.
q.r: That a business requested the person's credit report. An inquiry is a record that a business, such as a lender reviewing a credit application, requested the person's credit report. Inquiries from applying for credit can slightly lower a credit score. Savings balances do not appear on credit reports, disputes are handled separately from inquiries, and a credit score is calculated from the report rather than listed as an inquiry.
w: Savings balances are not part of a credit report at all, so an inquiry cannot show how much money the person has saved.
Disputes are handled as a separate process, while an inquiry is simply a record that a business asked to see the report.
A credit score is calculated from the report, but an inquiry only records who requested the report, not the score itself.

q.pt: Identify the types of information contained in a credit report
q.s: Before approving a car loan, Northbrook Credit Union reviews a document showing Ava's open accounts, balances, payment history and an old account sent to collections. The credit union is reviewing Ava's
o: income statement.
bank statement.
monthly budget.
credit report.
q.r: Credit report. A credit report lists a person's credit accounts, balances, payment history, collection accounts and public records, and lenders use it to judge the risk of lending. An income statement summarizes revenue and expenses. A bank statement shows deposits and withdrawals in one account. A monthly budget is a personal spending plan and does not show borrowing history.
w: An income statement summarizes revenue and expenses, not a list of Ava's accounts, payment history and a collection account.
A bank statement shows deposits and withdrawals in one account, not Ava's borrowing history across several accounts.
A monthly budget is a personal spending plan, while the credit union is reviewing a record of Ava's accounts, balances, payments and collections.

q.pt: Identify the types of information contained in a credit report
q.s: For each credit card and loan a person has, a credit report typically lists the account's
o: interest earned and dividends paid on the account.
purchase receipts and the names of the stores where they were made.
credit limit or loan amount, balance and payment status.
spending goals and monthly budget categories.
q.r: Credit limit or loan amount, balance and payment status. A credit report lists each credit account with its credit limit or original loan amount, the current balance and whether payments are current or late. This tells lenders how much a person owes and how reliably he or she repays. Interest earned and dividends relate to savings and investments, individual purchase receipts are not reported, and budget goals are personal plans that credit bureaus never collect.
w: Interest earned and dividends come from savings and investments, not from credit cards and loans, so they are not part of a credit report.
Credit reports show account totals and payment status, not individual receipts or the names of stores where each purchase was made.
Spending goals and budget categories are personal plans that credit bureaus never collect, so they do not appear on a credit report.

q.pt: Discuss how a borrower's credit history can impact their borrowing costs
q.s: Jordan has a long record of on-time payments. Sam has several late payments and an account in collections. If both apply for the same auto loan, the lender will most likely
o: offer both borrowers the same interest rate.
offer Sam a higher interest rate than Jordan.
offer Jordan a higher interest rate than Sam.
offer Sam a lower interest rate to help him rebuild.
q.r: Offer Sam a higher interest rate than Jordan. Lenders charge different interest rates based on the borrower's risk of nonpayment, which they judge from the credit report.
