Sam's late payments and collection account make him the riskier borrower, so he will likely be offered a higher rate, or be denied. Lenders do not charge every applicant the same rate, and they do not reward a weak history with a lower rate or penalize a strong one.
w: Lenders set rates based on each borrower's risk, so Sam's late payments and collection account would not earn the same rate as Jordan's clean record.
Jordan's long record of on-time payments makes Jordan the safer borrower, so Jordan would get the lower rate, not the higher one.
Lenders do not reward a weak credit history with a lower rate; they charge riskier borrowers like Sam more to cover the chance of nonpayment.

q.pt: Discuss how a borrower's credit history can impact their borrowing costs
q.s: Why do lenders charge higher interest rates to borrowers with poor credit histories?
o: The lender faces a greater risk of not being repaid
Borrowers with poor credit usually request larger loans
Higher rates help borrowers repay their loans faster
Processing these applications takes the lender longer
q.r: The lender faces a greater risk of not being repaid. A poor credit history suggests a greater chance that the borrower will pay late or not at all, so the lender charges a higher rate to make up for that added risk. This practice is called risk-based pricing. Poor credit does not mean a borrower requests larger loans, higher rates make repayment harder rather than faster, and processing time is not the reason rates differ.
w: Poor credit does not mean a borrower asks for a larger loan; the higher rate makes up for the greater chance of nonpayment.
Higher rates add to what a borrower owes each month, which makes repayment harder, not faster.
Processing time is not why rates differ; lenders charge more because a poor history suggests a higher chance the loan will not be repaid.

q.pt: Discuss how a borrower's credit history can impact their borrowing costs
q.s: Why should a person check his or her credit report at least once a year?
o: Credit reports expire unless the consumer reviews them
Reviewing the report raises the person's credit score
Lenders cannot see a report the consumer has not reviewed
Errors in the report could raise the person's cost of borrowing
q.r: Errors in the report could raise the person's cost of borrowing. Lenders set interest rates using information in the credit report, so a mistake such as a late payment that never happened could lead to higher rates or a denied application. Reviewing the report regularly lets the person find and dispute errors. Credit reports do not expire, checking your own report neither raises nor lowers your score, and lenders can access reports whether or not the consumer has reviewed them.
w: Credit reports do not expire when they go unreviewed; the real reason to check is to find mistakes that could raise borrowing costs.
Checking your own credit report does not raise your score, though finding and fixing errors on it might help.
Lenders can request a person's credit report whether or not the consumer has ever looked at it.

q.pt: Discuss how a borrower's credit history can impact their borrowing costs
q.s: Lenders often use a(n) __________, a number typically ranging from 300 to 850, to summarize a borrower's credit history and help set loan rates.
o: credit limit.
annual percentage rate.
credit score.
credit utilization rate.
q.r: Credit score. A credit score is a number calculated from the information in a person's credit report; the widely used FICO score ranges from 300 to 850. Higher scores signal lower risk and usually earn lower interest rates. A credit limit is the most a cardholder may borrow, the annual percentage rate is the yearly cost of credit, and the credit utilization rate is the share of available credit in use.
w: A credit limit is the most a cardholder can borrow, a dollar amount set by the lender, not a 300-to-850 number summarizing credit history.
The annual percentage rate is the yearly cost of borrowing shown as a percentage, not a score that summarizes a borrower's history.
The credit utilization rate is the percentage of available credit being used; it affects a score but is not the 300-to-850 number itself.

q.pt: Discuss how a borrower's credit history can impact their borrowing costs
q.s: Two borrowers each take out a one-year, $10,000 loan with simple interest. The borrower with excellent credit is charged 5%, and the borrower with poor credit is charged 11%. How much more interest does the borrower with poor credit pay?
q.r: $600. Simple interest equals principal times rate times time. The borrower with excellent credit pays $10,000 × 0.05 × 1 = $500, and the borrower with poor credit pays $10,000 × 0.11 × 1 = $1,100. The difference is $1,100 − $500 = $600. A weaker credit history raises borrowing costs. $500 and $1,100 are each borrower's total interest, and $60 misplaces the decimal.
w: $60 misplaces the decimal point; the real difference between $1,100 and $500 in interest is $600, not $60.
$500 is the interest the excellent-credit borrower pays, not how much more the poor-credit borrower pays.
$1,100 is the poor-credit borrower's total interest; you still need to subtract the other borrower's $500 to find the difference.

q.pt: Discuss how a borrower's credit history can impact their borrowing costs
q.s: Which action would most likely help a young adult build a credit history that leads to lower borrowing costs later?
o: Opening several new credit cards in the same month to raise credit limits
Paying bills only after the lender calls with a reminder
Paying cash for every purchase and never using any credit
Using a credit card for small purchases and paying it in full monthly
q.r: Using a credit card for small purchases and paying it in full monthly. Using a card lightly and paying the full balance every month builds a record of on-time payments and low balances, which leads to a strong credit history and lower rates later. Opening many accounts at once creates several hard inquiries and looks risky. Waiting for reminder calls usually means late payments, and using only cash builds no credit history for lenders to evaluate.
w: Opening several cards in one month creates many hard inquiries and makes a new borrower look risky, which can lower a score.
Waiting for a reminder call usually means paying late, and late payments damage the payment history that lenders rely on most.
Paying only with cash avoids debt, but it builds no credit record at all, so lenders have no history to judge.

q.pt: Explain why credit card interest rates tend to be higher than rates for secured loans, such as automobile loans
q.s: Credit cards usually charge higher interest rates than auto loans because credit card balances are
o: unsecured, so the lender has no collateral.
backed by the borrower's home.
insured by the federal government.
repaid in fixed monthly installments.
q.r: Unsecured, so the lender has no collateral. Credit card balances are unsecured: no property backs the debt, so if the cardholder stops paying, the issuer has nothing to take back and must rely on collections. That higher risk leads to higher rates. An auto loan is secured by the car. Card balances are not backed by a home, are not insured by the federal government and are revolving rather than repaid in fixed installments.
w: Credit card balances are not tied to the borrower's home; loans backed by a home, like mortgages, usually have lower rates because of that security.
The federal government does not insure credit card balances, so that cannot explain why card rates are higher than auto loan rates.
Credit cards are revolving credit that can be carried month to month, while it is the auto loan that is repaid in fixed installments.

q.pt: Explain why credit card interest rates tend to be higher than rates for secured loans, such as automobile loans
q.s: What is the main drawback of carrying a balance on a credit card from month to month?
o: The balance is added to the cardholder's income taxes
Interest is charged on the unpaid balance
The card is automatically converted to a debit card
The cardholder must start paying an annual membership fee
q.r: Interest is charged on the unpaid balance. When a cardholder does not pay the full statement balance, the issuer charges interest on the unpaid amount, and credit card rates are typically higher than rates on other loans. That interest makes every purchase cost more. Card balances have nothing to do with income taxes, a card does not become a debit card, and annual fees are set in the card agreement rather than triggered by carrying a balance.
w: Credit card balances have nothing to do with income taxes; the real cost of carrying a balance is the interest charged on it.
Carrying a balance does not turn a credit card into a debit card; the card stays a credit card and keeps charging interest.
Annual fees are set in the card agreement whether or not a balance is carried, so they are not the drawback of carrying one.

q.pt: Explain why credit card interest rates tend to be higher than rates for secured loans, such as automobile loans
q.s: Dana's bank charges 6% on auto loans and 23% on credit cards. Besides the lack of collateral, which factor helps explain the higher credit card rate?
o: The federal government requires card rates to be higher
Auto lenders earn most of their profit from annual fees
Card issuers lose more to balances that are never repaid
Card balances must be repaid within one month
q.r: Card issuers lose more to balances that are never repaid. A larger share of credit card balances ends in default and is written off than auto loan balances, partly because the issuer has no collateral to sell to recover the debt. Issuers charge higher rates to cover those losses. The federal government does not set card rates, auto lenders earn mainly interest rather than annual fees, and card balances can be carried from month to month.
w: The federal government does not set credit card rates, so it cannot explain why Dana's bank charges 23% on cards and 6% on auto loans.
Auto lenders earn mainly from interest, not annual fees, and that has nothing to do with why card rates are higher.
Card balances can be carried from month to month, so requiring repayment within one month is not true and would not explain higher rates.

q.pt: Explain why credit card interest rates tend to be higher than rates for secured loans, such as automobile loans
q.s: For the same borrower, which type of credit typically charges the highest interest rate?
o: Home mortgage
New car loan
Home equity loan
Credit card
q.r: Credit card. Credit cards typically charge higher interest rates than other common types of consumer loans because card balances are unsecured. A home mortgage and a home equity loan are secured by the house, and a car loan is secured by the vehicle, so the lender can claim the property if the borrower does not repay. That lower risk lets lenders offer lower rates on those loans.
w: A home mortgage is secured by the house, so the lender can take the home if the loan is not repaid, which keeps its rate lower.
A new car loan is secured by the vehicle, which lowers the lender's risk and usually earns a lower rate than a credit card.
A home equity loan uses the house as collateral, so it is less risky to the lender and typically has a lower rate than credit cards.

q.pt: Describe how a credit card user can minimize interest charges on their credit card purchases
q.s: Noor has a car loan at 7% APR, a credit card balance at 24% APR and a federal student loan at 5% APR. If she has extra money to pay down debt, she should first pay down the
o: credit card balance.
car loan.
student loan.
loan with the longest term.
q.r: Credit card balance. Putting extra money toward the debt with the highest APR saves the most interest, and that is usually the credit card. Each extra dollar on Noor's 24% card avoids far more interest than a dollar applied to the 7% car loan or the 5% student loan. The length of a loan's term does not determine which debt costs the most to carry.
w: The car loan's 7% APR is much lower than the card's 24%, so extra money there saves Noor far less interest.
At 5%, the student loan is Noor's cheapest debt, so paying it down first would save the least interest of all.
A loan's length does not decide what it costs to carry; the APR does, and the 24% card is Noor's most expensive debt.

q.pt: Describe how a credit card user can minimize interest charges on their credit card purchases
q.s: The best way to avoid paying interest on credit card purchases is to
o: pay the minimum payment every month.
pay the full statement balance by the due date.
make the payment shortly after the due date.
use the card only for large purchases.
q.r: Pay the full statement balance by the due date. Paying the full statement balance by the due date means no balance is carried forward, so the grace period applies and no interest is charged on those purchases. Paying only the minimum leaves a balance that is charged interest. A payment after the due date brings a late fee and interest, and the size of a purchase does not affect whether interest is charged.
w: Paying only the minimum leaves part of the balance unpaid, and that remaining balance is charged interest.
A payment after the due date usually brings a late fee and interest, so it is the opposite of a way to avoid interest.
Interest depends on whether the balance is paid in full on time, not on whether purchases are large or small.

q.pt: Describe how a credit card user can minimize interest charges on their credit card purchases
q.s: Jace and Omar each have a $2,000 balance on credit cards with the same APR and make no new purchases. Jace pays $50 a month, and Omar pays $200 a month. Which statement is true?
o: Jace will pay less total interest than Omar
Both will pay the same total interest
Omar will pay less total interest than Jace
Omar will be charged a higher APR than Jace
q.r: Omar will pay less total interest than Jace. Interest is charged on the balance that remains each month. Omar's larger payments shrink the balance faster, so less interest builds up and the debt is paid off sooner, for less total interest. Jace's small payments keep the balance high for much longer, so Jace pays more interest overall. The two cards have the same APR, and the payment amount does not change the rate.
w: Jace's $50 payments keep that balance high for much longer, so more interest builds up and Jace pays more total interest than Omar, not less.
The two pay at very different speeds, so interest is charged on larger balances for longer on Jace's card, making their totals differ.
Both cards have the same APR, and the size of a payment does not change the rate Omar is charged.

q.pt: Describe how a credit card user can minimize interest charges on their credit card purchases
q.s: Mara's credit card has a 25-day grace period, but she carried part of last month's balance forward. On most cards, interest on her new purchases this month will
o: be waived because of the grace period.
start building from the date of each purchase.
be charged only if she takes a cash advance.
be added only after the 25 days have passed.
q.r: Start building from the date of each purchase. On most cards, the grace period applies only when the previous statement balance was paid in full. Because Mara carried a balance forward, she loses the grace period, so new purchases begin collecting interest right away until she again pays the full balance. The grace period does not waive this interest, interest is not limited to cash advances, and it does not wait until 25 days have passed.
w: The grace period applies only when last month's balance was paid in full, so Mara's carried balance cancels it for new purchases.
Interest is not limited to cash advances; because Mara carried a balance, her regular purchases also start building interest.
Once Mara carried a balance, she lost the grace period, so interest does not wait 25 days; it starts on each purchase date.

q.pt: Identify financial institutions and businesses that offer consumer credit
q.s: Hollis wants to open a checking account and apply for a personal loan at the same institution. Hollis should go to a(n)
o: investment bank.
credit bureau.
retail bank.
insurance company.
q.r: Retail bank. A retail bank serves individual consumers with deposit accounts such as checking and savings, and it offers consumer credit such as personal loans, auto loans and credit cards. An investment bank helps businesses and governments raise money by issuing stocks and bonds. A credit bureau compiles credit reports but does not lend, and an insurance company sells protection against financial loss rather than checking accounts.
w: An investment bank helps businesses and governments raise money by selling stocks and bonds, not checking accounts and personal loans for individuals.
A credit bureau collects credit information and sells reports, but it does not open checking accounts or make loans.
An insurance company sells protection against financial losses, so Hollis could not open a checking account or get a personal loan there.

q.pt: Identify financial institutions and businesses that offer consumer credit
q.s: Which financial institution is owned by its members and often offers lower loan rates and fees than for-profit lenders?
o: Investment bank
Consumer finance company
Pawnshop
Credit union
q.r: Credit union. A credit union is a not-for-profit financial institution owned by its members. Because it returns earnings to members rather than to outside stockholders, it often offers lower loan rates and fees. An investment bank does not make everyday consumer loans. Consumer finance companies and pawnshops are for-profit lenders that usually charge higher rates, often to borrowers who have weaker credit or need cash quickly.
w: An investment bank serves businesses and governments raising money, and it is not owned by members or focused on everyday consumer loans.
Consumer finance companies are for-profit lenders that usually charge higher rates, not member-owned institutions offering lower ones.
A pawnshop is a for-profit business that lends against personal items, usually at high rates, and is not owned by its customers.

q.pt: Identify financial institutions and businesses that offer consumer credit
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a business that offers consumer credit:
o: A credit bureau that compiles and sells consumer credit reports
A furniture store that issues its own store credit card
A stock exchange that lists public companies
A tax preparer that files income tax returns
q.r: A furniture store that issues its own store credit card. Consumer credit is offered by banks and credit unions and also by businesses such as retailers and car dealers. A furniture store that issues its own store card lets customers buy now and pay later with interest. A credit bureau collects credit information but does not lend. A stock exchange is a marketplace for securities, and a tax preparer provides a service rather than credit.
w: A credit bureau gathers and sells credit information about consumers, but it does not lend money or let anyone buy on credit.
A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares of companies are bought and sold, not a business that lends to consumers.
A tax preparer is paid to file tax returns, which is a service, not a way for consumers to buy now and pay later.

q.pt: Compare lenders based on type of credit offered, interest rates, and fees
q.s: Consumer finance companies often lend to borrowers with weak credit histories. Compared with banks and credit unions, finance companies usually charge
o: lower interest rates and fees.
no interest on short-term loans.
the same rates, which federal law sets.
higher interest rates and fees.
q.r: Higher interest rates and fees. Interest rates and fees vary by type of lender. Consumer finance companies take on riskier borrowers, so they usually charge higher rates and fees than banks and credit unions to cover the greater chance of nonpayment. They do not offer lower costs or interest-free loans as a rule, and federal law does not set one uniform rate that every lender must charge.
w: Finance companies lend to riskier borrowers, so they usually charge more than banks and credit unions, not less.
Finance companies make money from the interest and fees they charge, so they do not generally offer interest-free short-term loans.
Federal law does not set one rate for every lender; rates and fees vary by lender and by the borrower's risk.

q.pt: Compare lenders based on type of credit offered, interest rates, and fees
q.s: When comparing loan offers from different lenders, which information gives a borrower the most complete picture of each loan's cost?
o: The APR, fees and repayment terms
The monthly payment the lender quotes
The advertised introductory interest rate
The distance to each lender's nearest office
q.r: The APR, fees and repayment terms. Together, the APR, fees and repayment terms show what each loan will really cost over its life. A low monthly payment can hide a long term that adds interest, and an advertised introductory rate may leave out fees or rise after the promotional period ends. The distance to a lender's office says nothing about the cost of borrowing, so it does not help the borrower compare offers.
w: A low monthly payment can hide a long term that adds much more interest, so the payment alone does not show a loan's full cost.
An introductory rate may leave out fees and can rise after the promotion ends, so it gives only part of a loan's cost.
How far away a lender's office is says nothing about how much the loan will cost, so it does not help compare offers.

q.pt: Explain how market conditions impact interest rates
q.s: When interest rates throughout the economy fall, consumers are most likely to
o: borrow less and save more.
face higher payments on new loans.
borrow and spend more.
stop using credit cards.
q.r: Borrow and spend more. Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, so consumers tend to take out more loans, buy homes and cars, and spend more. Market conditions affect the rates lenders charge. Borrowing less and saving more is the typical response to higher rates. New loans made at lower rates have lower, not higher, payments, and falling rates do not cause consumers to stop using credit cards.
w: Borrowing less and saving more is the usual response to higher rates; when rates fall, saving earns less and borrowing gets cheaper, so consumers tend to do the reverse.
New loans made when rates are lower come with lower payments, so falling rates would not raise what borrowers pay.
Lower rates make borrowing cheaper, which encourages more credit use, so consumers would not stop using credit cards.

q.pt: Explain how market conditions impact interest rates
q.s: The Federal Reserve raises its target interest rate to slow inflation. What will most likely happen to the rates banks charge on new car loans?
o: They will tend to decrease
They will tend to increase
They will stay the same because banks set rates independently
They will change only for loans that already exist
q.r: They will tend to increase. When the Federal Reserve raises its target rate, banks' own cost of borrowing rises, and they pass that cost on through higher rates on new loans, including car loans and credit cards. Rates move with market conditions, so they would not fall. Banks respond to the Federal Reserve's policy rather than ignoring it, and fixed-rate loans that already exist keep the rates in their contracts.
w: When the Federal Reserve raises its target rate, banks' own borrowing costs rise, so rates on new car loans would go up, not down.
Banks respond to Federal Reserve policy because it changes their own cost of money, so new loan rates would not stay flat.
Fixed-rate loans that already exist keep the rate in their contracts; the change shows up mainly in rates on new loans.

q.pt: Describe how lenders advertise loan costs to potential borrowers
q.s: Lenders advertise the yearly cost of borrowing, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed, as the
o: annual percentage rate (APR).
annual percentage yield (APY).
prime rate.
minimum payment.
q.r: Annual percentage rate (APR). The annual percentage rate (APR) is the yearly cost of credit expressed as a percentage of the loan principal, and lenders must disclose it so borrowers can compare offers. The annual percentage yield is what a savings account earns, not what a loan costs. The prime rate is a benchmark rate banks charge their best business customers, and a minimum payment is a dollar amount due on a card.
w: The annual percentage yield shows what a savings account earns in a year, not the yearly cost of borrowing money.
The prime rate is a benchmark rate banks offer their best business customers, not the cost lenders must advertise on each loan.
A minimum payment is a dollar amount due on a card each month, not a yearly percentage showing the cost of borrowing.

q.pt: Describe how lenders advertise loan costs to potential borrowers
q.s: Which federal law requires lenders to disclose the APR and finance charge to a consumer before the consumer signs a credit agreement?
o: Fair Labor Standards Act
Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act
Truth in Lending Act
q.r: Truth in Lending Act. The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to give borrowers clear written disclosure of credit terms, including the APR and the finance charge, so consumers can compare offers before they borrow. The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination in lending, and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act limits abusive practices by debt collectors.
w: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules for workers, not disclosure rules for loans.
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act bans discrimination in lending, but it is not the law that requires showing the APR and finance charge.
The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act limits abusive behavior by debt collectors after money is owed, not disclosures before a loan is signed.

q.pt: Describe how lenders advertise loan costs to potential borrowers
q.s: Jasmine is comparing two car loans for the same amount and term. Loan A has a 6.5% APR, and Loan B has a 7.9% APR. Compared with Loan B, Loan A will have
o: lower monthly payments.
higher monthly payments.
the same total interest.
a shorter repayment period.
q.r: Lower monthly payments. When the loan amount and term are the same, a lower APR means a lower cost of borrowing, so Loan A will have lower monthly payments and less total interest than Loan B. Its payments would not be higher, and the total interest cannot be the same because the rates differ. Both loans have the same term, so Loan A's repayment period is not shorter.
w: Loan A has the lower APR on the same amount and term, so its payments would be lower, not higher, than Loan B's.
Different APRs on the same amount and term produce different interest totals, so Loan A will cost less interest than Loan B.
Both loans have the same term, so the lower APR on Loan A does not shorten the time Jasmine takes to repay.

q.pt: Calculate APR, given annual interest and loan amount
q.s: Bryce borrows $2,500 and pays $200 in interest over one year. What is the annual percentage rate (APR) on Bryce's loan?
q.r: 8%. APR equals the annual interest divided by the amount borrowed, expressed as a percentage. Bryce's APR is $200 ÷ $2,500 = 0.08, or 8%. The answer 12.5% comes from dividing the loan amount by the interest ($2,500 ÷ $200), which reverses the formula. The answer 0.8% misplaces the decimal, and 20% has no basis in the numbers given.
w: 0.8% misplaces the decimal point; $200 divided by $2,500 equals 0.08, which is 8%, not 0.8%.
12.5% comes from dividing $2,500 by $200, which flips the formula; APR divides the interest by the amount borrowed.
20% would mean $500 of interest on a $2,500 loan, but Bryce paid only $200, so the numbers do not support this rate.

q.pt: Calculate APR, given annual interest and loan amount
q.s: Loan X is $1,800 with $270 in interest for one year. Loan Y is $2,400 with $312 in interest for one year. Which loan has the lower APR?
o: Loan X, with an APR of 15%
Loan Y, with an APR of 7.7%
Loan Y, with an APR of 13%
Loan X, with an APR of 6.7%
q.r: Loan Y, with an APR of 13%. APR equals the annual interest divided by the amount borrowed. Loan X: $270 ÷ $1,800 = 0.15, or 15%. Loan Y: $312 ÷ $2,400 = 0.13, or 13%. Loan Y charges more interest in dollars but has the lower APR because it is a larger loan. The 6.7% and 7.7% figures reverse the division, and choosing Loan X compares interest dollars instead of rates.
w: Loan X's APR really is 15%, but that is higher than Loan Y's 13%, so Loan X does not have the lower APR.
7.7% comes from dividing $2,400 by $312, which flips the formula; Loan Y's APR is $312 divided by $2,400, or 13%.
6.7% comes from dividing $1,800 by $270 instead of $270 by $1,800; Loan X's real APR is 15%, which is the higher one.

q.pt: Investigate what happens to a low introductory interest rate when the borrower misses a payment or makes a late payment
q.s: Jada's new credit card has a 0% introductory APR for 15 months. In month four, her minimum payment becomes more than 60 days past due. Jada should most likely expect
o: the introductory period to be extended to 19 months.
her credit limit to increase so she can catch up.
the introductory rate to end and a higher rate to apply.
the 0% rate to continue for the full 15 months.
q.r: The introductory rate to end and a higher rate to apply. Under the federal Credit CARD Act, an issuer generally cannot take away an introductory rate because a payment is a few days late, but once a minimum payment is more than 60 days past due, the issuer may replace it with a higher rate after 45 days' written notice. Issuers do not extend promotional periods or raise credit limits after a serious delinquency, and the 0% rate is unlikely to continue.
w: Card issuers do not reward a payment more than 60 days late by extending the promotion; serious lateness usually ends the low rate instead.
Issuers usually see a seriously late account as riskier, so they are more likely to cut or hold a credit limit than raise it.
Once a payment is more than 60 days late, the issuer may replace the 0% rate, so Jada cannot count on it lasting the full 15 months.

q.pt: Investigate what happens to a low introductory interest rate when the borrower misses a payment or makes a late payment
q.s: A low interest rate that a credit card company offers for a limited time to attract new customers is called a(n)
o: introductory rate.
penalty rate.
fixed rate.
prime rate.
q.r: Introductory rate. An introductory rate, sometimes called a teaser rate, is a low temporary rate used to attract customers; it rises to the regular rate when the promotional period ends and may end early if a payment is more than 60 days late. A penalty rate is a higher rate charged after late payments. A fixed rate does not change over time, and the prime rate is a benchmark banks use to set other rates.
w: A penalty rate is a higher rate charged after late payments, which is the opposite of a low rate used to attract new customers.
A fixed rate stays the same over time, while the question describes a low rate that lasts only for a limited period.
The prime rate is a benchmark banks use to set other rates, not a temporary low rate offered to win new cardholders.

q.pt: Describe the effect of higher interest rates and longer loan terms on the total cost of a loan
q.s: Ana and Ben each take out a $15,000 auto loan at the same APR. Ana chooses a 36-month term, and Ben chooses a 72-month term. Compared with Ana, Ben will
o: pay less total interest.
have higher monthly payments.
pay the same total interest.
pay more total interest.
q.r: Pay more total interest. The longer the repayment period, the larger the total interest a borrower pays, because interest is charged on the balance for more months. Ben's 72-month term means lower monthly payments than Ana's, but more total interest over the life of the loan. Ben will not pay less or the same interest, and Ben's monthly payments will be lower, not higher.
w: Ben's longer term means interest is charged on the balance for twice as many months, so Ben pays more total interest than Ana, not less.
Spreading the same loan over 72 months makes each of Ben's payments smaller than Ana's, not larger.
Ana and Ben have the same rate but different terms, and Ben's balance stays outstanding longer, so their total interest cannot be equal.

q.pt: Describe the effect of higher interest rates and longer loan terms on the total cost of a loan
q.s: Which change would increase the total amount of interest a borrower pays on a loan?
o: A larger down payment
A higher interest rate
A shorter repayment period
Extra payments toward principal
q.r: A higher interest rate. A higher interest rate increases the total interest because each month's interest is figured as a larger percentage of the balance. A larger down payment reduces the amount borrowed, a shorter repayment period gives interest less time to build, and extra payments toward principal shrink the balance faster. Each of those three changes lowers the total interest the borrower pays.
w: A larger down payment shrinks the amount borrowed, so there is less balance for interest to be charged on.
A shorter repayment period gives interest fewer months to build, which lowers the total interest paid.
Extra payments toward principal shrink the balance faster, so less interest is charged over the life of the loan.

q.pt: Describe the effect of higher interest rates and longer loan terms on the total cost of a loan
q.s: Darius borrows $3,000 at 5% simple interest per year for four years. What is the total amount Darius will repay?
q.r: $3,600. Simple interest equals principal × rate × time, so the interest is $3,000 × 0.05 × 4 = $600. The total amount repaid is the principal plus the interest: $3,000 + $600 = $3,600. The answer $600 is the interest only, $3,150 counts just one year of interest, and $3,646.52 compounds the interest each year, which simple interest does not do.
w: $600 is only the interest; the total Darius repays must also include the $3,000 that was borrowed, for $3,600 in all.
$3,150 adds just one year of interest ($150), but Darius borrowed for four years, so the interest is $600.
$3,646.52 compounds the interest each year, but simple interest is figured only on the original $3,000.

q.pt: For a given monthly payment, loan amount, and loan repayment period, calculate the total amount of interest paid by the borrower
q.s: Keisha borrows $11,500 to buy a used car. She agrees to pay $275 a month for 48 months. How much interest will Keisha pay over the life of the loan?
q.r: $1,700. To find total interest, multiply the monthly payment by the number of payments and subtract the amount borrowed. Keisha pays $275 × 48 = $13,200 in all, so her interest is $13,200 − $11,500 = $1,700. The answer $13,200 is the total amount repaid, not the interest. The answer $11,500 is the principal, and $275 is the monthly payment.
w: $275 is just one of Keisha's monthly payments, not the total interest she pays over all 48 months.
$11,500 is the amount Keisha borrowed, the principal, not the extra cost of interest on top of it.
$13,200 is the total Keisha repays over 48 months; you still need to subtract the $11,500 borrowed to find the interest.

q.pt: For a given monthly payment, loan amount, and loan repayment period, calculate the total amount of interest paid by the borrower
q.s: A $13,000 car loan can be repaid at $305 a month for 48 months or at $215 a month for 72 months. How much more interest does the 72-month option cost?
q.r: $840. The 48-month option totals $305 × 48 = $14,640, so its interest is $14,640 − $13,000 = $1,640. The 72-month option totals $215 × 72 = $15,480, so its interest is $15,480 − $13,000 = $2,480. The difference is $2,480 − $1,640 = $840. A longer term lowers the payment but raises total interest. The answer $90 is the difference in monthly payments.
w: $90 is just the difference between the two monthly payments, not the difference in total interest over each loan's life.
$1,640 is the total interest on the 48-month option alone, not how much more the 72-month option costs.
$2,480 is the total interest on the 72-month option; you still need to subtract the 48-month option's $1,640 to find the extra cost.

q.pt: Explain why using credit to finance education and housing could be beneficial
q.s: Why can borrowing to pay for a college education be a reasonable use of credit?
o: Student loans are forgiven when the borrower graduates
Education loans do not charge any interest
The education may increase the borrower's future earnings
College tuition decreases when students borrow
q.r: The education may increase the borrower's future earnings. Borrowing for education can be reasonable because a degree or credential can raise the borrower's lifetime earnings, so the future benefit may outweigh the cost and risk of the loan. Student loans must be repaid after graduation except in limited forgiveness programs. Most education loans do charge interest, and borrowing money does not lower the price of tuition.
w: Student loans must usually be repaid after graduation, with forgiveness only in limited programs, so that is not why borrowing can make sense.
Most education loans do charge interest, so the reason borrowing can be reasonable is the possible payoff in future earnings, not free money.
Borrowing does not lower the price of tuition; the loan just pays the same tuition with money that must be repaid.

q.pt: Assess the benefits and costs of using credit to finance education and housing versus using credit to purchase food and clothing
q.s: Which use of credit is most likely to cost the borrower more than it benefits him or her?
o: Financing a reliable car needed to get to work
Charging restaurant meals that are not paid off each month
Borrowing to complete a trade school program
Taking out a mortgage to buy a home the family will live in
q.r: Charging restaurant meals that are not paid off each month. Restaurant meals are consumed immediately and provide no lasting value, so carrying them on a card means paying interest long after the benefit is gone. Financing a car needed for work supports income, borrowing for job training can raise future earnings, and a home provides shelter and may gain value. In those three cases, the future benefits may outweigh the costs of borrowing.
w: A reliable car needed for work helps the borrower earn income, so financing it can pay for itself over time.
A trade school program can lead to better-paying work, so borrowing for it may produce benefits that outweigh the cost.
A home the family lives in provides shelter for years and may gain value, so a mortgage can be worth its cost.

q.pt: Justify the use of credit for a specific purchase
q.s: Elise is deciding whether to finance a $9,000 used car. Which factor best justifies using credit for this purchase?
o: The dealer is offering free floor mats with financing
Several of her friends recently financed brand-new cars of their own
She needs the car to commute to a job that will cover the payments
The loan would let her buy a more expensive car than she planned
q.r: She needs the car to commute to a job that will cover the payments. Using credit is easiest to justify when the purchase provides a lasting benefit and the borrower has a realistic way to repay. A car that gets Elise to a job, which in turn provides the money for payments, meets both tests. Free floor mats are a minor sales incentive, keeping up with friends is not a financial reason, and stretching to a pricier car increases debt without added need.
w: Free floor mats are a small sales extra and do not show that Elise needs the car or can afford the payments.
What friends buy is not a financial reason; borrowing to keep up with others adds debt without meeting a real need.
Using the loan to buy a pricier car than planned adds more debt without any added need, which makes borrowing harder to justify.

q.pt: Compare what happens if a borrower fails to make required payments on a secured loan, such as an auto loan or a home mortgage, versus failing to pay a credit card account
q.s: Ezra stops making payments on his auto loan for several months. Unlike an unpaid credit card balance, the auto loan allows the lender to
o: cancel the loan without damaging Ezra's credit.
lower Ezra's interest rate to help him catch up.
collect the payments from Ezra's employer automatically.
repossess the car that secures the loan.
q.r: Repossess the car that secures the loan. An auto loan is a secured loan, so the car is collateral; if the borrower defaults, the lender can repossess and sell the car to recover the money owed. An unpaid credit card is unsecured, so the issuer relies on fees, collections and legal action instead. Default damages the borrower's credit, lenders do not cut rates for nonpayment, and wages cannot be taken automatically without a court process.
w: Stopping payments for months is a default that damages Ezra's credit, and the lender would not simply cancel the loan.
Lenders do not lower interest rates because a borrower stops paying; missed payments make Ezra look riskier, not more deserving of a break.
Taking money from Ezra's paycheck requires a court process, so the lender cannot collect from the employer automatically.

q.pt: Describe how credit card grace periods, methods of interest calculation, and fees affect borrowing costs
q.s: Riley has a $1,500 credit card balance on a card with an 18% APR. About how much interest will be charged for one month if Riley makes no payments or new purchases?
q.r: $22.50. A card's monthly interest can be estimated by dividing the APR by 12 and applying that rate to the balance; issuers often use a daily rate, which gives a similar result. The monthly rate is 18% ÷ 12 = 1.5%, and $1,500 × 0.015 = $22.50. The answer $270.00 is a full year of interest ($1,500 × 0.18). The answers $18.00 and $27.00 come from applying the wrong rate to the balance.
w: $18.00 treats the 18% APR as if it were a dollar figure; applying the 1.5% monthly rate to $1,500 gives $22.50.
$27.00 uses 1.8% instead of the correct 1.5% monthly rate, which comes from dividing the 18% APR by 12 months.
$270.00 is a full year of interest at 18%; it forgets to divide the APR by 12 to get just one month.

q.pt: Compare the cost of borrowing $1,000 using consumer credit options that differ in rates and fees
q.s: Cole needs to borrow $1,000 for one year. Option A charges 15% simple interest with no fees. Option B charges 9% simple interest plus a $70 fee. Which option costs less, and by how much?
o: Option A, by $60
Option B, by $10
Option A, by $10
Option B, by $60
q.r: Option A, by $10. Option A costs $1,000 × 0.15 = $150 in interest with no fees. Option B costs $1,000 × 0.09 = $90 in interest plus a $70 fee, or $160. Option A is cheaper by $160 − $150 = $10. Comparing only the interest rates ($150 versus $90) makes Option B look cheaper by $60, which is why borrowers must include fees when comparing the cost of credit.
w: Option A is cheaper, but $60 compares only the interest amounts and leaves out Option B's $70 fee.
Option B's $90 interest plus its $70 fee totals $160, which is $10 more than Option A's $150, not $10 less.
$60 compares only the interest charges and ignores the $70 fee, which makes Option B look cheaper when it actually costs more.

q.pt: Identify the primary organizations that maintain and provide consumer credit reports
q.s: The three nationwide credit bureaus in the United States are
o: FICO, VantageScore and Equifax.
the FDIC, the Federal Reserve and the FTC.
Visa, Mastercard and Discover.
Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
q.r: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Equifax, Experian and TransUnion are the three nationwide credit bureaus that collect consumers' credit information and provide credit reports to lenders and consumers. FICO and VantageScore are companies that create credit scoring models, not bureaus. The FDIC, the Federal Reserve and the FTC are federal agencies, and Visa, Mastercard and Discover are payment card networks.
w: Equifax is a credit bureau, but FICO and VantageScore are companies that build credit scoring models, not bureaus.
The FDIC, the Federal Reserve and the FTC are federal government agencies, not private companies that keep credit reports.
Visa, Mastercard and Discover are payment card networks that process card transactions, not credit bureaus that compile reports.

q.pt: Explain how a person can get a free copy of their credit report and why this is advisable
q.s: Where can consumers request free copies of their credit reports from all three nationwide credit bureaus?
o: The Internal Revenue Service
Their credit card issuer's website
AnnualCreditReport.com
Their bank's loan department
q.r: AnnualCreditReport.com. AnnualCreditReport.com is the official site where consumers can get free credit reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, which now offer them weekly. Reviewing the reports helps a person catch errors and identity theft. The Internal Revenue Service handles taxes, not credit reports. Card issuers and banks may show a score or summary, but they do not provide free reports from all three bureaus.
w: The Internal Revenue Service handles federal taxes and does not provide consumers with credit reports.
A card issuer's website may show a score or summary, but it does not provide free full reports from all three bureaus.
A bank's loan department may pull a report when someone applies for credit, but it is not where consumers get free reports from all three bureaus.

q.pt: Outline the process of disputing inaccurate credit report information
q.s: While reviewing her credit report, Talia sees a late payment on a loan she always paid on time. What should Talia do?
o: Wait for the error to disappear in seven years
Dispute the error with the credit bureau that reported it
Open a new loan to offset the late payment on her report
Pay a credit repair company to delete all negative items from it
q.r: Dispute the error with the credit bureau that reported it. A consumer who finds inaccurate information should dispute it with the credit bureau that issued the report, and ideally with the company that supplied the information, including documentation. The bureau must investigate and correct or remove information it cannot verify. Waiting years lets the error raise her borrowing costs, a new loan does not fix the record, and no credit repair company can legally remove accurate negative items.
w: Late payments can stay on a report for about seven years, and waiting that long lets the mistake raise Talia's borrowing costs the whole time.
Opening a new loan adds debt and a hard inquiry but does nothing to correct the false late payment on Talia's report.
No credit repair company can legally delete accurate negative items, and Talia can dispute this error herself for free.

q.pt: Identify the main factors that are included in credit score calculations
q.s: Which factor generally carries the greatest weight in calculating a FICO credit score?
o: Payment history
Credit mix
New credit
Length of credit history
q.r: Payment history. Payment history, whether a person pays bills on time, carries the greatest weight in a FICO score, about 35%. Amounts owed, including credit utilization, is the next largest factor at about 30%. Length of credit history counts for about 15%, while new credit and credit mix each count for about 10%. Paying every bill on time is the most important habit for a strong score.
w: Credit mix, the variety of account types, counts for only about 10% of a FICO score, far less than on-time payments.
New credit, such as recent applications and accounts, counts for about 10% of a FICO score, much less than payment history.
Length of credit history matters, at about 15% of a FICO score, but it carries less weight than paying bills on time.

q.pt: Recommend ways that a person can increase their credit score
q.s: Theo has a $3,000 credit limit and a $1,800 balance on his only credit card. Which action would most likely raise his credit score?
o: Closing his credit card account
Paying his bill a few days late
Paying the balance down to $600
Applying for several store cards at once
q.r: Paying the balance down to $600. Credit utilization is the balance divided by the credit limit. Theo's is $1,800 ÷ $3,000 = 60%, which signals heavy credit use. Paying down to $600 drops it to $600 ÷ $3,000 = 20%, which tends to raise a score. Closing his only card removes available credit and shortens his history, late payments hurt payment history, and several applications create hard inquiries.
w: Closing his only card removes Theo's available credit, so any balance would push utilization up, and it shortens his credit history.
Paying a few days late can bring fees and, if it reaches 30 days, hurt the payment history that matters most in a score.
Applying for several store cards at once creates hard inquiries and new accounts, which tend to lower a score in the short run.

q.pt: Identify sources of assistance with debt management
q.s: Mateo is overwhelmed by credit card debt and wants help building a budget and a debt management plan. A good source of assistance is a
o: nonprofit credit counseling agency.
payday lender.
debt collection agency.
pawnshop that lends against personal property.
q.r: Nonprofit credit counseling agency. A nonprofit credit counseling agency helps consumers create budgets and can set up a debt management plan that may lower interest rates and combine payments into one monthly amount. A payday lender and a pawnshop provide expensive short-term credit that would add to Mateo's debt. A debt collection agency works to recover money for creditors, not to help the borrower plan.
w: A payday lender offers expensive short-term loans that would add to Mateo's debt instead of helping build a budget or a plan to pay it off.
A debt collection agency works to recover money for creditors, so its goal is collecting payments, not helping Mateo build a budget.
A pawnshop lends money against personal items at high rates, which adds more debt rather than offering budget or repayment help.

q.pt: Compare the results of liquidation versus reorganization bankruptcy
q.s: A legal process in which a court may sell a debtor's nonexempt assets to repay creditors and then erase many remaining debts is
o: Chapter 7 bankruptcy.
Chapter 13 bankruptcy.
debt consolidation.
credit counseling.
q.r: Chapter 7 bankruptcy. Chapter 7 bankruptcy is liquidation: a court-appointed trustee may sell nonexempt assets to pay creditors, and many remaining debts are then discharged. Chapter 13 bankruptcy is reorganization, in which the debtor follows a court-approved repayment plan, usually over three to five years. Debt consolidation combines several debts into one loan, and credit counseling provides guidance; neither is a court process.
w: Chapter 13 bankruptcy is a court-approved repayment plan over three to five years, not selling off assets and then erasing remaining debts.
Debt consolidation combines several debts into one loan, but it is not a court process and does not erase what is owed.
Credit counseling offers budgeting advice and repayment plans, but it is not a court process that sells assets or erases debts.

q.pt: Explain how using payday loans can cause a cycle of debt
q.s: Sierra takes out a $400 payday loan due on her next payday. When that day arrives, she cannot repay it, so she pays another fee to extend the loan two more weeks. This pattern can lead to
o: a lower interest rate.
a cycle of debt.
a reduction in the loan principal.
forgiveness of the loan.
q.r: A cycle of debt. Payday loans carry very high fees and are due in full within a short time. When a borrower cannot repay and pays a fee to roll the loan over, the fees add up while the principal stays the same, which can trap the borrower in a cycle of debt. Rollovers do not lower the rate, the extension fee does not reduce the principal, and the loan is not forgiven.
w: Paying a fee to roll over a payday loan does not lower its rate; the fees keep piling up instead.
The extension fee covers only the extra two weeks, so Sierra's $400 principal stays the same and is not reduced.
Rolling the loan over just pushes the due date back for another fee; the lender does not forgive what Sierra owes.

q.pt: Create a plan for a person who is having difficulty repaying debt
q.s: Which step should come first in a plan to get out of debt?
o: Apply for a new credit card with a higher credit limit
Stop paying the smallest debts to free up cash for the larger ones
Take out a payday loan to cover this month's bills
List every debt with its balance, rate and minimum payment
q.r: List every debt with its balance, rate and minimum payment. A plan to repay debt begins by listing every debt with its balance, interest rate, minimum payment and due date. With that list, the borrower can build a budget and decide which debts to target first. A new card adds borrowing capacity rather than reducing debt, skipping payments brings late fees and credit damage, and a payday loan adds very expensive new debt.
w: A new card with a higher limit adds more room to borrow, which can deepen debt rather than starting a plan to reduce it.
Skipping payments on the smallest debts brings late fees and credit damage, so it is not a sound first step out of debt.
A payday loan adds very expensive new debt to cover bills, which makes the overall debt problem worse.
